In the Name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-Shura

Its name was well known among the early generation (al-salaf) as ﴿Ha Mim, 'Ayn Sin Qaf﴾. Likewise al-Bukhari titled it in the Book of Tafsir, and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami', and it is named thus in a number of books of tafsir and in many copies of the Qur'an.

It is also called Surat al-Shura with the definite article (al-), as they said Surat al-Mu'min, and it is called so in many copies of the Qur'an and tafsir works. Sometimes they said Surat Shura without the alif and lam, quoting the wording of the Qur'an.

It is called Surat 'Ayn Sin Qaf without the words Ha Mim, for the sake of brevity.

[al-Suyuti] did not count it, in al-Itqan, among the surahs having two or more names. No report has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning its naming.

It is entirely Meccan according to the majority. He counted it, in al-Itqan, among the Meccan surahs, and al-Hasan ibn al-Hassar preceded him in this in his book on the abrogating and abrogated (al-nasikh wa al-mansukh), as al-Suyuti attributed it to him in al-Itqan.

From Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah it is reported that four verses are excepted, the first of which is His saying: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin﴾ [al-Shura: 23], to the end of the four verses.

From Muqatil it is reported that the exception is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants who believe﴾ [al-Shura: 23], up to His saying: "Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts." It is narrated that it was revealed concerning the Ansar, and it falls within the four verses mentioned by Ibn 'Abbas. In Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-Furs, from Muqatil: that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 27], and the rest of the verse, was revealed concerning the People of the Suffah, so it would be Madani. And in the same work, from him: that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 39], up to His saying: ﴿there is no path against them﴾ [al-Shura: 41], was revealed in Madinah.

It was revealed after Surat al-Kahf and before Surat Ibrahim, and it is counted as the sixty-ninth in the order of the revelation of the surahs according to al-Ja'bari, narrated from Jabir ibn Zayd.

If it is established that the verse ﴿And He it is who sends down the rain after they have despaired﴾ [al-Shura: 28] was revealed concerning the withholding of rain from the people of Makkah, as Muqatil said, then the surah was revealed around the eighth year after the Prophethood. Perhaps its revelation continued until the ninth year, after the chiefs of the Ansar believed on the night of 'Aqabah, for it has been said that His saying: ﴿And those who respond to their Lord, establish the prayer, and whose affair is consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 38] was meant to refer to the Ansar before the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to Madinah.

Its verses are counted as fifty according to the people of Madinah, Makkah, Syria and Basra, and as fifty-three according to the people of Kufa.

* * *

The Themes of This Surah

The first of its themes is an allusion to the challenge to those who attack the claim that the Qur'an is revelation from Allah, that they should produce speech like it. This challenge is not absent from the surahs that open with the disjointed letters, as has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

Allah argues against the obstinate that the revelation to Muhammad (ﷺ) is nothing but like the revelation to the messengers before him, in order to warn the people of Makkah and those around it of the Day of Reckoning.

And that Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, whose power cannot be opposed and whose wisdom cannot be doubted, before whom the higher worlds and those in them have submitted, and who is the Originator of creation, chooses whom He wills for His message. So it is no novelty that He legislates for the Muhammadan community of religion the like of what He legislated for those messengers before him, and Allah did not send messengers except from among mankind, to whom He revealed; He had not previously sent angels to address the general public directly.

And that the polytheists have no proof except the imitation of the leaders of disbelief who legislated polytheism for them and cast doubts upon them.

He warned them of the Day of Recompense, the nearness of the Hour, and what the polytheists will meet on the Day of Reckoning of punishment, while incidentally alluding to encouragement toward what the believers will receive of honour, and that if they reflected they would know that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not come with anything from Allah of his own accord, because Allah would not allow him to say about Him what He has not said.

And it mentions the proofs of His oneness, and that those signs are a blessing upon mankind, such as the evidence of sailing on the sea and what people are given of the blessings of this world.

And the consolation of the Messenger (ﷺ), that Allah is the one who will take charge of the recompense of the deniers, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) is not responsible for their reckoning in any way; his duty is only to persist in calling them to the upright truth. He reminded them that he does not seek any reward from them for his advice to them, but rather he seeks that they observe the ties of kinship between him and them.

He reminded them of Allah's blessings upon them, warned them against causing their severance through their evil deeds, and urged them to strive for the means of success in the Hereafter and to hasten to that before it is lost. The believers who rely upon their Lord have succeeded, and He praised their noble deeds and their avoidance of exposing themselves to His anger.

Interwoven with this is a reminder of many signs of His sole acts of creating and governing, which necessitate His sole divinity, as a refutation of shirk.

He concluded it with a renewal of the miracle of the unlettered one: that the Messenger (ﷺ) brought them a great guidance of religion, and they knew that he had not been among those who undertook such matters in the earlier part of his life. That is the greatest proof that what he brought is something revealed to him, so they must be guided by his guidance, and whoever follows his guidance has agreed with the will of Allah.

He ended this with a comprehensive statement containing entrusting the matter to Allah and awaiting His judgment, which is the saying: "Unquestionably, to Allah all affairs are returned."

﴿Ha Mim﴾ ﴿'Ayn Sin Qaf﴾.

It opens with the disjointed letters in the same manner as its counterparts began, like the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, because its opening points to the challenge of their inability to oppose the Qur'an, and that their inability to oppose it is proof that it is speech sent down from Allah, Exalted is He.

It is specially distinguished by the addition of the word (﴿'Ayn Sin Qaf﴾) to the openings of the surahs beginning with (Ali Ha Mim). Perhaps this is due to a state they were in of intense disparagement of the Qur'an at the time of the revelation of this surah, so the challenge to them by opposition was more severe, and so the challenge to them was increased with letters of spelling.

As for the Mim not being joined to the 'Ayn, unlike the Mim being joined to the Ra in the opening of Surat al-Ra'd, and as the Mim was joined to the Sad in the opening of Surat al-A'raf, and as the 'Ayn was joined to the Sad in the opening of Surat Maryam: this is because what follows the Mim in the three surahs is a single letter, so its connection to what precedes it is preferable. By contrast, in this surah what follows is three letters resembling a word, so separation was preferable.

[Page 27]

The position of the demonstrative in His words ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُوحِي إلَيْكَ﴾ ("Thus does He reveal to you") is like the position of His words ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ ("And thus We have made you a middle nation") (al-Baqarah 2:143). The meaning is: "Like this revelation, Allah reveals to you." The thing referred to is the act of revelation derived from the verb (يُوحِي, yuhi, "reveals").

As for ﴿وإلى الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾ ("and to those before you"), it is an incorporation (idmaj, the inclusion of one matter within another). The comparison, with respect to it, retains its original sense: that is, His revelation to you is like His revelation to those before you. The comparison is therefore used in both of its directions, just as a homonym (mushtarak) is used in both of its meanings. The purpose of the comparison is to establish equality: the revelation of Allah to you follows nothing but the same pattern as His revelation to the messengers before you, so His revelation to the messengers before you is no clearer than His revelation to you. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿إنّا أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ كَما أوْحَيْنا إلى نُوحٍ والنَّبِيِّينَ مِن بَعْدِهِ﴾ ("Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him") (al-Nisa' 4:163). That is, what he brought of revelation is only like what the earlier messengers brought, so the opposition of his people to it is nothing other than the opposition of the earlier nations to what their messengers brought. Thus this second meaning is achieved with utmost brevity together with the excellent placement of the digression (istitrad, a turn to a related point before returning to the main subject).

The attribute-pair (al-'Aziz al-Hakim, "the Almighty, the All-Wise") is applied to the Name of Majesty (Allah) rather than to any other, because these two attributes have a particular connection to the intended purpose, namely that Allah chooses whom He wills for His message. Thus al-'Aziz (the Mighty) is the One who disposes of things as He wills, and no one can repel Him. And al-Hakim (the All-Wise) loads His speech with meanings that no one else can reach. This is among the complements of the purpose with which the surah opens, which is the indication of the challenge to the obstinate to produce a surah like the surahs of the Qur'an.

The sentence ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُوحِي إلَيْكَ﴾ to its end is an independent sentence (ibtida'iyyah). The fronting of the prepositional phrase (majrur) (kadhalika, "thus") before (﴿يُوحِي إلَيْكَ﴾, "reveals to you") serves to give importance to the referent and to arouse interest by drawing minds to it. Since nothing preceding in the speech could be the referent of (kadhalika, "thus"), it is understood that the referent is an implied and known thing drawn from the verb that follows the demonstrative, namely the verbal noun derived from the verb. That is: "Thus, by this revelation, Allah reveals to you." This usage is established in parallel constructions of this kind, as already mentioned in His words ﴿وكَذَلِكَ جَعَلْناكم أُمَّةً وسَطًا﴾ in al-Baqarah. I think it is one of the innovations of the Qur'an, since I have not come across its like in Arabic speech before the Qur'an.

As for what al-Khafaji mentioned in al-Baqarah, comparing it with the verse of Zuhayr:

"Thus is their encampment, and every people has an encampment when adversity touches them."

It is not sound, because Zuhayr's verse is preceded by something that could be the referent. I had omitted to draw attention to this in the earlier verses, so combine what is here with what was said there.

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur, "the preposition and its object") is an attribute (sifah) of an omitted absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq, a cognate object) indicated by (yuhi, "reveals"). That is: a revelation like this wondrous revelation.

The shift from the past form to the present form in (yuhi, "reveals") serves to indicate that His revelation to him is renewed and does not cease throughout his blessed life, so that the polytheists would despair of his ceasing. This differs from His saying: ﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ رُوحًا مِن أمْرِنا﴾ ("And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command") (al-Shura 42:52) and His saying: ﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا إلَيْكَ قُرْآنًا عَرَبِيًّا﴾ ("And thus We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an") (al-Shura 42:7), since there is no purpose there in conveying the meaning of renewal. As for observing renewal here,

[Page 28]

it is because the intended subject of the verse is what was revealed to Muhammad ﷺ of the Qur'an, and His words ﴿إلى الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾ are an incorporation.

You may also consider the present form as regarded with respect to the two objects of the revelation, namely ﴿إلَيْكَ﴾ and ﴿وإلى الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكَ﴾, so that you make the present form serve to bring to mind the image of revelation to the messengers, where the polytheists considered its occurrence unlikely; it is thus presented as if it were being witnessed, in the manner of His saying: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي أرْسَلَ الرِّياحَ فَتُثِيرُ سَحابًا﴾ ("It is Allah who sends the winds, and they raise clouds") and His saying: ﴿ويَصْنَعُ الفُلْكَ﴾ ("and he was making the ark") (Hud 11:38).

The majority of readers read (يُوحِي, yuhi) in the active present form, with the Name of Majesty as the agent (fa'il, subject). Ibn Kathir read it (يُوحى, yuha) in the passive form, with (إلَيْكَ, "to you") as the deputy subject (na'ib fa'il, grammatical substitute for the subject). In that case the Name of Majesty is in the nominative as the subject of an independent nominal sentence, a resumptive explanatory sentence (istinaf bayani), as if, when he said "it is revealed to you," it was asked, "By whom is it revealed?", and it was answered: ﴿اللَّهُ العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾, meaning: it is revealed by Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise. This follows the manner of the saying of Dirar ibn Nahshal or al-Harith ibn Nahik:

"Let Yazid weep, one humbled by a lawsuit, and bewildered by what the calamities cast down."

This is because the transmission of the verse is in the passive form with a deputy subject.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 4:

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Mighty.﴾

The clause "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" confirms His description as "the Almighty, the Wise," because whoever owns whatever is in the heavens and on the earth as His dominion, might (ʿizzah) is realized for Him by the strength of His sovereignty (malakut), and wisdom (ḥikmah) is realized for Him because wisdom requires the creation of what is in the heavens and the earth and the perfecting of that order (niẓam) by which created beings proceed.

Because this clause confirms the meaning of the one before it, it stands in the position of emphasis (ta'kid), and so it is not joined to it by a conjunction.

The clause "and He is the Most High, the Mighty" is conjoined to it (ʿaṭf), confirming what the preceding clause established. For whoever is characterized by loftiness (ʿuluww) and greatness (ʿaẓamah), if he were not mighty, his loftiness and greatness would fail, and he would be none but wise, because his loftiness requires his exaltedness above base attributes and acts, and if he were not great, his will would be attached to base matters and he would descend to futile deeds.

The loftiness (ʿuluww) here is figurative (majazi), meaning exaltedness in perfection, such that He is more perfect than every perfect existent. The greatness (ʿaẓamah) is also figurative, and it is the majesty (jalalah) of His attributes and acts.

The form of the clause conveys the meaning of restriction (qaṣr), that is: there is no Most High and no Mighty other than Him, because whoever else He is, is not free of need for Him, so he has no loftiness and no greatness. This is a restriction of reversal (qaṣr qalb), meaning: in contrast to your gods, so they have no loftiness, as you claim. Abu Sufyan said: "Exalt Hubal!"

The meaning of these two clauses has already been discussed in the course of the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi) in Surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 5:

﴿يَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ مِن فَوْقِهِنَّ﴾ ["The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them."]

This is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustanafa) that confirms the meaning of the preceding sentence, "And He is the Most High, the Most Great." For that reason it is not conjoined to it by a conjunction. The meaning is: the heavens, despite their greatness, are almost splitting apart from the intensity of their being subjected (taskhir) to what God employs them for, of works that do not contradict what God has decreed for them. Also, it has been said that the meaning is: the heavens are almost splitting apart from the multitude of what is in them of angels and stars and the shifting of decrees. This would be in line with the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The sky has creaked, and it has the right to creak, for by Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, there is not a span's space in it but there is the forehead of an angel prostrating, glorifying God with His praise." It is preferred by his following it with the words of the Exalted: ﴿والمَلائِكَةُ يُسَبِّحُونَ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ["and the angels glorify their Lord with His praise"], as will come.

Nafi' alone and al-Kisa'i read (yakadu) with a ya' (yaʾ, third person) at its beginning. The rest read it with a ta' (taʾ, feminine). Both are permissible readings for a verb attributed to a plural of non-masculine-sound form, especially when there is no true feminine marking. Its occurrence in Surat Maryam, the saying: ﴿يَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ مِنهُ﴾ [Maryam 19:90], has already passed.

The majority read yatafattarna with a ya' then a ta', and its root is the present tense of tafattur, which is the reflexive (mutawaʿ) of tafṭir, the repeated form of splitting. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Ya'qub read it with a ya' then a nun, and it is the present tense of infaṭara, the reflexive of fatara (the triliteral), meaning to split. On both readings, what is intended is not the receiving of the effect of an agent, since there is no agent here for the splitting; rather what is intended is the report that the action occurs. This is common, as in their saying: "the light of dawn has split" (infashaqqa ḍawʾu al-fajr). So there is no attention here to what is generally intended in the pattern tafaʿʿala regarding repetition of the action, since there is no agent of the splitting here nor of its repetition. Thus the two readings are equal in the discipline of eloquence (balagha). Moreover, the use of the reflexive forms in the language has many modes and considerations, as al-Radi's commentary on al-Shafiya has indicated.

His words ﴿مِن فَوْقِهِنَّ﴾ ["from above them"] may be understood with the pronoun of "above them" referring to the heavens, so that the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb yatafattarna, meaning that their splitting occurs from their uppermost parts, and that is the most eloquent kind of splitting, for if their uppermost parts split, then the splitting of what is below them is more fitting, as has been said regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿وهي خاوِيَةٌ عَلى عُرُوشِها﴾ ["and it is fallen down upon its trellises"], as has passed in Surat al-Baqara and Surat al-Hajj. Here "min" is for the starting point (ibtida'iyya).

It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the earth, from His words, the Exalted: ﴿وما في الأرْضِ﴾ ["and what is in the earth"], by interpreting "the earth" as "earths" in view of the parts of the terrestrial sphere, or by interpreting "the earth" as its inhabitants, from the type of ﴿واسْألِ القَرْيَةَ﴾ ["and ask the town"].

In this case "min" is extra (za'ida), its extra use with adverbs (zuruf) serving to emphasize the sense of "above," so the adverb conveys the presence of the state of splitting and the state of its location. The splitting of the sky has been compared to the splitting of a rose in His words, the Exalted: ﴿فَإذا انْشَقَّتِ السَّماءُ فَكانَتْ ورْدَةً كالدِّهانِ﴾ [al-Rahman 55:37] ["And when the sky splits open and becomes rose-red like oil"]. The rose splits from its top when its bud opens, so if they split, they are on the verge of falling upon the earth; that is, this is nearly about to happen because of the spread of association and corruption in the earth, in the sense of His words, the Exalted: ﴿وقالُوا اتَّخَذَ الرَّحْمَنُ ولَدًا﴾ [Maryam 19:88] ﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتُمْ شَيْئًا إدًّا﴾ [Maryam 19:89] ﴿يَكادُ السَّماواتُ يَتَفَطَّرْنَ مِنهُ﴾ [Maryam 19:90] ﴿وتَنْشَقُّ الأرْضُ وتَخِرُّ الجِبالُ هَدًّا﴾ [Maryam 19:90] ["And they say, 'The Most Merciful has taken a son.' Indeed, you have done an atrocious thing. The heavens almost burst apart from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin."] This is supported by His following words: ﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِهِ أولِياءَ اللَّهُ حَفِيظٌ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ["And those who take protectors other than Him - God is Guardian over them"] [al-Shura 42:6]. And from Ibn 'Abbas: "The heavens are almost splitting apart" is from the words of the polytheists, "God has taken a son."

* * *

﴿والمَلائِكَةُ يُسَبِّحُونَ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّهِمْ ويَسْتَغْفِرُونَ لِمَن في الأرْضِ ألا إنَّ اللَّهَ هو الغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ ["And the angels glorify their Lord with His praise and seek forgiveness for those on the earth. Unquestionably, God is the Forgiving, the Merciful."] This is a sentence conjoined to the sentence "The heavens are almost splitting apart," because it confirms the meaning of God's greatness and majesty, indicated by His words "And He is the Most High, the Most Great."

The rank of the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud), glory be to Him, is that He is the people of transcendence (tanzih) and praise. The rank of the spiritual beings (ruhaniyyat), who are the angels, is that they are the intermediary of the Disposer, the Powerful, and the Bestower of good in executing His command, of creation, guidance, and the bestowing of good upon people. So when they receive His commands from God, they glorify Him and praise Him, and when the good things of their Lord overflow upon His servants, they seek forgiveness for those who receive them as believing servants of their Lord. That is an indication of the attainment of the fruits of their conveying, through its effect in ordering the conditions of the human world.

The rank of humanity, preferred by intellect, since its perfection is faith, is what is meant by "those on the earth."

[Page 32]

This sentence is coordinated with the sentence "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" [42:4], after what serves as proof that to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and on the earth, in His saying "He is the Most High, the Most Great" [42:4] and "the heavens are almost torn apart" [42:5], the two verses. The meaning is: the proof that He, exalted be He, alone possesses might, wisdom, loftiness and greatness has been established, and the believers knew it, so the angels sought forgiveness for them. As for those who did not perceive that proof, and for whom the evidences became obscured, do not concern yourself with their affair, for Allah is sufficient for them, and you are not a guardian over them. This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning his grief over their not believing in the oneness of Allah, exalted be He.

This is also an introduction to what the Messenger (ﷺ) will be commanded regarding the call, beginning with His saying "And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Towns" [42:7], the verse, then His saying "He has prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Noah" [42:13], the verses, then His saying "So invite, and remain steadfast" [42:15], and His saying "Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it" [42:23], the verse.

His saying "those who took protectors other than Him" is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause "Allah is Watchful over them" is the predicate (khabar) concerning "those who took protectors other than Him."

Al-hafiz (the Watchful) is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active): i.e., hafiz (one who guards). Its meanings vary, and they return to caring for a thing and attending to it. It is frequently used figuratively to mean watching over the conditions and deeds of the one watched over. As its meanings vary, its transitivity varies, either directly or with a preposition suited to the meaning. Here it is transitive with the preposition (ʿalā), as al-wakil (the guardian/disposer) is transitive with it, since it has the same sense.

Al-wakil is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive): i.e., the one to whom the performance of a matter or the pursuit of a right is entrusted. It is said: "he entrusted him with such-and-such" (wakkalahu ʿalā kadhā). From this comes agency (wakala) in financial dealings and litigation, and it is frequently used figuratively to mean watching over the conditions and deeds of the one entrusted. Here hafiz and (wakil) have been used in their figurative senses, with nearly the same meaning. Therefore the lexicographers may explain one of these two words by something close to the explanation of the other, like explaining a synonym by its synonym, and that is a loose usage.

So whoever wishes to distinguish between the two words must trace them back to the root sources of the roots (ḥ-f-ẓ) and (w-k-l). The root (ḥ-f-ẓ) requires that the action be performed by an agent and transitively reach an object. The root (w-k-l) requires that the action be performed by an agent, transitively reach an object, and then pass beyond that object to something else connected to it. Thus the verb (ḥafiza) conveys its meaning merely by mentioning its agent and object, without needing another complement, whereas the verb (wakala) depends for its complete meaning on a mention or on the implied presence of something additional beyond the object, one of its associated elements. Therefore the description (ḥafiẓ) is used here with attribution to the name of Majesty (Allah), because Allah is exalted above entrusting the guarding of anything to another; He is the agent of guarding. And the description (wakīl) is used with attribution to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the intended meaning is that Allah has not charged him with more than conveying the message. The meaning is: Allah is the Watcher over them, not you, and you are not one entrusted by Allah with compelling them to faith. Its meaning is similar to His saying at the end of this sūrah: "But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a watcher over them; your duty is only to convey" [42:48].

Also, this verse serves as an explanation of what is in the phrase "the heavens are about to split apart" [42:5], because among the causes of their nearly splitting is the multitude of angels in them.

Had it not been intended to add emphasis to the meaning of the clause "He is the Most High, the Most Great" [42:4], it would have been appropriate to separate it (fasl, without a conjunction), but the coordinating conjunction was preferred for the sake of stressing the loftiness and greatness of Allah, exalted be He. As for the explanatory relation (tabyīn), it is achieved merely by placing the clause "the heavens are about to split apart" [42:5] after it, as you have just understood.

So His saying "the angels" is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause "they exalt" is the predicate (khabar), and the aim is to inform of the majesty of Allah.

The angels' glorification of Allah with praise is humble submission to His greatness and loftiness, and glorification (tasbih) is declaring Him free of defects.

The angels' glorification may be an expression of their perception of the greatness of Allah, exalted be He, and so it is a spiritual response, like His saying, exalted be He: "And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear" [7:205]. It may also be an indication of declaring Him free of imperfection, by means of outward responses suited to angels, such as submission to obedience, or by speech suited to the angelic state. Likewise their praise of their Lord and their seeking forgiveness for those on the earth.

The object of "they exalt" is omitted, indicated by its being accompanied by "with the praise of their Lord." Its implied form is: "they exalt their Lord." The letter (bi) here denotes accompaniment, i.e., they glorify with a glorification accompanied by their praise of their Lord, that is, extolling Him with His attributes of perfection. Among extolling is what is thanks for His blessings upon them and upon others. So the meaning is: they glorify Allah and praise Him.

This is an implicit reproach to the polytheists, who turned away from glorifying and praising their Lord and occupied themselves with praising idols, which have no blessing upon them and neither benefit nor harm them.

Placing glorification before praise indicates that declaring Allah free of what is not befitting Him is more important than affirming the attribute of perfection for Him, because declaring Him free is a preparation for perceiving His perfections, exalted be He. For this reason the attributes expressed as attributes of negation (ṣifāt al-salbiyya) were placed before the attributes of meaning (ṣifāt al-maʿānī) and the attributes of the mind (ṣifāt al-maʿnawiyya), in the arrangement of the science of theology (ʿilm al-kalām), according to us.

Seeking forgiveness for those on the earth is asking for forgiveness for them by bringing about its causes, because the angels know the degrees of forgiveness and its causes. Since they are of the world of goodness and guidance, they are eager for the attainment of goodness for creatures and for their being guided to faith in Allah and to acts of obedience, and they converse with human souls with the motives of goodness, which are the angelic inspirations. So what is meant by "those on the earth" are those upon it who deserve the angels' seeking forgiveness, as He, exalted be He, said: "Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe: 'Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire'" [40:7]. Then He said: "and protect them from evil deeds" [40:9], in the sūrah of al-Mu'min (Ghafir). The Qur'an has also affirmed that the angels curse those upon whom the curse is due, in His saying, exalted be He: "Upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels" [2:161], in the sūrah of al-Baqarah. So the generality of "those on the earth" here is specified by what the verse of the sūrah of al-Mu'min indicates.

The clause "Unquestionably, Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful" [42:5] is a concluding appendix (tadhyīl) to the clause "and the angels exalt their Lord with praise" [42:5] to its end, to refute the polytheists' illusion that their associates intercede for them. For this reason this clause is formulated with the form of restriction (qaṣr), using the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), i.e., that none other than Allah forgives anyone. It is introduced with the particle of alerting (ḥarf al-tanbīh) to emphasize its meaning.

The verse has indicated the degrees of existent beings, which are: . . .

The intended meaning is to remove any responsibility from the Prophet (ﷺ) for their not responding to monotheism, i.e., do not fear that We will hold you to account for their not being guided, for your duty is only to convey. This was mentioned in His saying: "and you are not a guardian over them" [6:107], in the sūrah of al-An'am.

Since al-ḥafiẓ and al-wakīl have the same meaning, affirming that Allah is Watcher over them and negating that the Messenger (ﷺ) is a guardian over them gives the restriction of watching over them to Allah, exalted be He, and not to the Messenger (ﷺ), by a means other than the well-known forms of restriction. For this is clear restriction and explicit expression, not implication, and this is the basic form of restriction, though it is rare. From it is the saying of al-Samaw'al:

"Our souls flow upon the edges of swords, and they flow upon nothing but the edges of swords."

As for the well-known forms of restriction in the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-maʿānī), they belong to the style of concision (ījāz). The restriction here is restriction by reversal (qaṣr qalb), as is clear from its second part in His saying "and you are not a guardian over them." He treated the Messenger (ﷺ) as one who supposes that he is a guardian over their faith. From this treatment arises an implicit reproach to them: that they do not harm the Messenger (ﷺ) if they do not believe him.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 42, verse 7:**

﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Cities (Makkah) and those around it, and warn of the Day of Gathering, about which there is no doubt. A party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence ﴿Thus does Allah, the Mighty, the Wise, reveal to you and to those before you﴾ [al-Shura: 3], etc., on the basis of the difference between the coordinated sentence and the sentence it is coordinated with: the revealed content here is an Arabic Qur'an, and in the earlier sentence it is of the same kind as what was revealed to those before him.

The discussion of ﴿وكَذَلِكَ أوْحَيْنا﴾ is the same as the discussion of ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُوحِي إلَيْكَ﴾ [al-Shura: 3].

The phrase "and thus We have revealed" is repeated only so that "an Arabic Qur'an" can be built upon it, because of the separation that intervenes between them. The original structure is: "Thus does Allah, the Mighty, the Wise, reveal to you an Arabic Qur'an." Along with this, the repetition gives an emphasis (taʾkīd) that establishes this meaning in the best way.

The shift from the third-person pronoun to the pronoun of majesty ("We") is an iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person).

In this there is an indication that there is no difference between what was revealed to you and what was revealed to those before you, except the difference of languages, as the Exalted said: ﴿We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 4].

Al-Qur'ān is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "qaraʾa" (to recite), like ghufrān and subḥān. It is used here to mean "that which is recited," as an intensification (mubālagha) of its being recited, because of how much the reciters recite it, owing to its excellence and benefit. This name thus contains the meaning of perfection among recited things. ﴿ʿArabiyyan﴾ is a relative adjective (nisba) to al-ʿArabiyya, i.e., the language of the Arabs. Because its being a Qur'an indicates that it is speech, describing it as "Arabic" conveys that it is Arabic speech.

His saying ﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾ is a ground clause (taʿlīl) for ﴿We have revealed to you, and We enjoined﴾ [al-Shura: 13]. Its being Arabic suits the condition of those who are warned by it, namely the people of Makkah and those around it. They are the first addressees of the religion, owing to the divine wisdom that required the choice of the Arab nation to be the first to receive Islam and spread it among the nations. Had all the nations addressed by the call of Islam been taken into account, it would have required that it be revealed in countless languages. Therefore Allah chose for it the best of languages and chose its revelation upon the best of humankind.

Umm al-Qurā is Makkah. It was given this kunya (honorific nickname) because it is the oldest of the Arab cities, so the Arabs called it "Umm al-Qurā." The word "umm" (mother) is used for the origin of a thing, as in "umm al-raʾs" (the crown of the head), and for its point of return, as in their saying of a banner, "umm al-ḥarb" (the mother of war), and their saying "umm al-ṭarīq" (the mother of the road) for the great road around which are small roads.

Then, the warning of the Mother of Cities necessarily implies the warning of the rest of the cities, a fortiori. The Exalted said: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the cities until He sends in their mother a messenger﴾ [al-Qasas: 59]. This has already been discussed at His saying: ﴿and to warn the Mother of Cities﴾ [al-Anʿam: 92] in Surat al-Anʿam.

The intended meaning is: "that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities," so the name of the place is used for its inhabitants, as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82].

The people of Makkah are the Quraysh. As for "those around it" (man ḥawlahā), they are the tribes who settled around it, such as Khuzāʿa and Kināna. Among those around it are the Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir, who are the residents outside Makkah in its mountains.

Limiting the warning to the Mother of Cities and those around it does not imply that the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent to warn only the people of Makkah and those around it, nor that the Messenger (ﷺ) was restricted to warning rather than giving good news to the believers. This is because specifying the cause of an action by its motivating cause does not imply that the action so specified is restricted to that cause or to its related matters, since a single action may have several motivating causes. The Messenger (ﷺ) was sent to all people, as the Exalted said: ﴿We have not sent you except as a comprehensive messenger to humankind, bearing good tidings and warning﴾ [Saba': 28]. The limitation here to warning the people of Makkah and those around it is because they are the ones intended by the refutation, since they denied the prophethood of Muḥammad (ﷺ).

﴿Umm al-Qurā﴾ is in the accusative as the direct object of the verb ﴿tundhira﴾, treating the verb as if it were transitive to one object, since the one warned against (al-mundhar minhu), who would be the second object of the verb "to warn," is not mentioned with it. Because "anhara" (to warn) is transitive to two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 13], and in the hadith about the Dajjal (the Antichrist): "There is no prophet but that he warned his people." The meaning is: "that you may warn the people of the cities and those around it of the punishment they are to be warned of, in this world and in the Hereafter."

His saying ﴿and warn of the Day of Gathering﴾ repeats the verb ﴿tundhira﴾ to increase the awe of the matter of the Day of Gathering, because singling it out for mention after the general warning implies its magnitude. Also, the verb ﴿wa-tundhira﴾ takes ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾ as its object in a manner that differs from the warning of the Mother of Cities, because "the Day of Gathering" is the second object of the verb ﴿wa-tundhira﴾, i.e., "and you warn the people of the Day of Gathering." So the second object of ﴿li-tundhira﴾ is the thing warned of, and the first object of ﴿li-tundhira﴾ is the one warned.

﴿The Day of Gathering﴾ is in the accusative as the second object of the verb ﴿tundhira﴾, and its first object is omitted because of what precedes it, i.e., "and you warn them, namely the people of the Mother of Cities, of the Day of Gathering specifically," as in His saying: ﴿and warn them of the Approaching Day﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. This omission is what is called al-ḥadhf al-mutābaʿ (ellipsis that is followed by its context in use).

The Day of Gathering is the Day of Resurrection. It is called the Day of Gathering because creation is gathered in it for reckoning, as the Exalted said: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering﴾ [al-Taghabun: 9].

"Jamʿ" is a verbal noun, and it may also be a noun for those gathered, as in His saying: ﴿This is a host rushing in with you﴾ [Ṣād: 59], i.e., the Day of the assembly of all people.

The clause ﴿A party is in the Garden﴾ is resumptive and explanatory (istiʾnāf bayānī). The clause ﴿and a party is in the Blaze﴾ is coordinated with it. So the two clauses are an answer to a questioner who asks about the state of this gathering, if "gathering" is taken as a verbal noun: it is said, "a party (of those gathered on this gathering) is in the Garden and a party is in the Blaze." Or they are an answer to a questioner asking about the state of this gathering, if "jamʿ" is taken to mean "those gathered." The implied meaning is: "a party of them is in the Garden and a party of them is in the Blaze." The word ﴿al-Saʿīr﴾ was discussed at His saying: ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase them in blaze﴾ [al-Isra': 97] in Surat al-Isra'. The beginning of a sentence with ﴿fariq﴾ (a party), which is indefinite, is permitted because it occurs in the context of detailed explanation, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*69. So I advanced crawling on both knees; one garment I wore, and one garment I trailed.*

The clause ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the explanation and what is explained. The meaning of "there is no doubt about it" is that its evidences negate any doubt that it will occur, so the doubt of the skeptics about it is treated as nonexistent, because the causes of certainty about its occurrence are clear, as in His saying: ﴿This is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqara: 2] in Surat al-Baqara.

The attribution of the negated doubt to the pronoun of the Day (in "there is no doubt about it") is an instance of attributing an act or the like to the essence of a thing (ism al-dhāt). The intended meaning is that the act is attributed to some of its states indicated by the context, like ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], meaning its consumption. That is: there is no doubt about its occurrence.

The clause ﴿A party is in the Garden﴾ and what follows is parenthetical, and ﴿fariq﴾ (a party) is the predicate of an omitted subject, in the manner of ellipsis that is customary in usage, as al-Sakkākī named it, i.e., "they are a party in the Garden," and so on.

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 8:

﴿And if God had willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy; and the wrongdoers—they have no protector nor helper.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿A party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. The purpose of this conjunction is to convey that their being two parties is a matter that God willed to decree, meaning He brought about its causes by His wisdom. Had He willed, He would have decreed the causes for their unity upon one creed of guidance, and they would have been equal in their destination. The meaning is: they would all have been in the Garden.

This is brought to console the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers over their wish that all people be guided and all be in the Garden. By this you know that the intended meaning is not: "Had God willed, He would have made them one community in both matters, guidance and misguidance," because this second part is not what the present discourse aims to explain, although in reality, had God willed, it would have been so. The interpretation of this verse is therefore to be understood in light of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind together"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 13], and His saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99].

This is indicated by the exception (istidrak) in His saying: ﴿but He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾.

That is: but He willed a different will, which proceeded in accordance with His wisdom, namely that He created them capable of guidance and misguidance through the variations of their intellects and inclinations, empowered them to acquire their actions, and made clear to them the path of good and the path of evil through obligation. Thus among them were the guided, who are those whom God willed to admit into His mercy, and among them were the wrongdoers, who have no protector nor helper.

His saying ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ is one of two proofs for the implied meaning, since the sense is: "But He made them into two parties: a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze, so that He may admit whomever He wills of them into His mercy, which is the Garden." This also implies that He admits the other party into His punishment, and this is indicated also by His saying: ﴿and the wrongdoers—they have no protector nor helper﴾, because the negation of a helper is a metaphor (kinayah) for their being in misery, harm and subjugation, to the extent that they would need a helper if they had one. Thus the polytheists of Mecca are included among the wrongdoers by primary inclusion, since they are the cause of the revelation of this general statement.

The original construction is: "and He admits whom He wills into His wrath," but He turned away from it to what is in the verse, to indicate that the cause of their admission into His wrath is their wrongdoing, that is, their polytheism: ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13], together with the implication that they will not find a protector to repel His wrath from them, nor a helper to avenge them. The pronoun in (jaʿalahum) refers to the party of the Garden and the party of the Blaze, by consideration of the individuals of each party.

(أمْ) is used for the transitional *idrab* (a shift of topic, "rather"), as when one says: "Leave off concern with their affair and their warning, and let us return to the monstrousness of their condition in taking other than Allah as protectors."

After (أمْ) an interrogative hamza of denial (*hamza istifham inkari*) is to be understood. The meaning is: "Rather, have they taken other than Him as protectors?" That is, they committed an abomination when they took other than Him as protectors.

The pronoun in (اتَّخَذُوا) refers to ﴿those who have taken other than Him as protectors﴾ in the preceding sentence.

(Page 40)

The (فاء) in His words ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾ is the *fa'* of response to a condition that is implied (*shart muqaddar*), indicated by the context of denying that they took protectors other than Allah. This is because denying that implies that their protectors are not worthy of protection, and that they went astray in taking them as protectors. Thus a conditional is supplied whose meaning is: "If they sought a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector."

Al-Sakkaki said in *al-Miftah* (*Miftah al-'Ulum*): "The supplying of a condition on the basis of contextual indications is not impermissible. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾ [al-Anfal: 17], on the understanding: 'If you boast of killing them, then you did not kill them.' And He said: ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, on the understanding: 'If they sought a protector in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth, and there is no protector other than Him.'"

By *wilaya* (protection) in His words ﴿Have they taken other than Him as protectors? So Allah is the Protector﴾ is meant the protection of worship (*wilayat al-ma'budiyya*). The definite predicate in His words ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾ thus restricts the genus of "protector" in this sense to Allah (*qasr*, restriction). Since they worshipped other than Allah, it is determined that the intended meaning is to restrict true protection to Him, exalted is He.

The separating pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) in His words ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾ affirms the emphasis and confirmation of the restriction, and that there is no exaggeration in it, as a reminder that true protection in this matter belongs exclusively to Allah, exalted is He.

All of this is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, as consolation, reinforcement, and an allusion (*ta'rid*) to the polytheists, since they cannot avoid hearing it.

The conjunction of ﴿and He gives life to the dead﴾ to the sentence ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾ is an incorporation (*idmaj*) to re-affirm resurrection, to firmly establish the knowledge of the Muslims and to make it reach the ears of the deniers. This is because they denied it implicitly in taking other than Allah as protectors. When He invalidated their belief in the divinity of other than Allah, He followed it with the invalidation of what belongs to the connections of their polytheism, namely the denial of resurrection. This is not an argument against them for the invalidation of the divinity of their gods, because the occurrence of resurrection was already denied by them.

As for the conjunction of the sentence ﴿and He is over all things competent﴾, it serves to affirm this attribute for Allah, exalted is He, as a reminder of His sole possession of complete power. It also indicates an argument for the possibility of resurrection. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is He who originates creation and then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. It also indicates an argument for negating divinity from their idols, because whoever is not capable of everything is not fit for divinity. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17], and He said: ﴿They create nothing, while they are themselves created﴾ [al-Nahl: 20], and He said: ﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not recover it from it﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. The purpose of this is an allusion, so that it reaches the ears of the polytheists.

Since the intended aim is to affirm power for Allah, exalted is He, the sentence was conjoined to the one before it, because it is similar to it in conveying a judgment. The conveying of causation (*ta'lil*) through it was attained from its placement after it. Had causation been intended from the outset, the sentence would have been separated and not conjoined.

(Page 41)

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 10:

﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to God.﴾

It is possible that this is a completion of the parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), so that it is a statement addressed by God Most High to the people. It is also possible that it is the beginning of a statement connected to His words: ﴿That is God, my Lord; in Him I have put my trust﴾. In that case, the phrase "its judgment belongs to God" necessarily means that this whole statement is spoken by a single speaker, because the pronouns (rabbi, tawakkaltu, and unību) are his, and those pronouns cannot refer to God Most High. In the context of revelation there is no share for anyone other than the Prophet (ﷺ), so it is necessary to assume an imperative verb with a statement that the Prophet (ﷺ) is to say.

The sentence is coordinated with the sentences before it, because the address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the Muslims. The conjunction "wa" (and) links an imperative verb meaning "say." Omitting the verb "say" is common in the Qur'an when context indicates it, because the root of "differing" implies that the disagreement is between two parties, and the state of the two parties implies that the disagreement concerns matters of belief that the disbelievers denied, namely monotheism, resurrection, benefit, and harm.

The phrase ﴿from anything﴾ (min shay') explains the vagueness of "what" (mā), meaning: whatever thing you differ about. What is intended is: among the matters of religion and the affairs of God Most High.

The pronoun in ﴿its judgment﴾ (fa-ḥukmuhu) refers back to ﴿what you differ about﴾, in the sense that the judgment between you concerning it belongs to God. The meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection the one who is right and the one who is wrong will become clear to them regarding what they disagreed about, when they see the reward for the believers and the punishment for the polytheists. Then the polytheists will know that they were wrong in what they claimed.

﴿To God﴾ (ilā Allāh) is the predicate concerning its judgment. "Ilā" (to) indicates an endpoint, and this endpoint is a figurative, illustrative (tamthīlī) one. It likens the postponement of the judgment until the appointed time arrives with God Most High to the journey of a traveler toward a place where he will stop.

There is no connection between this verse and the disagreement of the scholars of the community in the foundations of religion and its subsidiary matters, because the judgment on that disagreement depends on examining the evidences and analogies (qiyās) for soundness and unsoundness. Issuing a judgment between the one who is correct and the one who is in error in these matters is easy if people are willing to deliberate and be fair. By this means the people of truth have reached the distinction between the correct and the mistaken, and the degrees of error in that. Moreover, this interpretation does not fit the context of the verses before and after it, nor the purposes of the Meccan surahs. Those who deny analogical reasoning (nufāt al-qiyās) have argued from this verse, but it is an argument that no skilled physician (naṭṭās) would accept.

* * *

﴿That is God, my Lord; in Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.﴾

It is possible that this sentence is the quoted speech of an omitted verb of saying, indicated by His words: ﴿so that you may warn the Mother of Towns﴾, the verse, in which case it is an independent statement, because warning requires something to be warned about. It is also possible that it is connected to the sentence ﴿and what you differ about, from anything﴾ as a completion of the statement addressed from God. In that case, in His words "my Lord" there is an iltifāt (a shift from address to first-person speech), and the estimated meaning is: ﴿That is God, your Lord﴾. The two sentences ﴿in Him I have put my trust﴾ and ﴿to Him I turn in repentance﴾ would then be parenthetical.

The demonstrative is used to distinguish the thing pointed to, which is what is understood from ﴿its judgment belongs to God﴾. This distinction serves to remove the confusion, on the part of the polytheists, about the reality of divinity and lordship, since they named idols as gods and lords.

The demonstrative used for what is distant is chosen to express glorification, through the conceptual distance that necessarily accompanies sublimity and high rank, meaning: that God who is Great. From this one arrives at the glorification of His judgment. The meaning is: God, who is Great in His judgment, is my Lord, in whom I have put my trust, so He is sufficient for me against you.

Tawakkul (putting one's trust) is a form of tafa''ul from wakl, which is delegation in action. It was discussed earlier, at His words, ﴿So when you have resolved, then rely upon God﴾ (3:159), in the surah of Āl 'Imrān.

Ināba (turning in repentance) means returning. What is intended here is a metonymy (kināya) for abandoning reliance on others, because returning to a thing implies that what is sought is not found with anyone else. Ināba was discussed earlier, at His words, ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, grieving, and repentant﴾ (11:75), in the surah of Hūd.

The verb ﴿I have put my trust﴾ (tawakkaltu) is in the past tense, and the verb ﴿I turn in repentance﴾ (unību) is in the present tense, to indicate that his trust in God preceded the appearance to him of his people's hostility toward him. His people's hostility met a servant who was already trusting in his Lord. Since his trust preceded his people's hostility, its continuation after they bared their fangs of enmity is certain.

As for the verb ﴿I turn in repentance﴾, it is in the present tense to indicate the renewal of repentance and the seeking of forgiveness. Its realization in the past is known by its being paired with the phrase ﴿in Him I have put my trust﴾, because one who trusts is one who turns in repentance. This may be an instance of ihtibāk (a rhetorical device in which a term is omitted from each of two parallel elements, each being supplied from the other). The estimated meaning is: in Him I have put my trust and I [do] put my trust, and to Him I have turned in repentance and I [do] turn in repentance.

Placing the two complements first, in ﴿in Him I have put my trust﴾ and ﴿to Him I turn in repentance﴾, serves to convey exclusivity, meaning: I put my trust in none but Him, and I turn in repentance to none but Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 11:

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth.﴾

This is a second predicate of the pronoun in His saying, ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), as you have just learned, following it with the statement that He is Able over all things, since the creation of the heavens and the earth is among the most prominent effects of the attribute of power, which belongs to Him alone.

Al-Fatir means al-Khaliq (the Creator), and this was discussed at the beginning of Surat Fatir.

* * *

﴿He has made for you mates from among yourselves, and of the cattle mates, by which He multiplies you.﴾

This is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the pronoun of (Fatir), because its content is a circumstance of the origination of the heavens and the earth. The creation of humankind and of the cattle is among the most wondrous circumstances of the creation of the earth.

It is also permissible for it to be a third predicate of the pronoun in ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾.

The meaning is: He ordained, in the creation of the human species, mates for its individuals. Since that ordainment was concurrent with the origin of the species, the past tense verb was used.

The address in His saying "for you" (lakum) is to all people. The address is a shift (iltifat) from the third person. The lam is for causation (ta'lil). The placement of lakum before the other objects of ja'ala (made) is so that it is recognized as an object of that verb and it is not supposed to be a qualifier of azwajan (mates), and so that the causation by it is considered in the conjoined phrase "and of the cattle, mates".

Azwaj (mates) is the plural of zawj, which is that which joins with a single one so that each of the two becomes a mate for the other. The intended meaning here is the males and females of humankind: that is, He made for your collective mates; males have mates from females, and females have mates from males. This is for the sake of all, because by that making there was achieved the pleasure of companionship and the blessing of offspring.

The meaning of "from among yourselves" (min anfusikum) is from your own kind and from among you, like His saying, "greet one another" (fasallimu ala anfusikum), and His saying, "do not kill yourselves" (la taqtulu anfusakum) [al-Nisa: 29]. That the mates are from among themselves is a perfection of the blessing, because if one of the two spouses were made of another kind, the delight of intimacy would be lost. As for the claim of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic era that a man may marry a jinn woman or a ghoul, that is among the falsehoods and imaginings of some of them; and perhaps some people suffer a mental derangement specific to this, so they imagine it and speak of it, and it circulates among every fool.

His saying, ﴿and of the cattle, mates﴾ is conjoined to the first (azwajan), so it is like an object of (ja'ala), and the estimate is: and He made of the cattle mates, that is, He made from them mates, some of them for others. The benefit of mentioning the mates of the cattle rather than the mates of wild animals is that in the kinds of cattle there is benefit for human life, because they live with him and do not shy away from him; he benefits from their milk, wool, meat, offspring, and their labour, such as carrying and tilling. So by making them mates, most of their benefit was achieved for humankind.

* * *

Al-dhar' (multiplying) is the spreading and increasing of creation. In it is the meaning of successive generations over the passage of time, since there is no benefit for people from the mates of cattle, considered as mates, except what comes from their offspring.

The pronoun of address in His saying (yadhra'ukum) refers to those addressed by His saying (ja'ala lakum). Its intended scope includes the making of mates among the cattle mentioned earlier; for the mention of the mates of the cattle was not idle but intended to increase the favour, since the multiplying of human offspring is a blessing for people and the multiplying of the offspring of cattle is another blessing for people. For this reason he was content with mentioning the mates in the case of the cattle instead of mentioning the multiplying, since there is no benefit for people in the mating of cattle except what results from their offspring.

Since the pronoun is a pronoun of a group of rational beings, and is a pronoun of address while the cattle are neither rational nor addressed, the rational beings have been given precedence in that pronoun, since no pronoun suitable for both rational and non-rational beings was mentioned, such as saying "yadhrauka" with a kasra on the kaf, interpreting it as addressing the group.

There is also in it the precedence of address over the third person, so there are two instances of precedence. It is a subtle precedence, since two kinds of precedence are gathered in a single word, as Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) and al-Sakkaki indicated in the section on precedence (taghlib) in al-Miftah.

The pronoun in (fihi) refers back to the making (al-ja'l) understood from His saying (ja'ala lakum), that is, in the making mentioned, in accordance with the saying: "Be just; that is nearer to piety."

The imperfect was used in (yadhra'ukum) to indicate renewal, and renewal is more fitting to the expression of favour.

The particle (fi) is used figuratively for the meaning of causation, likening the cause to a container in that it contains its effects, as a spring contains its water and a mine contains its earth. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179].

* * *

﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

This is a third or fourth predicate of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾ [al-Shura: 9]. The position of this clause is like the conclusion of the proof, for when He mentioned what are great blessings, it became clear that God is not like any of the things in His governance and bestowal of favour.

The meaning of ﴿There is nothing like His likeness﴾ is: there is nothing like Him. The kaf of comparison has been inserted before "mithl" while it has the same meaning, because the meaning of mithl is comparison, so it is determined that the kaf conveys emphasis on the meaning of mithl. This is a verbal emphasis by a synonymous word of a different kind, and what made it acceptable is that the emphasized word is a noun, so it resembles what follows the kaf of comparison, which contradicts the meaning of the kaf, and so it lacks the heaviness found in the verse of Khitam al-Mujashi'i:

"And scorching ones, as if they were set upon stones (kama yu'thfayn)."

Since the likeness was occurring within the scope of negation, the kaf is an emphasis of its negation, so it is as if He negated likeness from Himself by two clauses, teaching the Muslims how to refute the likeness of idols to God Most High.

This view is the opinion of Tha'lab, Ibn Jinni, al-Zajjaj, al-Raghib, Abu al-Baqa, and Ibn 'Atiyyah.

Al-Zamakhshari made it a second possibility, and he preceded it by saying that the kaf is not additional, and that the estimate is: "There is nothing like the likeness of Him." The intended meaning is: nothing is like the essence of Him. So he affirmed a likeness for His essence and then negated that likeness from having a like, as a metonymy for negating a like for the essence of God Most High, that is, by way of the implication of an implication, since if He negates likeness from His likeness, likeness is negated from Him, for if He had a likeness it would not be correct to say, "there is nothing like the likeness of His likeness." He considered it of the type of the Arab saying: "So-and-so's peers have reached maturity," meaning that he himself reached maturity, so the maturing of his peers was used as a metonymy for his own maturing.

And the saying of Ruqayqa bint Sayfi in the hadith of the watering of 'Abd al-Muttalib: "Behold, among them is the good and pure one, his peer," meaning: and the good and pure one will be with them, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn al-Munir followed him in this in al-Intisaf. Some scholars say: it is like your saying, "My brother Zayd has no brother," meaning the negation that Zayd has a brother, for if Zayd had a brother, Zayd would be a brother to his brother; so when you negate that his brother has a brother, you have negated that Zayd has a brother. But it should not be relied upon, for in it there is artificiality and ambiguity, and both are things the context rejects.

The negation of likeness also includes the refutation of what they attributed to God, the daughters, and this is the reason it occurs right after His saying, "He has made for you mates from among yourselves."

The hadith of the watering of 'Abd al-Muttalib, that is, the report of his request for rain for Quraysh, is that Ruqayqa bint Abi Sayfi said: "Successive years came upon Quraysh that dried up the udder and crushed the bone. Then while I was sleeping, a caller called out: 'O assembly of Quraysh, verily this Prophet who is to be sent from among you, his days have drawn near over you. Look then for a man among you, of the middle rank, great of body, white, with long eyelashes, smooth-cheeked, with a high-bridged nose; let him and his son withdraw. Behold, among them is the good and pure one, his peer; let a man from every clan go down to him, let them pour water and touch perfume, then let them climb Abu Qubays, and let the man seek rain, and let them say Amen; then you will be given what you wish.'" etc. They said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was with them, and he was then a boy.

Know that this verse negated that any existent thing could be a likeness to God Most High. A likeness is, when used absolutely, understood as its most perfect instance. Fakhr al-Din said: "The two likes are those each of which stands in the place of the other in its reality and quiddity." Thus no one is truly called a like except the one that is alike in reality and quiddity and their parts and necessary attributes, not accidents. So the verse negated that any existent thing is alike to God Most High in the attributes of His essence, because the essences of created things do not resemble the essence of God Most High; and it follows from this that whatever is established for created things in the perceptible aspects of their essences is negated of the essence of God Most High.

Accordingly this verse has been a foundation, in the view of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil), for the declaring of God Most High free of limbs, senses, and organs. Those who affirmed for God Most High what came in the Qur'an of what we call the ambiguous (mutashabih) affirmed it together with exemption from its apparent sense, since there is no disagreement about applying His saying, "There is nothing like unto Him," and that He has no equal and no peer.

Since we have agreed on this foundation, no dispute remains regarding the interpretation of the texts that give the appearance of likeness, except that the interpretation of our predecessors was an interpretation in summary (jumli), while the interpretation of their successors was a detailed interpretation (tafsili), such as their interpreting "yad" (hand) as power, "ayn" (eye) as knowledge, the spreading of the two hands as generosity, the face as the essence, and descent as the representation of the state of answering and acceptance by the state of a high one descending from his lofty place to where his petitioners are, so as to grant them what they asked. For this reason they said: "The way of the predecessors is safer, and the way of the successors is more knowledgeable."

Since His saying, "There is nothing like unto Him," conveyed the negative attributes, He followed it with the affirmation of the attribute of knowledge for God Most High, which is among the attributes of meaning (ma'nawiyyah), by describing Him as "the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing," both indicating the connection of His knowledge to existent things among audible and visible objects, as a reminder that the negation of the likeness of things to God Most High should not be taken to mean that God is exempt from being described by the perfect attributes of meaning which created things are described by, such as life and knowledge. But the attributes of created things do not resemble His attributes in their perfection, because in created things they are accidental, whereas they are necessary for God Most High in the utmost perfection. Thus His being All-Hearing and All-Seeing is among the attributes that fall under the shade of interpretation by way of being understood under the generality of His saying, "There is nothing like unto Him," so they do not require limbs.

And the following of that saying with these two attributes was like following a question with its example.

A fourth or fifth predicate of the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And He is powerful over everything﴾ [al-Shura: 9]. The position of this sentence is like the position of the one before it. It stands in the place of a conclusion drawn from what precedes it, because once it is established that God is the Protector (al-Waliyy), and that what the sentences after it contain, up to His saying ﴿He multiplies you thereby﴾, comes from His sole act of creating, it follows that He alone is the One who provides sustenance (al-Raziq).

Al-maqalid (the keys): the plural of iqlid, used irregularly, or the plural of miqlad, which means the key. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ in Surat al-Zumar.

[p. 49]

Placing the prepositional phrase first (al-majrur) serves to express exclusivity (al-ikhtisas), meaning: they belong to Him and not to anyone else.

Al-maqalid here is a metaphor by implication (isti'ara bi'l-kinaya) for the good things of the heavens and the earth. The good things are likened to treasures, and something belonging to the terminology of the thing likened to, namely keys, is attributed to them. The meaning is that He alone disposes of the good things that benefit people. As for what appears to be the disposal of some people over earthly good things, through giving and withholding, restriction and extravagance, it is not taken into account, because its benefit is small in comparison with God's disposal.

The sentence ﴿He extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾ explains the content of the sentence ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾. Extending provision (basṭ al-rizq) means widening it, and restricting it (qadr) is an implicit expression (kinaya) for its scarcity. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿God extends provision for whom He wills and restricts it﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26] in Surat al-Ra'd.

The sentence ﴿Indeed He is All-Knowing of everything﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (istinaf bayani), which functions as the cause for His saying ﴿for whom He wills﴾. That is, His will proceeds according to His knowledge of what suits the conditions of those who are provided for, whether through extension or restriction.

The explanation of this appears in His later saying ﴿Had God extended provision to His servants, they would have rebelled in the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 27].

[p. 50]

This is a transition from praising God for worldly blessings to praising Him for the blessing of the spirit. It turns to address the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, both to highlight the religion of Islam and to hint at the disbelievers who turned away from it. So the sentence is independent (ibtida'iyya).

The meaning of *shara'a* ("He has prescribed") is "he made clear and explained to you the paths of what He has obligated you with." The original sense of *shara'a* is "to make a wide path." Its use for laying down laws and religions became common, and so religion is called *shari'a* (the sacred law). Here *shara'a* is used metaphorically for "explaining," as in the verse: ﴿Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾ [Ash-Shura 42:21]

It was mentioned in His saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:48], in the surah of Al-'Uqud (Al-Ma'idah).

The definite article in *al-din* ("the religion") is the article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), and it covers the earlier divine religions. The *min* ("of") is partitive (lil-tab'id).

*Tawsiya* (enjoining) means commanding something while urging its performance and practice.

The meaning of His having prescribed for the Muslims "of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah" is that Islam is a religion like what He commanded Noah and urged him to follow. So His saying ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ implies an omitted noun, meaning "like what He enjoined upon Noah." Or the comparison is understood through the particle of comparison (ka), in the manner of the eloquent comparison (al-tashbih al-baligh), in emphasis of the strength of the resemblance, to the point that the like becomes as if it were the very same as its like. This is a common construction, like the saying of Waraqa ibn Nawfal: "This is the Namus that was sent down to Jesus."

The intended meaning is resemblance in the foundations of religion, concerning what is obligatory for God regarding His attributes, and in the foundations of the law, concerning the universal principles of legislation. The greatest of these is the Oneness of God, then what follows it of the five universal necessities (al-kulliyyat al-khamsa al-darruriyyat, the five essentials of religion, life, intellect, lineage and property), then the needs (al-hajiyyat) without which the order of human life cannot be upheld. Every element contained in the aforementioned religions of this kind has been deposited in the religion of Islam in a similar form.

The earlier religions commanded monotheism, belief in resurrection and the afterlife, and piety toward God by obeying His commands and avoiding what He forbids in general, and by noble moral conduct according to what is recognized as good. God said: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself﴾ [Al-A'la 87:14] ﴿and mentions the name of his Lord and prays﴾ [87:15] ﴿But you prefer the worldly life﴾ [87:16] ﴿while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [87:17] ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾ [87:18] ﴿the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [87:19]. They differ in the details of these matters and their branches.

The religion of Islam was not devoid of these foundations, even if it differed from them in the branches, by narrowing or broadening. This law was distinguished by giving reasons for rulings, blocking the means to harm (sadd al-dhara'i'), commanding reflection on the evidences, lifting hardship, leniency, and a strong connection with the natural disposition (fitra). I have explained this in my book *Maqasid al-Shari'a al-Islamiyya* (The Objectives of Islamic Law).

Alternatively, the intended resemblance is in what follows it in His saying "that establish the religion," etc., on the basis that *an* (that) is explanatory (tafsiriyya), meaning: He prescribed for you the obligation to establish the religion revealed, and not to be divided in it, as will come. In any case, the purpose is that Islam does not contradict these named laws, and that following it brings what they brought of the good of this world and the Hereafter.

The restriction to mentioning the religions of Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus is because Noah was the first messenger God sent to people, so his religion is the foundation of the religions. God said: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [An-Nisa 4:163]. And because the religion of Abraham is the origin of the *hanifiyya* (primordial monotheism), and it spread among the Arabs through the call of Isma'il to it, so it is the best known of the religions among the Arabs, and they were upon a remnant of it in the pilgrimage, circumcision, hospitality and chivalry. The religion of Moses is the broadest of the earlier religions in the legislation of rulings. As for the religion of Jesus, it is because it is the religion that immediately preceded the religion of Islam, and there was no other religion between them, and so that it would include a preparation for the call of the Jews and Christians to the religion of Islam.

Following the mention of Noah's religion with what was revealed to Muhammad, peace be upon them both, is to indicate that the religion of Islam is the seal of the religions. So it is conjoined to the first of the religions, uniting the two ends of the religions. Then the other three are mentioned after them, because they are intermediate between the two religions mentioned before them. This is a wondrous arrangement in the composition of speech. Had it not been for this consideration, the mention of Islam would have been put first, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [An-Nisa 4:163], and His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [Al-Ahzab 33:7], in the surah of Al-Ahzab.

Al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) mentioned, regarding the verse of Al-Ahzab, that the mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) is placed first in the detail to show his superiority, because the context there is listing those from whom the covenant was taken. As for the verse of Surah Ash-Shura, it is presented in the context of describing the religion of Islam with originality and uprightness. So it is as if God said: He prescribed for you the original religion which He sent with Noah in the old covenant, and sent with Muhammad (ﷺ) in the recent covenant, and sent with those who came between them.

So His saying "and what We revealed to you" refers to what was revealed before this verse of the Qur'an, with its rulings. He conjoined it to "what He enjoined upon Noah" because of the difference between them in additional detail and branching. And He mentioned it after "what He enjoined upon Noah" for the reason already mentioned.

[p. 52]

In His saying ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ and His saying ﴿and what We enjoined upon Abraham﴾, the relative pronoun *ma* is used, while in His saying "and what We revealed to you" the relative pronoun *alladhi* is used. It may appear at first glance that this is merely variation, avoiding repeating the same word three times in succession, and that is sufficient for this variation. But it is not far from my view that this difference is for a semantic purpose, a subtle distinction in the use of eloquent speech. Namely, *alladhi* and its counterparts are the original relative pronouns; they are established from their basic usage to refer to someone identified by a known state, which is the content of the relative clause. So *alladhi* indicates something known to the addressee by its clause.
