As for the relative *ma*, its origin is a general, indefinite, vague noun needing a qualifier, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah admonishes you with what is excellent﴾ [An-Nisa 4:58], according to Al-Zamakhshari and a group. They interpreted it as: "How excellent is a thing with which He admonishes you." So *ma* is an indefinite specifier (tamyiz) with *ni'ma* ("how excellent"), and the clause "He admonishes you with it" is a qualifier of that indefinite. Sibawayh said, regarding His saying: ﴿This is what is ready with me﴾ [Qaf 50:23], that the meaning is "this is a thing ready with me." And they cited the poetry:

"For a beneficial thing the intelligent person strives, so do not be one who strives for a thing whose benefit is far away in time."

That is, "for a beneficial thing." Here its qualifier came as a singular noun, by the evidence of its contrast with the phrase "for a thing whose benefit is far away." Then *ma* becomes definite through frequent use as an indefinite noun qualified by a clause, so it became definite through its qualifier and resembled the relative pronoun in being bound to the clause following it. For this reason, *ma* as a relative pronoun was frequently used for non-rational beings. Therefore, choosing *ma* with "what He enjoined upon Noah, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus" suits the fact that these are laws whose time has long passed, so they were not known to the addressees except in general outline, and thus they were indefinite nouns that are distinguished only by their qualifiers. As for choosing *alladhi* for what was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), it is because it is a law well known and current among them. So the meaning is: He prescribed for you a thing He enjoined upon Noah, and a thing He enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and the thing revealed to you. Perhaps this is one of the overlooked subtleties of the inimitability of the Qur'an.

In the shift from the third person (*ghayba*) to the first person (*takallum*) in His saying "and what We revealed to you," after His saying "He prescribed for you," there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

He mentioned for the four earlier laws the verb "enjoined" (*wassa*), and for the law of Muhammad (ﷺ) the verb "revealed" (*awha*), because the laws that preceded the law of Islam were temporary laws, expecting that another law would come after them. So acting upon them was like the act of a trustee over something until its owner comes. And this is so that the connection would occur between the verb "We revealed to you" and His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Thus does He reveal to you and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the Wise﴾ [Ash-Shura 42:3].

The "that" (*an*) in His saying "that establish the religion" may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle, since it enters upon a verbal clause whose verb is inflected, and the verbal noun derived from it stands in the position of a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) from the first or the last "what." If it is a substitution from one of them, it has the sense of a substitution from all its counterparts, because they are equal in being objects of the verb "prescribed" through the conjunction. So the command to establish the religion and the prohibition against division in it are among what the enjoining of the religions included.

It may also be explanatory (tafsiriyya) of the sense of "enjoined," because it includes the meaning of saying without its letters. So the meaning is: establishing the religion and the unity of the word upon it is what God enjoined on each messenger of the messengers He named. This view requires that what was described as the law in the earlier religions is this meaning, namely the establishment of the prescribed religion as it is. The "establishment" is general, and what is in each religion of branches explains it.

Establishing a thing (*iqama*) means making it standing. It is a metaphor for being zealous in acting upon it, as in His saying: ﴿and they establish the prayer﴾, which was discussed in Surah Al-Baqarah.

The pronoun in "establish" (*aqimu*) is intended to refer to the communities of those messengers, though they were not previously mentioned explicitly, but their presence is indicated by the sense of conveying (tabligh) contained in the verb "enjoined."

He followed the command to establish the religion with the prohibition against division in the religion.

Division (*tafarruq*) is the opposite of gathering together. Its original meaning is the distancing of entities, meaning the widening of the distance between them. It is often used metaphorically for strong disagreement in states and opinions, as it is here. It includes division among the community through belief in the messenger versus disbelief in him, meaning: do not disagree about your prophets. It also includes division among those who believed, by becoming sects and factions. That is the community's disagreement about matters of its religion, meaning about its foundations, principles and objectives, since disagreement about the foundations leads to neglecting some of them, so part of the basis of the religion is undermined.

The meaning is: do not divide regarding its establishment, such that some are energetic in establishing it while others abandon it, since without agreement on establishing the religion its affairs fall into disorder. The reason is that when souls agree, their influence converges upon a single aim, so that influence becomes stronger and the result comes more quickly, since each member of the community becomes a helper to the others, and their aim of establishing their religion becomes easier. But if division and disagreement occur, this leads to the loss of the affairs of religion in the midst of that disagreement. Then it soon casts the community into enmity among themselves, and may even drive some of them to wait for misfortunes to befall others. For this reason God said: ﴿and do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart﴾ [Al-Anfal 8:46].

As for disagreement regarding its branches according to the deductions of the scholars of religion, that belongs to the jurisprudence (*tafaqquh*) to which the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) refers: "Whomever Allah wishes good for, He gives him understanding in the religion."

* * *

﴿It is grievous to the polytheists what you call them to﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 13 (part 2 of 2):

This is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion﴾ and the clause ﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them﴾. It may also be taken as an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), answering the question of one who wonders at the disbelievers' turning away from Islam, although it is a religion confirmed by the divine laws that preceded it. The answer is given in summary: it was difficult (kabura) for the polytheists, and they found it repugnant (tajahhamuhu). Here (kabura) means "it was hard," and close to it is the usage "it weighed heavily" (thaqula), meaning that they were unable to accept what you call them to. Thus "greatness" (al-kibar) is a metaphor (majaz) borrowed for a thing the soul does not find at rest in accepting. Originally, al-kibar indicates the massiveness of a substance, because a massive thing is generally hard to carry. Because the verb includes the sense of "weighed heavily" (thaqula), it is construed with ('ala).

The call of Islam is expressed by the relative pronoun (ma), in consideration of the polytheists' denial of this call, their astonishment at it, and their regarding it as an improbable absurdity. It was difficult for them in three respects:

The first is the caller, because he is a human like them. They said: ﴿Has God sent a human as a messenger?﴾ (17:94). And because he had not been among the great men of the two towns before the call: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns?﴾ (43:31).

The second is the content of the call. They reckoned that God does not address the Messenger except through a book sent down to him from heaven all at once. They said: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a book to descend upon us that we may read it﴾ (17:93). And those who do not expect to meet Us said: ﴿Why are the angels not sent down to us, or do we not see our Lord?﴾ (25:21). And those who do not know said: ﴿Why does God not speak to us?﴾ (2:118). The speakers here are the polytheists.

The third is what the call contained that their desires did not support. They said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ (38:5). ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who tells you that when you are torn to pieces, completely torn apart, you will be in a new creation?﴾ (34:7).

The present tense verb is used in (they call them, tad'uhum) to indicate the renewal and continuity of the call.

* * *

﴿God chooses for Himself whom He wills, and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), answering the question of one who asks: How was the call of Islam so difficult for the polytheists? The answer is that God chooses whom He wills. The polytheists, who did not draw near to God's guidance, were not chosen (mujtabayn) by God, since He did not will to choose them. That is, He did not decree guidance for them.

It may also be a rebuttal of one of the doubts that led them to deny his message, namely that God chooses whom He wills. He is not bound to observe your customs regarding leadership and selection.

Ijtiba' (choosing) means bringing near and selecting. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They said: Why have you not chosen it?﴾ (7:203). Whomever God wills to choose is whomever He guides to His religion from among those who turn back in repentance. He knows best the secrets of His creatures.

The fronting of the subject (musnad ilayhi), which is the name of Allah, before the verbal predicate serves to restrict (qasr), in rebuttal of the polytheists who considered the message of a human from God to be impossible. And when they considered it great that the weak among the believers should be better than them.

[Page 55]

[Page 56]

﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, for a specified term, the matter would have been decided between them.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the clause "and do not be divided therein," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), as you know. The speech contains an ellipsis (ḥadhf) indicated by His saying "and they did not become divided," whose implied reading is: "so they became divided." The pronoun in (tafarraqū) refers back to what the pronoun in ﴿that establish the religion and do not be divided﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13] refers to, namely the communities of the mentioned messengers. That is, We enjoined upon them, through their messengers, that they establish the religion. The meaning of "enjoined" (waṣṣā) includes the sense of "conveying," as has preceded, which indicates this implied reading.

Knowledge (al-ʿilm) is the perception of the intellect, whether certain or presumed.

The coming of knowledge to them indicates that their messengers made clear to them the harms of division from the time of Noah, as God related about him in His saying: ﴿Then indeed I called them openly. Then indeed I announced to them and I spoke to them secretly in private﴾ [Nūḥ: 8], up to His saying ﴿roads, wide ways﴾ [Nūḥ: 20], in the Surah of Noah. Their scholars received that knowledge.

It is also permissible that "knowledge" means the cause of knowledge, that is: "except after the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ) with his attributes, which agree with what is in their Book, so they became divided by fabricating slanders and false excuses in order to deny the correspondence of the attributes." This would be like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not become divided except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4], according to one of its two interpretations.

The meaning is: their communities did not become divided in their religions except after knowledge had come to them through their messengers, prohibiting division in religion, together with their clarifying to them the corruptions and harms of division. That is, they divided while knowing the corruptions of division, not excused by ignorance. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not become divided except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4], according to the other interpretation.

He mentioned the cause of their division in His saying: "out of rebellion among themselves," meaning they divided for the sake of enmity among themselves, that is, among those who divided, meaning they did not safeguard the injunctions of the messengers.

This is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the polytheists in their turning away from the call of Islam, out of their enmity toward the believers.

[Page 57]

His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, etc., is a warning to the believers against the like of that disagreement. The indefiniteness of (kalima, "a word") is for variety (tanwīʿ), because for each group of those who divided in religion there is a word from God concerning their delay. It is thus in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And over their eyes is a covering﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. The indefiniteness of (ajal, "term") is also for variety, because for each community among those who divided there is a specified term, so the terms vary in length and brevity and differ according to times and places.

What is meant by "word" is what God willed of respite for them and delay of their being seized until a term for them which His wisdom required within the order of this world. He may delay them and then punish them in this world, or He may delay them until the punishment of the Hereafter, and all of that falls within the specified term, and for each of these there is His word. So "word" here is used figuratively (mustaʿāra) for will and decree. Its preceding means its being prior to the time of their division, and that is the precedence of God's knowledge of it and His will for it at a time that He knew and decreed. A parallel to this word has already been mentioned in Surah Hūd and in Surah Ṭā-Hā.

* * *

﴿And indeed those who were made to inherit the Book after them are in disquieting doubt concerning it.﴾

This is a conjunction on the clause ﴿And they did not become divided except after knowledge had come to them﴾ up to His saying ﴿the matter would have been decided between them﴾. This clause is the real purpose of the clause ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13] up to His saying ﴿and do not be divided therein﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13], because the intended people are the People of the Book who existed at the time of the revelation of the verse.

Since among the communities to whose messengers God revealed there were two communities existing at the time of the revelation of this verse, namely the Jews and the Christians, and since both had divided regarding what knowledge had brought them, and since God had delayed the judgment between those of them who differed until a specified term, and since when the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) reached them they doubted whether the attributes mentioned in the Book applied to the description of the promised Prophet, the meaning is: just as their predecessors divided in religion before the sending of the promised Prophet, their successors divided in the same way and increased in division in applying the attributes of the promised Prophet, a division arising from hesitation and doubt,

[Page 58]

that is, without exerting effort to attain certainty. So doubt remained their habit.
Thus, those reported about as being in doubt are those who were made to inherit the Book after their predecessors.

The structure of the verse is concise (ījāz) and can bear these many meanings and what branches from them. The pronoun in (minhu, "concerning it") was used after words that could serve as its referent: the word (al-dīn, "religion") in His saying (min al-dīn, "of the religion"), the word (alladhī, "that which") in His saying: ﴿and that which We revealed to you﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13], and the relative (mā, "what") in His saying: ﴿what you call them to﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13]. These three refer to Islam. There is also the word (mā waṣṣaynā, "what We enjoined") which governs Moses and Jesus, and the word (al-kitāb, "the Book") in His saying: ﴿And indeed those who were made to inherit the Book﴾. These two refer to the Books of the People of the Book.

Those who were given the Book are those existing at the time of the revelation of the verse. Reporting about them that they are in a doubt arising from those hostilities toward the message means that the extent of their disbelief and obstinacy does not exceed the state of doubt concerning the truth of the Muhammadan message. That is, they were not, in spite of this, certain that Islam is false, but they hesitated, then they proceeded to deny it out of envy and obstinacy. Among them are those whose state remained in doubt, and among them are those who became certain that Islam is true, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their own sons, and indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. It is also possible that the meaning is: "in doubt about the truth of the Qur'an," or "in doubt about what is in their Book of the matters over which they divided," or "about what is in their Book of the indication of the coming of the promised Prophet and his attributes."

These are many meanings which the verse bears, and all of them apply to the People of the two Books. By this it becomes clear that there is no need to turn the word (shakk, "doubt") away from its literal meaning.

The meaning of (ūrithū al-kitāb, "were made to inherit the Book") is: the knowledge of the Book about which their predecessors differed came to them, so the word "inheritance" (irth) is borrowed for succession in the knowledge of the Book.

The definite article in (al-kitāb, "the Book") is for the genus, so that it includes the Book of the Jews and the Book of the Christians.

[Page 59]

So the pronoun in (min baʿdihim, "after them") refers back to what the pronoun in (tafarraqū, "they divided") refers to, namely those who were addressed by His saying: ﴿and do not be divided therein﴾ [al-Shūrā: 13].

The adverbial sense of His saying (fī shakk, "in doubt") is a figurative adverbial sense, and it is a subsidiary metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya): it likens the settling of doubt into their souls to the encompassing of a container around what it contains.

The (min, "from/concerning") in His saying (lafī shakkin minhu, "in doubt concerning it") is the "min" of origin, and it is a figurative origin, meaning accompaniment and association, that is: a doubt connected to it, or "in doubt because of it." So in the particle (min) there is a subsidiary metaphor, the particle (min) being placed in the position of the "bāʾ" of accompaniment or causation.

The emphasis of the report with (inna, "indeed") is for concern and merely to affirm it to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. This concern is a metonymy (kināya) for urging caution against their deception and against leaning toward them, because of the clear manifestation of their enmity, lest they incline toward them. It is likely that the Jews at that time began to sow doubt among the Muslims and mingled with them in Makkah in order to observe the state of the Muhammadan call.

This is the way of understanding this verse, and it is the one that accords with what precedes it and with His saying after it: ﴿So do not follow their desires, and say: "I believe in whatever Book God has sent down, and I have been commanded to act justly among you. God is our Lord and your Lord."﴾ [al-Shūrā: 15], and so on.

Murīb (disquieting) means that which causes doubt (rayb), and rayb is suspicion. So the meaning is: "in a doubt that leads to suspicion and accusation," that is, a doubt mixed with denial. Thus (murīb) is an active participle (ism fāʿil) from (arāba), whose hamza is for transitivity, meaning "one who causes doubt." It is not the hamza of (arāba) which is for making, as in their saying "arābanī" ("he made me doubt him"), meaning he caused me to suspect him, while he is not one who causes suspicion. This is as in the verse of Bashshār:

"Your brother, if you suspect him, says, 'You only made me suspect,' and if you rebuke him, his side softens,"

according to the reading with the fatḥa on the tā' in (arabta, "you suspected"). The saying of His, exalted is He, has already preceded in Hūd: ﴿And indeed we are in disquieting doubt about that to which you call us﴾ [Hūd: 62].

[Page 60]

﴿So for that, call, and be upright as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires. Say: "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down, and I have been commanded to act justly between you. Allah is our Lord and your Lord. For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. There is no argument between us and you. Allah will gather us together, and to Him is the final return."﴾

The *fa'* (ف) here is the *fa'* of consequence (*tafri'*), attached to His words: ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ [al-Shura 42:13], up to the end of the verse. That verse is explained by His words: ﴿that you establish the religion and do not divide over it﴾ [al-Shura 42:13]. Its parts are separated by intervening clauses, from His words "It is grievous to the polytheists" up to "whoever turns back [to Him]."

The *lam* (ل) may be causal (*lam al-ta'lil*), with the demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") referring to what has been mentioned, namely the entire preceding command to establish the religion, the prohibition against dividing over it, the polytheists' rejection of the call with aversion, the believers' acceptance of it with submission and turning back, and the People of the Book's reception of it with doubt. So the meaning is: "For the sake of all that has been mentioned, call and be upright", that is, for the sake of all that has preceded: the guidance granted to those whom Allah has guided, the polytheists' disgust, and the doubt of the People of the Book, call.

The object of "call" (*ud'u*) is not stated, because what precedes it indicates it. The meaning is: call the polytheists, those who were given the Book, and those who have been guided and turned back.

The fronting of *li-dhalika* before its governed element, the verb "call", serves to emphasise what the demonstrative contains, since it is a collection of reasons for the command to persist in the call.

The *lam* in His words *fa-li-dhalika* may also be the *lam* of reinforcement (*lam al-taqwiya*), in which case it and its genitive complement are the object of "call", and the demonstrative refers to the religion in His words ﴿He has ordained for you of the religion﴾ [al-Shura 42:13]. The meaning is: "So call to that religion."

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governed element serves to emphasise the religion.

The imperative "call" (*fa-ud'u*) is used to mean perpetual persistence in calling, as in His words ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:136], with the indication of His words "as you have been commanded". In this there is a refutation of [the polytheists'] doubt on the third point mentioned earlier, at His words "It is grievous to the polytheists that you call them to it."

[Page 61]

The *fa'* in "fa-ud'u" may be a reinforcement of the preceding *fa'* of consequence, or it may be taken as implying the meaning of a conditional response (*jaza'*), because of the similarity of meaning to a conditional that is produced by fronting the prepositional phrase, as in His words: ﴿so let them rejoice in that﴾ [Yunus 10:58].

*Al-istiqama* (الاستقامة) means moderation and uprightness. The *sin* and *ta'* in it are for intensification, like *ajaba* and *istajaba* (to answer, and to respond). The intended meaning here is metaphorical uprightness, namely the balance of inner affairs through piety and noble character. The command to be upright, that is, to persist in it, is given to indicate that the perfection of calling to the truth is not achieved unless the caller is himself upright.

The *ka* (ك) in "*kama umirta*" ("as you have been commanded") expresses the meaning of similarity (*tashbih*), that is: a call and uprightness like that which you have been commanded, meaning in accordance with it, meaning fulfilling what you have been commanded. This *ka* is one of those called the *ka* of causation (*ka al-ta'lil*), as in His words ﴿remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqara 2:198]. Causation is not, strictly speaking, one of the meanings of *ka*, but it is an implied meaning that arises in the use of *ka* when the intention is to liken its governing element to what follows it, in the sense of conformity and agreement.

*Al-ittiba'* (الاتباع, following) is used metaphorically for accommodating and agreeing with someone, and for imitating and resembling someone in action. Both senses are intended here, so that the prohibition returns to a prohibition against opposing the two commands mentioned in "call and be upright."

The pronoun in "*ahwa'ahum*" (their desires) refers to those mentioned earlier, the polytheists and the People of the Book. The intended meaning is the prohibition of the Muslims from that, by way of the principle of ﴿if you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65]. Do you not see His words in Surat Hud: ﴿so be upright as you have been commanded, and [so also] those who turned back with you﴾ [Hud 11:112]?

It is also possible that the meaning of "do not follow their desires" is: do not let them lead you astray in your dealings. That is, let their attacks on your call not prevent you from mentioning the virtues of their messengers and the guidance of their books, apart from what they have altered in them. So declare that you believe in their books. For this reason, His words "and say: I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down" are joined by a conjunction to His words "do not follow their desires." The conjunctive *wa'* (و) here has the same function as the *fa'* of consequence.

[Page 62]

The meaning is like His words: ﴿and let not the enmity of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'ida 5:8], in Surat al-Ma'ida.

*Al-ahwa'* (الأهواء) is the plural of *hawa* (هوى), which means love, and which came to be used specifically for love of what has no benefit in it. That is, call them to the truth even if they dislike it; and be upright, you and those with you, even if the People of the Book are hostile to you. They love that you follow their religion. This is part of the meaning of His words: ﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from Allah no protector or helper﴾ [al-Baqara 2:120].

His words, "*wa-qul amantu bima anzala Allahu min kitab*" ("Say: I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down"), coming after "call" (*fa-ud'u*), are a command to oppose the Jews, who said: "We believe in part," meaning the Torah, "and we disbelieve in part," meaning the Gospel and the Qur'an. So the Messenger (ﷺ) and the Muslims were commanded to believe in the three books revealed by Allah, as He said: ﴿and you believe in the Book entirely﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:119]. The meaning is: say it to those whom this statement concerns, namely the Jews. He was commanded to say this as a public declaration and to make it known to the ears of the Jews, so that he would not answer their denial of the truth of his Book by denying the truth of their Book. In this there is a display of the fairness that his call contains.

*Min kitab* (من كتاب) is an explanation of "*ma anzala Allah*" ("what Allah has sent down"). The indefiniteness of *kitab* is for classification (*nau'iyya*), that is: with whatever Book Allah has sent down. There was no well-known book at that time other than the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an.

The pronoun in "*baynakum*" (between you) is addressed to those whom this statement was commanded to be directed at, namely the Jews. That is: I have been commanded to establish justice among you, by calling you to the truth and not wronging you because of your enmity. But I carry out God's command concerning you, and I do not align myself with the Jews or the Christians.

The meaning of "*baynakum*" is that I establish justice between you, so that you do not see any injustice from me between you. Thus *bayn* here is a unified (*muttahid*), undivided adverbial, meaning "in the midst of the group and within it." This is unlike *bayn* in the saying: "He judged between the two litigants," or "He divided the wealth among the seekers." So the meaning is not "that I may be just between your factions," since the context does not require it.

Along with the fact that this verse was revealed in Mecca at a time of weakness for the Muslims, it contains a miraculous foretelling (*i'jaz bil-ghayb*), indicating that the Messenger (ﷺ) would have authority over the Jews of the Arabian lands, such as the people of Khaybar,

[Page 63]

Taymaʼ, Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa'. He did act justly toward them and left them in their affairs, until they backed the confederates against him, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Ahzab.

The *lam* in His words "*li-a'dila*" (so that I may act justly) is a *lam* that frequently occurs after verbs of command and will, as in His words: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:26]. The discussion of it has already been given. Some grammarians regard it as superfluous (*za'ida*).

The clause "Allah is our Lord and your Lord" is part of what he was commanded to say. The whole clause, therefore, is a resumptive statement (*jumla mustani'a*) that follows the clause "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down," confirming its content. This is because the purpose of the whole clause "Allah is our Lord and your Lord" is His words "there is no argument between us and you." So it confirms the content of "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down." The two clauses "Allah is our Lord and your Lord" and "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds" were introduced as a preparation for the intended point, which is "there is no argument between us and you." For this reason, all these clauses are separated from the clauses "I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down" and "I have been commanded to act justly between you."

The intended meaning of "Allah is our Lord and your Lord" is that we agree on the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, as in His words: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we will not worship except Allah and not associate anything with Him"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:64], that is, Allah is the Witness over us and over you, since you have denied a Book that was sent down from Him. So the statement is used for recording and obligation.

The clause "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds" is a call to fairness, meaning that Allah repays each person according to his deeds. This statement is used as a warning and an alert to error.

The clause "There is no argument between us and you" is the intended point after His words "and I have been commanded to act justly between you," that is: I act justly between you, and I will not dispute with you over your denial of my truthfulness.

*Al-hujja* (الحجة) is the evidence which shows the truth of the claim of the one who presents it. An argument exists only between people who differ over a claim. The negation of *hujja* is a negation of the genus, which may be a metonymy (*kinaya*) for negating the disputation that normally involves argument, and a metonymy for not engaging them in their quarrel. So the meaning is: refrain from disputing with them, because the truth has become manifest and they are obstinate in it. This is an allusion that debating with them is of no benefit.

[Page 64]

It is also possible that the negated item is the genus of effective argument, understood through context, like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book" [a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim]. The meaning is that continuing to argue against them after evidence has been made clear to them would be futile. This is an allusion that they are obstinate.

Whichever is the case, this negation is not used to forbid engaging them in argument, for the Qur'an did argue with them in many verses revealed after this one, and the Prophet (ﷺ) argued with them over the matter of stoning. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:46]. The exception is explicit in permitting their disputation.

The repeated *bayn* in "*baynana wa-baynakum*" (between us and you) is a unified adverb distributed over the groups or individuals of the speaking subject and the addressees, as one says: "He divided it among them," and this differs from the *bayn* mentioned just before.

The word "gather" in His words "Allah will gather us together" means the gathering on the Day of Judgement for the final decision, when the one who is right will be distinguished from the one who is wrong. This is a statement of fairness. Since such words are only uttered by one confident of his truth, their address to them is used in the sense of disengagement and separation: I will abandon arguing and disputing with you, since it is of little use among you, and I entrust my affair to Allah, who will judge between us on the Day when He gathers us. This is an allusion that the judgement will be against them.

The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate in "Allah will gather between us" serves to strengthen the statement, that is, to confirm the occurrence of this gathering; otherwise the addressees, who are the Jews, do affirm the Resurrection. The *bayn* here is a distributed adverb like the one in "there is no argument between us and you."

The clause "and to Him is the final return" is coordinated with the clause "will gather between us." The definite article in "*al-masir*" (the final return) is for comprehensiveness, that is: the return of all people. Thus the clause serves as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) with the generality it contains: our return, your return, and the return of all creation.

These four clauses require a separation (*muhajaza*) between the believers and the Jews. It is a separation in speech and an abandonment in fighting at that time, until Allah permitted fighting against them when they backed the confederates.

[Page 65]

There is nothing in the forms of these clauses that requires the abandonment to be permanent, since there is nothing in them that requires the generality of all times. Therefore, the command to fight some of them after the day of the confederates does not abrogate (*naskh*) this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 16:

﴿And those who dispute concerning God after He has been responded to—their argument is baseless in the sight of their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿Say: I believe in what God has sent down﴾ [al-Shura: 15], etc., and it entails a shift in the discourse. So when he had completed the portion concerning the People of the Book in the matter of disputation with them, he returned to the polytheists on this matter with his saying: ﴿And those who dispute concerning God﴾, the verse.

The change of style by using the explicit relative noun, and the fact that its relative clause is the matter of argumentation, indicates a change of purpose regarding those being spoken of, together with the appropriateness of what was attached to it: his saying ﴿by which those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Shura: 18] and his saying ﴿Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what God has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura: 21]. Therefore, what is intended by ﴿those who dispute concerning God after He has been responded to﴾ is the polytheists, because they dispute concerning the matter of God, which is His oneness, and not the Jews among the People of the Book, for they do not dispute concerning God's singularity in divinity.

It is reported from Mujahid that he said: ﴿Those who dispute concerning God﴾ are men who hoped that the days of ignorance (jahiliyya) would return after people had entered Islam. And it occurs in the words of Ibn ʿAbbas, in al-Tabari: that they are the Jews and the Christians.

So the meaning of their disputing concerning God is their disputing concerning the religion of God, i.e., their introducing doubt into people's minds about the validity of the religion of Islam or about its being superior to Judaism and Christianity. Their disputation is what they cloak it with against the Muslims in order to introduce doubt about them in following Islam, like the saying of the polytheists: ﴿What is wrong with this messenger, that he eats food and walks in the markets? Why was an angel not sent down to him to be a warner with him?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and their saying about the idols: ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18], and their saying in denying resurrection: ﴿When we have died and become dust, that is a far return﴾ [Qaf: 3], and their saying: ﴿If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land﴾ [al-Qasas: 57].

And like the saying of the People of the Book: "We are those upon the religion of Abraham," and their saying: "Our book is earlier than the book of the Muslims."

The application of the name "argument" (hujja) to their doubts is a figurative accommodation to them by way of mockery (tahakkum), and the indicator is his saying: ﴿baseless in the sight of their Lord﴾.

The object of "yuhajjuna" (they dispute) is omitted, indicated by his saying ﴿after He has been responded to﴾, and the estimated meaning is: they dispute with those who respond to God after they have responded to Him, i.e., they responded to His call through the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ.

The agent of "ustujiba" (He has been responded to) is omitted for brevity, because the intended meaning is after the occurrence of the well-known response.

Al-Dahiḍa is that which has slipped (dahaḍat), from the verb with the ḥāʾ vowelled with a fatḥa: it is said dahaḍat rijluhu yadḥaḍu, with fatḥa on the ḥāʾ, duḥūḍan, i.e., his foot slipped. The word dahḍ is used metaphorically for falsehood, by the common feature of lack of stability, just as a foot does not stand firm on a slippery place. He did not specify the aspect of its slipping, being content with what was made clear in the course of the proofs revealed in the Qur'an concerning the corruption of the plurality of gods, the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, the possibility of resurrection, and what was visibly manifest of the increase of Muslims day after day and their security from being attacked.

The wrath (ghadab) is the wrath of God; it was indefinitely expressed to indicate its severity. There was no need to attach it to the Divine Name or to a pronoun, because the intended meaning is clear from his saying: ﴿their argument is baseless in the sight of their Lord﴾. So the estimated meaning is: and upon them is the wrath of God.

He placed the predicate before the subject in his saying "and upon them is wrath" for the sake of emphasis on the wrath falling upon them, as is required by the figurative preposition of elevation (ʿalā).

The same applies to ﴿and for them is a severe punishment﴾. Perhaps what is meant by it is the punishment of the sword in this world through killing on the day of Badr.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 17:

[p. 67]
﴿Allah is the One who sent down the Book with truth, and the Balance. And what will make you know that the Hour may be near?﴾

You already know that among the arguments of the polytheists concerning Allah, and among the most contentious of them in their own claim, is their argument by denying resurrection, as in their saying: ﴿Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you are completely disintegrated, you will be in a new creation? Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ [Saba': 7]. Shaddad ibn al-Aswad said:

"The Messenger informs us that we shall live again, but how can there be life for echoes and skulls?"

Allah has refuted their argument in several places in His Book, by negating its impossibility and by the proof of its possibility, and here He alludes to what its affirmation requires, so He makes clear that resurrection and recompense are truth and justice. How then would the One who governs the universe and sends down the Book and the Balance not determine it? Many verses point to this meaning, among them His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], and He said: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except with truth, but most of them do not know. Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38–40].

Most of these verses are arranged in the same order as the arrangement of this verse, beginning with what reminds of the wisdom of creation, and that the completion of the wisdom is through recompense for deeds.

So His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who sent down the Book with truth, and the Balance﴾ is a preparation for His saying: ﴿And what will make you know that the Hour may be near?﴾, because His saying: ﴿And what will make you know that the Hour may be near?﴾ indicates an omitted element that the meaning requires. Its estimate is: He made recompense for those who follow the truth and those who deviate from it on the Day of the Hour, so there is no escape for the servants from meeting recompense. And what will make you know that the Hour may be near? So it refers to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. The position of this sentence relative to the sentence ﴿And those who dispute concerning Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 16] is the position of a proof, and proof is a kind of clarification; for this reason the sentence is separated from the one before it, because its meaning is closely connected to the meaning of the other.

The reference to the name of Allah by a relative clause whose content is His sending down the Book

[p. 68]
and the Balance, is for the sake of the allusion inherent in the relative form to the basis on which the following predicate is built, and that it is of the kind of truth and justice, like the relative in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who are too arrogant to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated﴾ [Ghafir: 60].

The definite article in (al-Kitab) is for the generic definition, i.e., the sending down of books, and it looks to His saying just before: ﴿And say: I believe in whatever Book Allah has sent down﴾ [al-Shura: 15].

The ba' in (bil-haqq) is for accompaniment, i.e., He sent down the Books accompanied by truth, far from falsehood.

Al-haqq: everything that is due (yahiqqu), i.e., that must be done in matters of righteousness, and it may be explained as correct and beneficial purposes.

Al-mizan is literally the instrument of weighing, and weighing is the estimation of the weight of a body. The mizan is an instrument with two balanced pans suspended at the ends of a level, even rod, which has a loop at its middle, such that neither pan tilts over the other when the rod is held by its loop.

Al-mizan here is used metaphorically for justice and guidance, by the indication of His saying (sent down), for the religion is what is sent down, and religion calls to justice and fairness in disputation about religion and in giving rights. So it is likened to the balance in the equality of the tilt of its two pans. He, exalted, said: ﴿And We sent down with them the Book and the Balance so that people may establish justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25].

The sentence ﴿And what will make you know that the Hour may be near?﴾ is coordinated with the sentence ﴿Allah is the One who sent down the Book with truth, and the Balance﴾, and the connecting reason is what we mentioned, namely that the former sentence signals an omitted element.

The phrase (wa-ma yudrika) functions as a proverbial expression, and the kaf in it is an address to an unspecified person, meaning: perhaps you know; i.e., perhaps the one who knows [would know]. So (ma) is interrogative, and the interrogation is used for alerting and preparing. (Yudrika) derives from al-diraya, meaning knowledge, and the verb (yadri) has been suspended from acting by the particle of hope.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Every occurrence of the verb in (ma adraka) means that Allah informed him of it, i.e., explained it to him, immediately after the phrase (ma adraka), as in: ﴿And what will make you know what it is? A blazing fire﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 10]. And every occurrence in which (wa-ma yudrika)

[p. 69]
is used without Allah informing him of it, i.e., not followed by what clarifies its ambiguity, as in: ﴿And what will make you know that the Hour may be near?﴾ and ﴿And what will make you know that he might purify himself?﴾ [Abasa: 3]. The meaning of this statement is that usage has restricted each of these two forms to this usage, so reflect on it.

The meaning: What will inform you, O listener, that the Hour is near? I.e., the requirement of your knowledge is abundant. So the address is to an unspecified person. Its like is His saying: ﴿And what will make you aware that when they come they will not believe?﴾ [al-An'am: 109] in Surat al-An'am.

The predication of the Hour by (qarib), which is not feminine, is because the usage of qarib and ba'id for the masculine form, in consideration of something, has become predominant, as in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know that the Hour may be [in fact] near?﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]; and this was discussed earlier in Surat al-A'raf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 18:

﴿They seek to hasten it, those who do not believe in it; but those who believe are apprehensive of it and know that it is the truth.﴾

It is permissible that the clause "yasta'jilu biha" (they seek to hasten it) through to its end be a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "al-Sa'ah" (the Hour). It is also permissible that it be an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Shura: 17], because of what it contains of warning and preparation with respect to both groups: the believers in the Hour and those who do not believe in it. So it mentions the state of both groups in face of that warning. As for the polytheists, they receive it with mockery and obstinate denial of it, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿They seek to hasten it, those who do not believe in it﴾. And those who believe in it act for that by which they will attain success on account of it; for this reason, after it there comes the clause ﴿Surely those who dispute about the Hour are in far-off error﴾, as will come.

Al-istti'jal (seeking to hasten) is seeking speed. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿their hastening [request] for good﴾ [Yunus: 11] in Surat Yunus. That is, those who do not believe in the Hour ask the Prophet ﷺ that God hasten the arrival of the Hour so that his truthfulness may be shown, by way of derision, mockery, and as a metonymy for their taking its delay as evidence that it will not occur, while they are despairing of it, as His saying in its counterpart indicates: ﴿and those who believe are apprehensive of it﴾. This meaning has recurred from them in various expressions mentioned amid the verses of the Qur'an,

Page 70

such as His saying: ﴿They say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48], and ﴿They said, "Our Lord, hasten for us our portion before the Day of Reckoning"﴾ [Sad: 16].

Al-ishfaq (apprehension) is expectation of the occurrence of what is disliked; that is, they are apprehensive of its terrors. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿and they are apprehensive of His dread﴾ [al-Anbiya: 28]. He made the apprehension concern the Hour itself only to convey the magnitude of its terrors, so that its states are as though they were the Hour itself, following the manner of attributing a judgment and the like to entities, as in ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. So they strive to be saved from it through obedience and piety; that is, they do not seek to hasten it, but rather they seize upon their remaining in this world for righteous action and repentance.

By ﴿those who do not believe﴾ is meant the polytheists, and they are expressed by the relative form because the relative clause indicates the cause of their seeking to hasten it. By ﴿those who believe﴾ is meant the Muslims, for this is a title for them. Thus in the speech there is ihtibak (interlocking omission), its estimate being: "They seek to hasten it, those who do not believe in it, so they are not apprehensive of it; and those who believe are apprehensive of it, so they do not seek to hasten it."

The clause ﴿and know that it is the truth﴾ is conjoined to ﴿apprehensive of it﴾ to convey that their apprehension of it is apprehension arising from certainty and conviction, not apprehension arising from doubt and fear that reality might reveal the report about it to be untrue, with that being an equally probable possibility in their view.

The definiteness of al-Haqq in His saying ("innaha al-Haqq") is the definiteness of genus, and it conveys restriction of the predicate to the subject, a restriction of emphasis for the perfection of the genus in the subject, as in: "'Antarah is the brave one," meaning: they are certain that it is the truth entirely, because the signs of its occurrence are manifest, to the extent that it is as though there is no truth other than it.

* * *

﴿Surely those who dispute about the Hour are in far-off error﴾

This clause is a tadhyil (concluding appendix) to what precedes it, both explicitly and implicitly, because its explicit meaning is the affirmation of error for those who deny the Hour, and its implicit meaning is the affirmation of guidance for those who believe in the Hour. This tadhyil is a summary (fadhlakah) of the clause that precedes it.

The opening of the clause with the particle "ala" (indeed/take note), which serves to call attention, is for the purpose of giving care to the speech.

Al-muma'arah is a mufa'alah from al-miryah, with a kasra on the mim, which is doubt. Al-muma'arah is contentious dispute, because it introduces doubt into the disputant. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿so do not dispute concerning them﴾ [al-Kahf: 22] in Surat al-Kahf.

He made error like a container for them, as a comparison of their being immersed in error with an object being in its container, so the particle "fi" (in) is for figurative containment.

Describing error as "far-off" is a figurative description: He likened disbelief to the error of a traveler on a road, which is greater when the road is far, and this is a metonymy for the difficulty of returning him to the intended goal.

The meaning is: surely they are in severe error. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿then he has certainly strayed into far-off error﴾ [al-Nisa: 116] in Surat al-Nisa.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 19:

﴿Allah is Subtle with His servants; He provides for whom He wills, and He is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾

This sentence is a preparatory introduction (tawti'ah) to the sentence ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾ [al-Shura: 20], because what will be mentioned in the following sentence is one of the effects of Allah's subtlety (lutf) toward His servants, His gentleness with them, and the provision He facilitated in this world for both believers and disbelievers among them, and then what He specially granted to the believers of provision in the Hereafter. Therefore the sentence is a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i) that serves as a prelude to the resumed sentence that it introduces, namely ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾ [al-Shura: 20] and what follows.

As for the placement of the sentence ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20] and so on, we will explain it.

Al-Latif (the Subtle) means: the one who is kind, strongly kind (al-barr al-qawiyy al-birr). This includes many bounties. Some exegetes interpreted (al-Latif) as "the one who bestows some of them," but this is an illustrative interpretation (tafsir tamthil) that does not restrict the indication of the attribute to it. The verb lataf comes from the pattern of nasara and takes the preposition bi as here, and li as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills﴾ [Yusuf: 100], as was mentioned earlier in Surah Yusuf. The reality of the meaning of His name al-Latif, may He be exalted, has also been previously verified.

Page 72

And ('ibadihi, His servants) is general for all servants, and they are the species of humankind, because it is a plural construct (jam' mudaf).

The sentence ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾ is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to the name of Majesty (Allah), or in the position of a predicate (khabar) about it.

Al-Rizq (provision) is the giving of what benefits. In our view it is not restricted to what is lawful (halal), whereas according to the Mu'tazilah it is restricted to it, and the dispute is a terminological one.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended here is the provision of this world, because the discourse is a preparation for His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20].

Al-Mashi'ah (will) here is the will of determining provision for each individual among the servants, so that the general nature of subtlety toward the servants remains; thus His saying (whom He wills) does not carry the sense of repetition, for it would become: He provides for whomever He wills from among His servants, who are all treated with subtlety, and provision is only part of subtlety, so it would become part of the meaning already conveyed. Therefore it is certain that the will here is directed toward the will of determining provision according to its measures.

The meaning is: because of His subtlety toward all His servants, He does not leave any of them without provision, and He preferred some of them over others in provision, in accordance with His will.

This meaning raises the question of the disagreement among the imams of the principles of religion (usul al-din) concerning the blessing upon the disbeliever, and among its branches is the provision of the disbeliever. From Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari it is reported that the disbeliever is not favored with a worldly blessing (ni'mah dunyawiyyah), because the pleasures of the disbeliever are a respite (istidraj), and since they lead to punishment in the Hereafter, they are not a blessing. By "worldly" they mean the opposite of "religious" (diniyyah). It seems that the Shaykh's intention with this is to establish the meaning of Allah's anger toward the disbelievers, as came in many verses; so his meaning is that the disbeliever is not favored with the blessing of approval and honor, but it is a blessing of mercy because of his affiliation to creaturehood toward Allah, may He be exalted.

Abu Bakr al-Baqillani said: the disbeliever is favored with a worldly blessing. The Mu'tazilah said: he is favored with a worldly and religious blessing: the worldly is evident, and the religious is like the capacity to reflect that leads to knowledge of Allah.

This is a question whose disagreement the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) traced back to wording and to building upon terminologies

Page 73

and considerations that accord with the subtleties of the schools, since no one disputes the blessing upon those among them who are favored, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of blessing﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

The conjunction of ﴿He is the Strong, the Mighty﴾ upon the attribute "Subtle" or upon the sentence ﴿He provides for whom He wills﴾ is a glorification of Allah, may He be exalted, with these two attributes. It also serves as a safeguard against the assumption that His subtlety comes from incapacity or flattery, for He is Strong and Mighty, who neither lacks power nor flatters; or against the assumption that His provision for whomever He wills comes from miserliness or scarcity, for He is the Strong, and from the Strong the causes of miserliness are negated, and the Mighty is negated from the cause of poverty. So His provision for whom He wills, in what He wills, is bound to a wisdom He knows concerning the states of His creation in general and in particular, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Had Allah expanded provision for His servants, they would have rebelled in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27], and so on.

The predication about the name of Majesty (Allah) with the predicate defined by the article al-lam (al-Qawiyy al-'Aziz, "the Strong, the Mighty") conveys the meaning of restricting strength and might to Him, may He be exalted. This is a restriction of genus (qasr al-jins) for the sake of emphasis, given His perfection in them, to the point that the strength of others and the might of others are as nothing.

**[Page 74]**

This verse is connected to His words: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are apprehensive of it﴾ (al-Shura: 18) and what follows, because it contains the existence of two groups: the group of believers, whose greatest concern is the life of the Hereafter, and the group of those who do not believe, whose aspiration is limited to the life of this world. So this verse came to detail how God deals with the two groups differently, although they are equal in being His servants and in being objects of His kindness. The sentence ﴿God is Gentle with His servants﴾ (al-Shura: 19) was thus a preparation (tamhid) for this sentence, and this sentence is a detailed account of the portions of the two groups concerning belief in the Hereafter and its denial.

Because of this connection between it and the sentence ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾ (al-Shura: 18), its conjunction (ʿatf) to that sentence was omitted, and the conjunction of its preparatory sentence was likewise omitted. Because of the connection between it and the sentence ﴿God is Gentle with His servants﴾ (al-Shura: 19), the conjunction of its preparatory sentence to that sentence was omitted, since the purpose is connected to the preparation.

Al-ḥarth (tilling, cultivation): its original meaning is the verbal noun of ḥaratha, when one tills the land in order to sow seed in it or to plant trees in it. It was applied to the land in which there is crops or trees, and this is a very common usage, as in His words: ﴿Go out early to your tilth, if you are going to harvest﴾ (al-Qalam: 22), meaning your garden. This is in line with His words before it: ﴿We tested the people of the garden﴾ (al-Qalam: 17). And He said: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: of women, children, heaped treasures of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilth﴾ (Al ʿImran: 14), and it was discussed earlier in Surat Al ʿImran.

In this verse, al-ḥarth is a metaphor for devoting oneself to acquiring what the earner regards as a benefit from which he hopes for abundant gain, like the farmer's devotion to tilling and sowing the land so that he obtains many ears of grain and fruit from the crop. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*We are both, when one of us attains something, it escapes the other,*
*and whoever tills my field and yours will grow lean.*

The attribution of tilling to the Hereafter and to this world is in the sense of the lam (the particle "for"), as in His words: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it﴾ (al-Isra: 19). This is the lam of specification (lam al-ikhtisas), and in such a case it denotes the specification of the thing caused to its cause. The lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil) is nothing but one of the variants of the lam of specification.

The meaning of ﴿desires the tilth of the Hereafter﴾ is: seeks work for the sake of the Hereafter. The one who desires it is the believer in the Hereafter, because the believer in the Hereafter cannot be free of desiring the Hereafter in some of his deeds, whether many or few. The one who desires the tilth of this world is meant to be the one who strives only for worldly work, by the indication of the contrast with the one who desires the tilth of the Hereafter. So it is determined that the one who desires the tilth of this world in this verse is the one who does not believe in the Hereafter. A parallel to this is His words in Surat Hud: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be shortchanged therein﴾ (Hud: 15). ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did therein is nullified, and what they used to do is vain﴾ (Hud: 16). Do you not see His words: ﴿for them there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire﴾ (Hud: 16), and His words in Surat al-Isra: ﴿Whoever desires the hasty (life of this world), We hasten for him therein what We will, for whomever We wish; then We have made Hell for him, to burn therein, blameworthy and rejected﴾ (al-Isra: 18), ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it, while being a believer, those—their striving will be appreciated﴾ (al-Isra: 19).

[Page 75]

The verb ﴿We will increase for him in his tilth﴾ admits of two meanings:

First: that the increase is in the reward for the deed, as in His words: ﴿and He causes charities to grow﴾ (al-Baqarah: 276), and His words: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and God multiplies for whomever He wills﴾ (al-Baqarah: 261). Soon there will come His words: ﴿And whoever earns a good deed, We will increase for him therein its goodness﴾ (al-Shura: 23). On this view, the attachment of the increase to the tilth is a rational metaphor (majaz ʿaqli): the increase is attached to the tilth, though its proper attachment is to its cause, which is the reward. So the meaning requires an elided modifier (ellipsis of a possessive noun).

Second: that the increase is in the deed itself, i.e., We will decree for him help in increasing righteous deeds, and make that easy for him, so that he increases in righteous works. On this view, the attachment of the increase to the tilth is literal, and so it is the use of the compound expression in its literal and rational-metaphorical senses.

The meaning of ﴿We will give him of it﴾: We will decree for him of the enjoyments of this world, of a lifespan, health, and provision, because God has decreed for His creatures their provisions and their sustenance in this world, and He made the portion of the Hereafter specific to the believers, as He said: ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it, while being a believer﴾ (al-Isra: 19). The verse of Surat al-Isra included another group not mentioned here: those who believe in the Hereafter and seek salvation in it, but have not embraced Islam, like the People of the Book. This group is also mentioned in Surat al-Balad with His words: ﴿But he did not attempt the steep path. And what can make you know what the steep path is? It is freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ (al-Balad: 11–14), up to His words: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ (al-Balad: 17).

Let no one suppose that this verse and others like it prevent the Muslim from enjoying the portions of this world when he has fulfilled the due of faith and religious obligation, nor that they bar him from combining worldly portions with the portions of the Hereafter when he fulfils both, nor that combining the two portions contradicts sincerity, such as seeking coolness along with ablution, or seeking health along with voluntary fasting, provided that the primary intent is the fulfilment of the religious duty.

This question was addressed by Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi in the first section of the sixth issue of the fourth category of the book of Purposes (al-Maqasid) in his book al-Muwafaqat. He mentioned in it two differing views of al-Ghazali and Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi, and he preferred the view of Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi, so refer to it.

[Page 76]

Al-naṣīb (portion): what is designated for one person from a divided thing. It is of the pattern faʿīl from naṣaba, because the portion is set up (yuṇṣab), i.e., it is made like a heap for its owner. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Those will have a portion of what they earned﴾ (al-Baqarah: 202) in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 21:

﴿Or do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion what Allah has not permitted?﴾

(Am) is for the transitional turning away (al-idrab al-intiqali), a shift from the discussion of the division among the adherents of the earlier religious laws regarding their laws, both those who have perished and those who remain, such as the People of the Two Books, to the discussion of what resembles that of disagreement over the foundation of the religion. This is the opposition of the polytheists to all the laws and their acceptance of the religion of association from the leaders of disbelief and the commanders of misguidance.

The meaning of the interrogation required by (am) used for transitional turning away is here for reproach and mockery. The reproach refers to their having instituted in religion what Allah has not permitted, and the mockery refers to those who instituted polytheism for them. So they were asked about those who prescribed for them the religion of polytheism: are they other partners whom they believed to be partners of Allah in divinity and in the legislation of religions, just as Allah legislated religions for people? This is mockery of them, because this kind of partner was not claimed by the polytheists among the Arabs. This meaning is what supports the indefiniteness of (partners) and its description by the clause ﴿who have instituted for them in religion﴾.

It is also possible that the one asked about, who instituted for them, is the idols they worship, which is what the exegetes have followed. Then (for them) would be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to (partners).

The purpose is to expose the enormity of their polytheism by denying that it is attributed to Allah. That is, if it was not legislated by the true God, then it was legislated by the false gods, who are the partners. It is evident that those gods are not fit to legislate a religion, because they do not reason and do not speak, so it is established that the religion of polytheism is a religion without any basis. Close to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus their partners have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137].

Page 77

It has also been said that what is meant by the partners is the leaders of the religion of polytheism, and the name of partners was applied to them figuratively by the relation of causation.

The two pronouns in (for them) refer either to ﴿those who do not believe in it﴾ [al-Shura: 18] or to ﴿those who dispute concerning Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 16].

The definiteness of (the religion) is generic, meaning: they instituted for them of the kind of religion what (i.e., a religion) Allah has not permitted, that is, He did not permit its legislation, that is, He did not send with it a messenger from Himself, nor reveal it through His angels.

* * *

﴿And had it not been for a decisive word, they would have been judged between﴾

This is like His saying earlier: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord for a specified term, they would have been judged between them﴾ [al-Shura: 14].

The decisive word is what Allah decreed and willed concerning their being given respite. And (al-fasl) means the decisive, that is, that about which there is no hesitation.

* * *

﴿And indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment﴾

This is conjoined to the clause ﴿And had it not been for a decisive word﴾, and the purpose is to affirm that their being given respite until a specified term does not release them from being held accountable for what they wronged. By the wrongdoers is meant the polytheists: ﴿Indeed, association is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

The painful punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter for all of them, and the punishment of this world by the sword and humiliation for those who were postponed until its appointed time of arrival, such as their killing on the day of Badr.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle of emphasis is because this statement is directed at them, since they hear this speech and know that they are the ones intended by it.

[Page 78]

﴿You see the wrongdoers apprehensive of what they have earned, while it befalls them. But those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in the meadows of the gardens; they will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty.﴾

The clause ﴿You see the wrongdoers apprehensive of what they have earned﴾ explains the clause ﴿Indeed, for the wrongdoers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 21]. It describes the state of this punishment by describing the state of those who suffer it at the time they expect it to descend, and that is sufficient to indicate its terror.

The address with ﴿you see﴾ is not directed at a specific person, so it includes everyone who is able to see on that Day, as in His saying: ﴿And you would see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ [al-Shura: 44] and ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled by humiliation﴾ [al-Shura: 45]. The purpose is to bring before the mind of the listener an image of the state of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection.

Ishfaq (apprehension) is the anticipation of a harmful thing, and it is the opposite of wishing (tamanni).

What they have earned (ma kasabu) refers to their evil deeds. What is meant is their recompense, by the indication of the context.

The clause ﴿while it befalls them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: apprehensive with an apprehension that approaches despair, and this is the most intense apprehension, when they know that what they fear cannot be averted by caution. This is because apprehension that occurs before the feared thing draws near may lead the apprehensive one to seek means of escape from it, but when the punishment has actually come, its barrier has prevented any escape. The meaning is: apprehensive of the punishment for their deeds at the time the punishment descends upon them. It is not the meaning that they are apprehensive in this world of their evil deeds, because they do not believe in that; so whatever exegesis is built upon that possibility is not clear.

The preposition bi in His saying ﴿befalls them﴾ indicates elevation (isti'la'), as in the verse of Ghawi al-Sulami:

"Is it a lord upon whose head the foxes urinate?"

This usage is close to the figurative sense of attachment (ilsaq majazi).

The pronoun in ﴿it befalls﴾ refers to ﴿what they have earned﴾ by considering an implied noun, meaning

[Page 79]

the recompense of what they have earned, i.e., in a state in which the recompense befalls them.

The clause ﴿But those who believed and did righteous deeds will be in the meadows of the gardens﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, with the waw being the waw of circumstance, meaning: you see the wrongdoers in apprehension, while those who believed are at ease in the meadows of the gardens. In this circumstance there is an indication that those who believed have already settled in the meadows before the wrongdoers are presented for reckoning and before their apprehension of its consequences. This is part of the contrast between the conditions of the two groups in the Hereafter, the reverse of what they were in this world, mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it, while those who believe are apprehensive of it﴾ [al-Shura: 18]. That is, today the apprehension of the believers has turned into tranquility, and the tranquility of the polytheists has turned into apprehension. The difference between the two tranquilities and the two apprehensions is vast, and it is by this opposition in the two states and their causes that it is correct to consider the existence of those who believed in the Garden as a circumstantial clause from the wrongdoers.

Rawdat (meadows) is the plural of rawda, which is a name for a collection of water and trees surrounding it, with greenery around it.

The clause ﴿they will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾ is a second predicate about those who believed, and ʿinda (with, in the presence of) is an adverbial complement attached to the stable predicate (al-kawn) to which the prepositional phrase in ﴿they will have﴾ is attached.

The phrase ʿinda (in the presence of) is an honour that conveys the sense of exclusivity expressed by the lam in His saying ﴿they will have﴾, and it expresses care for what they are given of desired things. The meaning is: what they wish is their right, preserved with their Lord. It should not be taken that ʿinda is attached to the verb ﴿they wish﴾, because then ʿinda would be an adverb of their wishing, meaning a wish of theirs directed toward their Lord, so the wish would be interpreted as a request that He give them what they ask, and the purpose of honour and care would be lost.

You may also make ʿinda rabbihim (with their Lord) a third predicate about those who believed, meaning: they are in the presence of their Lord, that is, in His hospitality and His entertainment, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and a river, in a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 54]. The arrangement of the three predicates would then follow the pattern of ascent from the good to the better: He informs about them that they have descended into the best dwelling, then He brings to them what they desire, then He rises to what is greater, which is their being in the presence of their Lord, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And approval from Allah is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]. Among the subtleties of this interpretation is that it follows the order familiar in actual occurrence: a guest or arriving visitor first alights in a place of honour upon arrival, then the hospitality is brought to him, then the master of the house mixes with him and draws near to him.

[Page 80]

The clause ﴿That is the great bounty﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil). The demonstrative refers to the content of His saying ﴿in the meadows of the gardens, they will have whatever they wish with their Lord﴾, by interpreting it as: that which has been mentioned.

The demonstrative for the distant is used metaphorically to indicate that the referent is of distant rank, after a figurative elevation, which is nobility.

Al-fadl (bounty) may be a verbal noun meaning nobility and superiority over others, in which case it means their excellence (fadluhum). It may also be a noun for what is bestowed as a favour, in which case it means: that is Our bounty upon them. In this latter sense there is an indication that the reward for deeds is a bounty from Allah, because the obedience of servants is obligatory upon them; when they perform it, they have done only what they cannot avoid doing. So if they were not rewarded for it, their not being rewarded would not be injustice.

The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) here conveys a figurative restriction (qasr idda'i) for the sake of emphasis on the supreme greatness of the bounty. Al-fadl can be taken as if it were attached to the object, meaning Allah's bounty upon them, or as if it were attached to the subject, meaning their bounty, i.e., their nobility and blessing. In the latter case the sense of restriction becomes: the bounty that came to those who believed and did righteous deeds is the greatest bounty.

[p. 81]

﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants who have believed and done righteous deeds.﴾

The demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*, "demonstrative noun") emphasizes its counterpart mentioned before it. That is, what has been mentioned, which is a bounty that they will receive in Paradise, is also good news for them in this worldly life.

The returning pronoun (*al-a'id*, the pronoun that refers back) from the relative clause (*al-sila*, the clause that completes the relative pronoun) to the relative pronoun is omitted. Its estimated form is: "that which Allah gives good news of to His servants." Its omission here is because it has been treated as if it were an object pronoun, with the preposition omitted, in the manner of its omission in such a phrase as His words: ﴿And Moses chose from his people﴾, with the estimate "from his people." Since it was treated like an object pronoun, it was omitted just as an object pronoun is omitted.

[p. 81 continues]

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and Khalaf read (*yubashshiru*) with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ba'*, with the *shin* doubled and kasra-vowelled. It is from *bashsharahu*, meaning: when he informs him of an event that pleases him. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (*yabshuru*) with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, a sukun on the *ba'*, and a *damma* on the *shin* without doubling. It is said: *bashartu al-rajula* with the *shin* lightened, *abshuruhu*, from the pattern of *nasara*, meaning: when I make him happy with an event that pleases him.

The plural *'ibad* ("servants"), when it is annexed to the Name of Majesty or to its pronoun, has come to be used in the Qur'an predominantly in contexts of drawing near and of elevating rank. For this reason, the phrase ﴿those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾ [al-Fussilat: 8] here occupies the position of an explicative apposition (*'atf al-bayan*, appositive clarification) to what is in His words: ﴿Indeed, the allies of Allah—there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve, those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾ [Yunus: 62], since ﴿those who have believed﴾ occupies the position of an explicative apposition to ﴿the allies of Allah﴾.
