* * *

[p. 82]

﴿Say, "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except affection among relatives."﴾

This is a fresh beginning of speech (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new independent sentence), occasioned by the mention of what has been prepared for the polytheists of punishment and what has been prepared for the believers of good. The pronoun of the group addressed is meant to refer, undoubtedly, to the polytheists. There is nothing in the preceding discourse that could be supposed to be an answer to it, such that it would be: "Say, I do not ask you." Therefore it is established that the clause ﴿Say, I do not ask you for it any reward﴾ is an independent statement beginning a new discourse.

It appears from what al-Wahidi related in *Asbab al-Nuzul* from Qatadah that the polytheists gathered in an assembly of theirs, and some of them said to others: "Do you see Muhammad asking a reward for what he undertakes?" Then this verse was revealed. (They meant: if that is the case, we shall gather wealth for him, as they had said to him more than once.) It is that it has no connection with what precedes it. When the occasion of its revelation arose, it was revealed in the midst of the revelation of the verses before it and after it. Thus it is an independent clause. Its placement here is due to the relation with what came before of mention of the polytheists' disputation and obstinacy, for its connection with the verses that accompany it is evident, since it is among what the Qur'an addressed against the polytheists' argumentation, negating their illusions, and opening their insight to consider the signs of the truthfulness of the Messenger. So it is an independent clause that came as a parenthetical insertion (*mu'taridah*) between the clause ﴿And those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾ [al-Shura: 22] and the clause ﴿And whoever earns a good deed﴾.

It begins with "Say" (*qul*), either because it is a reply to a statement that came from them, or because it is among what is important to convey to them, just as its counterparts begin with something similar, such as His words: ﴿Say, "Whatever reward I have asked of you, it is for you"﴾ [Saba': 47], and His words: ﴿Say, "I do not ask you for any reward for it, and I am not of the pretenders"﴾ [Sad: 86], and His words: ﴿Say, "I do not ask you for it any reward"﴾ [al-An'am: 90], ﴿My reward is only from Allah, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ [Yunus: 72]. The pronoun in ("for it") refers to the Qur'an, which is understood from the context.

The reward (*al-ajr*) is the recompense that someone is given for a deed he does. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him a great reward﴾ [al-Tawbah: 22] in the surah "Bara'ah" (al-Tawbah).

Affection (*al-mawaddah*) is love and good treatment resembling the treatment of those who love one another. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿affection among you in the life of this world﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25] in the surah al-'Ankabut. The statement is according to an omitted modifier: that is, the treatment of affection, i.e., courtesy; by the indication that love cannot be asked for, because it is an inner emotional movement and affect.

[p. 83]

"In" (*fi*) is for figurative (*majazi*) locative sense, because its object, which is "kinship" (*al-qurba*), is not suitable to be something contained in it.

The meaning of the figurative locative sense here is causation (*ta'lil*), which is a meaning that frequently occurs for the particle "in," as in His words: ﴿And strive in the cause of Allah﴾ [al-Hajj: 78].

*Al-qurba* is a verbal noun (*ism masdar*), like *al-ruj'a* and *al-bushra*, and it is kinship by lineage. Allah says: ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾ [al-Isra': 26], and Zuhayr said:

"And the wronging of kinsmen is most bitter in its sting..." [the rest of the verse]

It was discussed earlier at His words: "and for the near of kin" in surah al-Anfal.

The meaning of the verse according to what its arrangement requires: "I do not ask you for any reward for the Qur'an, except that you show affection to me," i.e., that you treat me with the treatment of affection, that is, not the treatment of enmity, for the sake of the kinship that is between us in lineage through the Quraysh.

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari and the *Jami'* of al-Tirmidhi, Ibn 'Abbas was asked about this verse in the presence of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Sa'id hastened and said: "The near kin of Muhammad." Ibn 'Abbas said: "You have been hasty; there was no clan of Quraysh except that it had kinship with him among them." He (Sa'id) said: "Except that you join what is between me and you of kinship."

Al-Qurtubi related from al-Sha'bi that he said: "The people argued much about us concerning this verse, so we wrote to Ibn 'Abbas asking him about it, and he wrote that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the middlemost of the people among Quraysh, so there was no clan among their clans except that he was born to it. Then Allah said to him: ﴿Say, 'I do not ask you for it any reward, except affection among relatives'﴾, meaning: except that you show affection to me in my kinship with you, i.e., that you observe what is between me and you, so that you affirm me. So the kinship here is kinship of blood, as if he had said: follow me for kinship if you do not follow me for prophethood." The words of al-Qurtubi end.

As for what some commentators explained, that the meaning is: "except that you show affection to my relatives," it is a contrived meaning, derived from an understanding that does not look to Arabic usage, and no reliable report is transmitted for it from anyone whose understanding is relied upon.

As for the fact that the love of the family of the Prophet (ﷺ) for the sake of the love of what has connection with him is a moral trait of Muslims, this is established from other proofs, and the detailed delimitation of its limits is in al-Shifa' of 'Iyad.

The exception is disconnected (*istithna' munqati'*, exception not of the same kind), because affection for the sake of kinship is not from the reward for conveying the call through the Qur'an, but is among what manhood requires. So its exception from the general negated reward is not a real exception. The meaning is: "I do not ask you for a reward for the conveying, but I ask you for affection for the sake of kinship."

He asked them for affection only because their treating him with affection helps spread the call of Islam, since through that treatment their obstinacy softens, so they leave off opposing him, and he is able to convey the call of Islam in a more complete manner. Thus this affection became a religious purpose with no benefit for the person of the Prophet (ﷺ) himself.

In some of the fabricated reports (*al-akhbar al-mawdu'ah*) about the occasions of revelation, it is said that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was that when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina, misfortunes befell him that what was in his hands could not cover. The Ansar said: "This man, Allah guided you through him, so let us gather wealth for him." They did so, then brought it to him, and it was revealed.

[p. 84]

In another narration: the Ansar said to him one day: "Our souls and our wealth are for you," and it was revealed. It was also said that there was revealed ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants﴾ up to His words: ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. For this reason, a group said that these verses are Medinan, as was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah, and these are weak reports.

The verse includes that the Prophet (ﷺ) is exalted above seeking from people any recompense for conveying guidance to them, since prophethood is the greatest rank in teaching the truth, and it is above the rank of wisdom. The wise have avoided taking a wage for teaching wisdom, since wisdom is abundant good, and abundant good is not matched by the goods of this world. For this reason Allah commanded His messengers to be exalted above seeking any recompense for conveying the message. He said, relating about Noah: ﴿And I do not ask you for it any reward; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 109]. Likewise He related about Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb.

* * *

[p. 85 — continuing in the following text]

﴿And whoever earns a good deed—We increase for him therein in goodness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Appreciative.﴾

This is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a closing statement that generalizes) for the clause ﴿That is what Allah gives good news of to His servants who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾. The meaning: whenever a believer does a good deed, We increase him in goodness from that great bounty. This is in the meaning of His words: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. The conjunction "and" is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*).

*Al-iqtiraf* is a reflexive form (*iftial*) from *al-qarf*, which is earning/acquiring. So *al-iqtiraf* is an intensification of acquiring, equivalent to *al-iktisab*, and it is not restricted to acquiring evil, though it has predominated in that usage. Its root is from *qarafa al-shajarah*, when one peels its *qirf*, with a kasra on the *qaf*, which is its bark, i.e., the peel of its wood. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿and that they may earn what they are earning﴾ [al-An'am: 113] in surah al-An'am, and at His words: ﴿and wealth that you have acquired﴾ [al-Tawbah: 24] in surah "Bara'ah."

*Al-hasanah* is the deed possessing goodness. It is an adjectival form (*sifah mushabbahah*, a quasi-adjective) that has become predominant in the usage of the Qur'an and the Sunnah for obedience and devotion, so that it became like the fixed nouns, a proper designation by predominance. It is derived from *al-husn*, which is beauty of form. *Al-husn* is the opposite of ugliness, and it is a quality in the thing itself that makes its appearance acceptable in the souls of those who see it and inclines them to continue beholding it. Non-physical matters are described as beautiful, and by this is meant that the deed or quality is praiseworthy to the intellects and desirable to be characterized by.

Since *al-hasanah* is taken from *al-husn*, the increase in it is made an increase in goodness, observing the original derivation. So the mention of goodness is paired with it by what is called paronomasia of derivation (*jinas al-ishtiqaq*), like His words: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. The meaning becomes: "We increase for him therein something similar to it."

It is necessarily understood that the increase in it is an increase not from his own deed, and the increase is not by a deed done by someone else, for that would become a deed that itself deserves increase, so the increase would never end. Therefore it is established that the meaning is an increase in the reward of its equivalents with Allah. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-An'am: 160], and His words: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever intends a good deed and then does it, Allah records it with Him as ten good deeds up to seven hundred times."

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Appreciative﴾ is a concluding statement and a justification for the increase, to establish it, by stating that Allah's forgiveness is abundant for whoever deserves it, and His appreciation is abundant for those who draw near to Him. The purpose of the justification is the attribute of Appreciative. As for the attribute of Forgiving, it was mentioned to point toward encouraging those who commit evil deeds to seek forgiveness and repent, so that they may be forgiven and not despair of Allah's mercy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 24:

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented a lie against Allah"? But if Allah willed, He would seal up your heart, and Allah would obliterate falsehood and establish the truth by His words. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾

This is a transitional digression (idrab intiqali), in conjunction with His saying: ﴿Or do they have partners who have instituted for them in religion that which Allah has not permitted?﴾ [al-Shura: 21]. That is the discourse being turned away from and transitioned from, and the intent is a transition to another rebuke. The interrogative hamza implied after (am) is an interrogation of reproach, for they did say this and so deserve reproach for it. The meaning is: "Or do they say, 'He has invented it,' and [do] they say it?"

The verb (yaqulun), "they say," is in the present tense so that the reproach targets their persistence in this abominable statement despite the evident proofs of its falsehood. If their saying is an abominable utterance, then persisting in it is more abominable.

Following upon this rebuke, He says: ﴿But if Allah willed, He would seal up your heart﴾. This is a consequence (tafri') that contains some obscurity and subtlety, because what is immediately understood from a consequence is that what follows the fa' is a refutation of what they attributed to him of inventing a lie against Allah, and a confirmation of the rebuke. So how is this refutation derived from the conditional and its response, which are themselves consequences of the rebuke?

Commentators have many understandings regarding the explanation of this consequence and its relation to what precedes it, most of which are not free from artificiality and weak persuasion.

The correct explanation is that this conditional and its response, which in the apparent wording are consequences of the rebuke and the refutation, are evidence of the intended meaning, with the consequence suited to rebuking them and refuting their claim. The consequence is to be construed thus: "How could the invention come from you against Allah, when Allah does not allow anyone to lie about Him? Had He willed, He would have sealed up your heart," that is, deprived you of the intellect by which you think about falsehood, so that you would be struck dumb from speech and unable to fabricate against Him. That is, there is no barrier preventing the will of Allah from that, were you to invent against Him. Thus the conditional is a metonymy for the absence of invention, since Allah does not allow one who lies about Him to speak. Through this composition there results a wondrous brevity, and the verse is close to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if he had attributed to Us some [false] sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44-46].

Ibn 'Atiyyah has a few words that support the sense of this interpretation, relying on the saying of Qatadah, taken according to the apparent wording, that what follows the fa' is the consequence, and the statement is a metonymy for turning away from their saying, "He has invented a lie against Allah." That is, Allah addresses His Messenger with this, by way of allusion to the polytheists. The meaning: their claim that he invented against Allah should not concern you to the point that you show enmity to Muhammad (ﷺ). Allah is more entitled than you to be jealous over the violation of the sanctity of His message and to defend His majesty. So do not make this claim your concern, for if Allah willed, He would seal up your heart, depriving you of the ability to attribute speech to Him.

These two interpretations are the ones suited to the position of the verse, to the consequential fa', to the futurity in the conditional, and to the verb of the condition being in the present tense. Thus the pause is at His saying (ʿala qalbika), "upon your heart," which is the end of a statement.

The clause ﴿And Allah would obliterate falsehood﴾ is coordinated with the consequence and is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), intending that Allah obliterates the falsehood and deceit of the polytheists and realizes what His Messenger (ﷺ) brought. In accordance with this meaning, a group of exegetes proceeded, such as al-Kisa'i, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari, and they did not make (wa-yamuh) a coordination with the verb of the response, because what is immediately understood is that this is a promise from Allah of the manifestation of Islam and a warning to the polytheists that their religion is doomed to vanish. This is what is immediately understood from the nominative (wa-yuhiqqu), upon which the reciters agree. The meaning of "obliteration" here is removal. The falsehood intended is the known falsehood, namely the religion of polytheism; and the truth intended is the known truth, namely Islam.

Or the meaning is that it is among the way of Allah, Exalted, to remove falsehood and expose it by creating the causes of its disappearance, and to make the truth clear by creating the causes of its manifestation, until its manifestation exposes the falsehood. Thus, if the Qur'an were a lie invented against Allah, Allah would expose its falsehood and manifest the truth. In this case, "falsehood" means the genus of falsehood, and "truth" the genus of truth, and the clause serves as a tadhyil (concluding summation) to the consequence. The first meaning is more fitting to the resumption, and because it conveys the threat of removing what they are upon and granting the Muslims victory over them.

On both meanings, His saying ﴿And Allah would obliterate falsehood﴾ is a resumptive statement, not coordinated with the response of the condition, for the meaning is not "If Allah wills, He will obliterate falsehood," but rather it is an affirmation of His obliterating falsehood, like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra': 81], as indicated by the nominative of ﴿and establishes the truth by His words﴾. Thus the verb (yamhu) is nominative, and its original form bears a waw at its end, but it was dropped for ease of pronunciation, and its written form followed its dropping in pronunciation, in consideration of the state of speech, just as the waw was dropped in ﴿We will call the guards of Hell﴾ [al-'Alaq: 18] and the waw in ﴿and man supplicates for evil as he supplicates for good﴾ [al-Isra': 11]. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in al-Kashshaf that the waw was present in some of the codices, but he did not specify it, nor did anyone else mention it, as far as I have seen.

The manifestation of the name of Allah in His saying ﴿And Allah would obliterate falsehood﴾, rather than saying "and would obliterate falsehood," serves to strengthen the establishment of the subject in the mind and to show Allah's care for obliterating falsehood.

He turned to a nominal sentence in the formation of ﴿And Allah would obliterate falsehood﴾, and did not say "and Allah obliterates falsehood," because the intent is that the renewal and recurrence implied by the present verb indicates that this is Allah's way and custom, which does not fail; and he did not intend to affirm and establish this, since the implication of recurrence demands it by way of metonymy, so both purposes are achieved.

The bi in (bi-kalimatihi) denotes causation, and the "words" (kalimat) are: the words of the Qur'an and revelation, as in His saying: ﴿They want to change the words of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 15]; or the intended meaning is the words of creation (kalimat al-takwin) related to bringing into existence according to His knowledge, as in His saying: ﴿There is no changer of His words﴾ [al-An'am: 115].

This response to them came in the mode of address to the Prophet (ﷺ), because that is more forceful in attending to instructing him in replying to their denial, since the context is one of censuring their slander. This is the reason for the difference between the style of this verse and the style of His saying: ﴿Say, "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it"﴾ [Yunus: 16], because that was not driven toward refuting a statement issued by them.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the whole of the two clauses: "If Allah willed..." up to His saying "by His words", that is, because nothing is hidden from Him, neither the fabrication of the fabricator nor the truthfulness of the one who is right. "Dhat al-sudur" means the intentions and purposes that people conceal in their minds. "Al-sudur" (breasts) means the minds; the word "breasts" was applied to them according to Arabic usage, and it has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾ [al-Anfal: 43] in Surat al-Anfal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verses 25–26:

﴿He it is who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds, and He knows what you do﴾ ﴿and responds to those who believe and do righteous deeds, and increases them from His bounty; but as for the disbelievers, there is a severe punishment for them﴾

When the warning concerning those who dispute about God in order to support their falsehood had come, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who dispute about God after it has been responded to, their argument is void with their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 16], it was followed by a description of the wretched state they will be in on the Day of Recompense, in His saying: ﴿You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 22], and it was contrasted with a description of the bliss of those who believe, in His saying: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds will be in the meadows of the gardens﴾ [al-Shura: 22]. Since this might break the souls of the people of obstinacy and misguidance, it was followed by informing them that it is part of God's nature to accept the repentance of whoever of His servants repents, and that His pardon, by that, covers what of their evil deeds has passed.

This information is an allusion that urges hastening to repentance, and for this reason the verb is given in the present tense, which is suitable for the future. It is also good news to the believers that He has accepted their repentance from the polytheism and ignorance they were in, for the One whose nature is to accept repentance in the future has already accepted the repentance of those who repented before, by the implication of the speech's wording or its import, and that it is part of His nature to respond to those of His servants who believe and do righteous deeds. All of this follows the Qur'anic custom of following intimidation with encouragement and vice versa. All of this includes a promise to the believers that their faith will be accepted, and to the disobedient that their repentance will be accepted.

So the clause: ﴿He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And indeed, for the wrongdoers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 21] and what is connected to it of what was mentioned earlier, especially the clause: ﴿And God effaces falsehood﴾ [al-Shura: 24].

Expressing the information with this clause in nominal form serves to convey the stability and permanence of its judgment.

The predicate being a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) serves to convey that God is characterized by the content of its relative clause, and that this is an attribute among God's attributes, known to be firmly established for Him without exception, because it suits His wisdom, the greatness of His station, and His independence from His creation.

The choice of the relative clause in the present tense serves to convey the renewal and recurrence of its content, so that they know that this is a promise that does not fail and does not vary.

The verb (qabila) is transitive with min (the initial "min") at times, as in His saying: ﴿And nothing prevented them from having their contributions accepted from them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 54], and His saying: ﴿Never will there be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91]. It then conveys the sense of taking the accepted thing from the one from whom it is taken. It is also transitive with 'an (from/away from), which conveys the sense of the accepted thing passing away from, or separating from, its giver and bestower. This is more emphatic in the meaning of the verb than transitivity with the particle min, because it implies a metaphor for the thing bestowed being held with the one to whom it is given, such that it is not returned to its bestower.

Thus there are four intensifications in the clause ﴿He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾: the clause being nominal, being a relative construction, being in the present tense, and the verb of the relative clause being transitive with 'an rather than min.

Repentance (tawbah) is abandoning the act of disobedience in compliance with obedience to God. Its discussion has already been given at His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] in Surat al-Baqarah. The acceptance of repentance is a favour from God Exalted, for if He had willed, He would not have been pleased with the one who committed the transgression; but He made it acceptable out of His wisdom and bounty.

In mentioning the name "servants" rather than something like "people," or "those who repent," or otherwise, there is an indication that God is gentle with His servants by virtue of the station of servanthood, for the Creator and Maker loves the well-being of His creation.

Al-'Afw (pardon) is not holding the offender to account for his crime. Al-sayyi'at (evil deeds) are the transgressions, because they are evil in the sight of the Law. Pardon of evil deeds occurs by means of repentance, by pardoning the evil deeds that the sinner committed before his repentance; and it occurs without that, like pardon of evil deeds following an accepted Hajj, and like pardon of evil deeds for the sake of martyrdom in the way of God, and like pardon of evil deeds due to the abundance of good deeds, whereby from the sinner's evil deeds is erased an amount equal to a measure of his good deeds in a manner known to God Exalted, and like pardon of minor sins through avoiding major sins.

The definite article in (al-sayyi'at) is the definite article of genus, intended for comprehensiveness; it is general but specified by exclusion of shirk. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with [in worship]﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. You may also take it as a substitute for the genitive complement, i.e., "the evil deeds of His servants," so that it embraces all servants with a generality specified by the evidences for this ruling, as in the first aspect.

The clause ﴿and He knows what you do﴾ is parenthetical between the conjoined clauses, or in the position of a circumstantial clause. The intended meaning is that nothing of the deeds of His servants, good or bad, is hidden from Him.

Al-Jumhur read (ma yaf'aluna) with the ya' of the third person, i.e., "what His servants do." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim and Khalaf read it with the ta' of address, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

Al-istijabah (responding) is an intensified form of ijabah (answering), and in usage the word istijabah is restricted to complying with a call or command.

The apparent structure of the verse is that the subject of (yastajibu) is a pronoun referring to what the pronoun in ﴿He it is who accepts repentance﴾ refers to; that ﴿alladhina amanu﴾ is the object of (yastajibu); and that the clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿yaqbalu al-tawbah﴾.

The common usage is to say istajaba lahu, as in His saying: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. They sometimes omit the lam and use the verb transitively, as in the words of Ka'b ibn Sa'd:

"And a caller who called, 'O you who respond to the summons,' but on that occasion no responder responded to him."

The meaning is that God grants them what they hope for from Him of reward, and what they call upon Him for.

It is also possible that alladhina amanu is the subject of (yastajibu), i.e., they respond to God and obey Him, and the clause (wa yastajibu) is conjoined to the whole clause ﴿He it is who accepts repentance﴾, meaning: that is His nature, and this is the nature of His believing servants.

The meaning of ﴿and increases them from His bounty﴾ on both readings is that He gives them what they hoped for from their supplication and their deeds, and more than what they hoped for when they responded to Him and His Messenger; and that He gives them more reward than what they did of righteous deeds, since He made a good deed worth ten like it up to seven hundred times, as in the hadith; and that He gives them of the good of this world what they did not ask Him for. All of this is because He is Gentle with them and Manager of their interests.

Since responding and increasing are an honour for the believers, the name of "those who believe" is stated explicitly and brought in as a relative construction, to indicate that faith is the reason for their being responded to and for their being increased.

The clause ﴿and the disbelievers, for them is a severe punishment﴾ is a parenthetical clause returning to what preceded in His saying: ﴿You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned, and it will befall them﴾ [al-Shura: 22], as an emphasis of the threat and a warning against persisting in disbelief after the door of repentance has been opened to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 27:

page 92
﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth. But He sends down in measure what He wills. Indeed He is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing.﴾
This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿And He increases them of His bounty﴾ [al-Shura: 26], or upon the whole of what comes from the clause ﴿And He responds to those who believe﴾ [al-Shura: 26] and from the clause ﴿And He increases them of His bounty﴾ [al-Shura: 26].

Its place in meaning is that of istidrak (qualification, correction) and ihtiras (precaution against misunderstanding), for it points to an answer to an implicit question in the listener's mind. When he hears that Allah responds to those who believe and that He increases them of His bounty, he may ask himself: since believers ask for abundance of provision and ease in it, and the believers in the early days of Islam were in need and narrow provision, when the polytheists withheld their provisions and boycotted their dealings, the answer is given: if Allah were to expand provision for all people, its expansion would corrupt them, because the one who becomes rich is open to forgetting his reliance upon Allah, and it drives him to transgress against people. So it was among the best interest of the believers, in the long run, that provision not be expanded for them. This was bound up with a wisdom which Allah intended in the ordering of this world, one that applies to people, believers and unbelievers alike. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, man does transgress﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 6] ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 7].

In this there was another benefit for the believer: that his wealth should not preoccupy him from the work by which he succeeds in the Hereafter, so that his possessions do not distract him from it. This consideration is what the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to when he said to the Ansar, when they came before him after the dawn prayer, and wealth had come to him from Bahrain: "By Allah, I do not fear poverty for you, but I fear that the world will be spread out over you as it was spread out over those before you, and you will compete for it as they competed for it, and it will destroy you as it destroyed them."

This verse came in a universal manner, because His saying (to His servants) encompasses all servants. Through this universality there is achieved the benefit of the specific answer concerning believers, together with the conveying of the general wisdom of this created order. Thus this clause, in this respect, stands in the place of a concluding statement (tadhyil) for what it contains of generality, meaning: Allah established the order of this world upon general laws, and it is not part of His wisdom to single out His friends and His party with a worldly created order; rather He singled them out with the meanings of nearness, approval and success in eternal life.

page 93
And perhaps He singled them out with what He willed to specify for them of what pertains to the establishment of the truth.
Al-baghy: transgression and injustice, i.e., some would transgress against others, because wealth is the seat of insolence and arrogance when it encounters a corrupt soul. A poet of the Hamasa, from Banu Jarm of Tayy, said:

When you are fertile, you become enemies, and when you are barren, you become dependents.
And for one of the Arabs, whom al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) cited:

The rain of spring has made grow between us
and between the Banu Ruman, nabʿ and shawhat (trees).

As for poverty, it has rarely been a cause of transgression, except a transgression mixed with fear, like the transgression of the hungry man who seizes by force; that is rare and is not taken into consideration. Moreover, the context is for explaining the wisdom of provision being given in measure, not for explaining a wisdom in poverty.

Thus the implication between the condition and its answer in His saying ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel﴾ is established by this causal relation, regardless of whether this cause may sometimes be replaced by its opposite as well. Moreover, between the expansion of provision and poverty there are other levels: sufficiency, narrowness of provision, want, and poverty, which vary, so there is no difficulty in the reasoning.

It is related from Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "This verse was revealed about us. We looked at the wealth of Banu al-Nadir, Banu Qurayzah and Banu Qaynuqa, and we wished for it, so it was revealed." This is among what led some people to think this verse is Madani, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah. If this is correct from Khabbab, then it is his interpretation, because the verse is Meccan, and Khabbab was an Ansari, so perhaps he heard some of them citing this verse for one another and had not heard it before.

It is also narrated that it was revealed concerning the People of the Suffa, who wished for expansion of provision, so it was revealed. This report is weak.

The meaning of the verse: if Allah had made all people enjoy expansion of provision, the order of their life would be disrupted by some transgressing against others, because some of the rich are moved by their souls to transgress, given the abundance of the causes of aggression, as you know; then the one transgressed against finds resistance, and so on, and that leads to the disruption of their order.

From this you know that the expansion of provision for some servants, as is observed, does not lead to such corruption, because wealth may encounter a good soul and a soul that has a restraint from religion, so it is not a cause of transgression. If it encounters a corrupt soul with no restraint, that is a rare condition, one of the bad conditions in the world, and there are things that oppose it in the Sharia, the judicial decision, and the jealousy of the community, so it does not lead to general corruption or disruption of the order.

The application of the verb "to send down" to the giving of provision in His saying ﴿but He sends down in measure﴾ is a metaphor (istiʿara), because it is a gift from one of exalted rank, so it is likened to something descending from a height. Such usage recurs in the Qur'an.

Al-qadar, with two fathas: measure and determination.

The meaning of (what He wills): His will, exalted is He, proceeds in accordance with His knowledge and with what He facilitates for Him of the arrangement of causes according to the differing interests of His creatures and the conflict of some with others. All of this is disposition and determination that none encompasses except His knowledge, exalted is He. All of it falls under His saying ﴿Indeed He is, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾, and this clause stands in the position of a causal explanation for what precedes it.

It is opened with (inna), which is not meant to emphasize the statement, but merely to draw attention to the statement and to signal the causal explanation, because (inna) in such a context takes the place of the resultative fa' and conveys causation and connection, so the clause is in the sense of a clause joined by fa'.

The combination of the two attributes "Khabir" and "Basir" is because the attribute Khabir indicates knowledge of the interests and conditions of the servants before their determination and the determination of their causes, i.e., knowledge of what will be. The attribute Basir indicates knowledge related to their conditions that have already occurred, and there is a difference between these two relations of divine knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 28:

Page 95
﴿And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy. And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy.﴾
This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿But He sends down by measure whatever He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27]. Rain is a great means of provision, and what Allah sends down of it is by a measure He knows best. In it is a reminder of this great blessing upon people, of which the greater part of their true sustenance comes, for them and for their livestock.

He singled it out for mention, apart from the other worldly blessings, because it is a blessing about which people do not differ, since it is the foundation of the continuation of life through the provision of wholesome food for people and animals. By this the force of His saying becomes clear: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed in them of living creatures﴾ [al-Shura: 29], coming right after His saying here ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain﴾.

The use of the present tense in (yunazzilu) is to indicate the recurrence and renewal of the sending down.

The use of the past tense in His saying ﴿after they have despaired﴾ is to indicate that the despair had occurred and become established through the passage of a period of time over it.

Al-ghayth (the rain) is the rain that comes after drought. It was named ghayth by way of the verbal noun, because through it people in distress are relieved (yughathu). It was discussed at His saying ﴿wherein people will be given relief﴾ [Yusuf: 49] in Surah Yusuf.

Al-qunut is despair, and it was discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not be of those who despair﴾ [al-Hijr: 55] in Surah al-Hijr. The meaning is: after they had despaired of the rain, with the cessation of the usual signs of rain and the narrowing of the time for sowing.

The form of restriction (qasr) in His saying ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain﴾ conveys qasr al-qalb (restriction by reversal of belief), because among the listeners there are polytheists who think that the sending down of rain is from the influence of the stars, and among them are heedless Muslims, who were treated as one who thinks the sending down of rain is tied to the usual causes of rain. This is because in the Jahiliyyah they believed that rain came from the influence of the stars' risings (anwa').

In the hadith of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us after a rain that had fallen during the night, and said: 'Do you know what your Lord has said?' He said: 'In the morning, among My servants there are those who believe in Me and those who disbelieve in Me. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by the grace of Allah and His mercy, he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star. As for the one who said: We have been given rain by the rising of such-and-such and such-and-such, he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star.'"

Page 96
This restriction, with respect to the polytheists, is a original qasr al-qalb, and with respect to the Muslims it is a qasr al-qalb of tanzil (applied correction).

Al-nashr is the opposite of folding (al-tayy), and it was discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a book he will find spread open﴾ [al-Isra: 13] in Surah al-Isra.

It is used here metaphorically for extension and expansion. The mercy here is His mercy through water; it was also said: through the sun after the rain. The pronoun in ﴿after they had despaired﴾ refers to (His servants) in His saying: ﴿And He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25].

It has been said: "The verse was revealed concerning the lifting of drought from Quraysh through the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ for them, after the drought had persisted over them for seven years, during which they ate carrion and bones, and this is what is alluded to in His saying in Surah al-Dukhan: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]."

In the Sahih, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called Quraysh, they denied him and rebelled against him, so he said: "O Allah, help me against them with seven [years] like the seven of Yusuf." Then Abu Sufyan came to him and said: "O Muhammad, your people have perished; so pray to Allah to remove it from them." So he prayed. Then he said: "You will return [to it] again." This was in Madinah, and it is supported by what is reported that this verse was revealed concerning "the Prophet ﷺ's seeking rain when a Bedouin asked him while he was delivering the Friday sermon."

In a narration, the one who spoke to him was Ka'b ibn Murrah. And in some narrations in the Sahih, the Prophet ﷺ said: "O Allah, upon Quraysh; O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar; O Allah, make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read (yunazzilu) with a fatha on the nun and tashdid on the zay. The rest read it with a sukun on the nun and a light zay.

The mention of the two attributes ﴿the Protector, the Praiseworthy﴾ rather than others is because they suit the giving of relief: the Protector (al-Wali) does good to those under His care, and the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid) gives what is worthy of praise. The attribute (Hamid) is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul.

Al-Mahdawi mentioned the explanation of (yanshuru rahmatahu) as the rising of the sun after the rain.

[Page 97]

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and of the living creatures He has scattered throughout them. And He is able to gather them whenever He wills.﴾

When the sending down of rain combined being a blessing with being a sign that points to the wondrous craftsmanship of God Most High and the immensity of His power, which requires that He alone be God, the discourse moved from mentioning it to mentioning other signs that point to God Most High's sole divinity. These are the sign of the creation of the great worlds and what is in them that is visible to people, without the intent of showing favor. This transition is an *istitrad* (digression) and an *i'tiraḍ* (interjection) between the topics of the context in which these verses appear.

*Al-Ayat* (the signs) is the plural of *ayah*, which means a sign or evidence of something. The context indicates that the intended meaning is the signs of divinity. *Al-Samawat* (the heavens) are the higher worlds that are not visible to us, the stars, and what lies beyond the earth of the atmosphere. *Al-Ard* (the earth) is the sphere on which animals and plants live. *Al-Bath* (scattering) is placing things in many places.

*Al-Dabbah* (living creature) is that which crawls on the earth, that is, walks, and so it includes birds, because a bird walks when it lands. It is among what is intended by His words here, *fihima* (in them), meaning in the earth and in the sky, that is, in part of what is called the sky, which is the atmosphere, the thing that appears to the observer like a blue dome over the earth during the day. God Most High said: ﴿Have they not considered the birds, held in the air of the sky?﴾ (al-Nahl: 79). So applying the term *dabbah* to birds is based on the fact that birds frequently walk on the earth to pick up grain and other things.

As for the beings in the high heavens, such as angels and spirits, the term *dabbah* is not applied to them. It is possible that in some of the heavens there are beings that crawl, since the stars are among the heavens. Scholars hesitate over affirming inhabitants of the stars, and some later scholars allowed that there are inhabitants on the planet Mars. God Most High said: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ (al-Nahl: 8). Moreover, the meaning of the expression *fihima* (in them) may be the locative sense of the whole rather than of each part, that is, what He has scattered in the totality of the earth and the sky of living creatures. The living creatures are only upon the earth. Since the earth and the heavens were mentioned together, and mention of living creatures came after them, the living creatures were made to be contained in them, because the earth is enclosed by the heavens and is, as it were, contained within them, like something contained within its container, and what is contained within a container is contained within the container of its container. This is as God Most High said: ﴿He released the two seas, meeting each other﴾ (al-Rahman: 19), then He said:

[Page 98]

﴿From them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ (al-Rahman: 22). The pearl and the coral emerge from only one of the two seas, which is the salt sea, not from the fresh sea.

The clause ﴿And He is able to gather them whenever He wills﴾ is an interjected clause within the interjection, for the purpose of *idmaj* (incorporation), that is, including the possibility of resurrection within the presentation of evidence for God's great power and His sole divinity.

The meaning is this: the One who is able to create the heavens and the earth and what is in them from non-existence is able to recreate some of what is in them for the resurrection and recompense, because all of that is equally within the scope of His power. So how can you consider it impossible?

The plural pronoun in His words *jam'ihim* (their gathering) refers to what He has scattered in them of living creatures, in view of the fact that those whose gathering for recompense the will is directed toward on the Day of Gathering are the rational among the living creatures, that is, humankind.

What is meant by *jam'ihim* (their gathering) is their assembly for recompense. God Most High said: ﴿The day He gathers you for the day of gathering﴾ (al-Taghabun: 9).

It is reported in authentic hadith that some living creatures will be gathered for retribution against those who wronged them. *Idha* (when) is a temporal particle referring to the future, and here it is stripped of the conditional sense. So the meaning is: "at the time He wills, in future time," and it is connected to *jam'ihim* (their gathering). This temporal particle is a second *idmaj*, to nullify their argument that the Day of Resurrection is delayed, so that it is supposed not to happen, as is reported of them in God Most High's words: ﴿They say, "When is it?" Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ (al-Isra': 51) ﴿They say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ (Saba': 29) ﴿Say, "For you is an appointed day from which you cannot delay an hour, nor can you advance it."﴾ (Saba': 30).

[Page 99]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 30 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much.﴾

When the favour of sending down rain after despair was followed by the statement that the people had been struck by a hardship of famine that had brought them to the point of despairing of rain, he followed this with a warning, alerting them to the fact that the misery that had struck them was a recompense for the polytheism (shirk) they had committed. This warning is meant to rouse them, and to rouse the community, to consider their own conduct with a view to seeking the pleasure of their Creator and taking account of themselves. So that they do not suppose that the recompense with which they were threatened is confined to the recompense in the Hereafter, but rather know that God may afflict them with what is a recompense for them in this world. Since what befell the Quraysh of famine and hunger was in response to the supplication of the Prophet ﷺ against them, as has already been mentioned, and since that supplication arose from the harm they inflicted on him, which he had no power to resist, it was inevitable that what befell them was a consequence of what their hands had earned.

Thus the sentence is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿And He it is who sends down the rain after they have despaired﴾ [Ash-Shura: 28]. The phrase "what their hands have earned" is used, by way of metaphor (majaz) with the relation of generality (ʿalaqat al-iṭlaq), to refer to the deeds and words that are condemned. That is, it refers to what proceeded from you of words of polytheism, of harm to the Prophet ﷺ, and of committing the abominations that arise from the religion of polytheism.

The address is initially to the polytheists, because they are the intended audience of the whole context of the verses, and they are the most in need of this admonition, since they did not believe in the threat of the Hereafter. It also includes the believers by way of analogy (qiyas), and by what indicates the inclusion of this ruling for them from sound reports and from other verses.

The particle "bi" (bāʾ) expresses causation (sababiyya), meaning that the cause of what befalls you of affliction is your deeds. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar recited ﴿bi-mā kasabat aydīkum﴾ with "mā" as a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and it is the subject (mubtadaʾ). The phrase ﴿bi-mā kasabat aydīkum﴾ is a fixed adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) which is the predicate (khabar) of the subject. Likewise it is written thus in the Codex (muṣḥaf) of Medina and the Codex of Syria. The rest recited ﴿fa-bi-mā kasabat aydīkum﴾ with a fāʾ before the bāʾ, and likewise it is written thus in the Codex of Basra and the Codex of Kufa, with "mā" understood as containing the meaning of a conditional (sharṭ), so that its predicate is joined with the fāʾ for that reason; or else it is a conditional particle and the fāʾ is the linking element for the answer of the condition. The verb of the condition is in the past tense to indicate certainty.

The "min" (min) is explanatory (bayāniyya) according to both readings, because of the vagueness contained in the relative pronoun and in the conditional particle.

The word "muṣība" (affliction) is a noun for an event that strikes with harm and something disliked. The feminine ending (tāʾ) has become attached to it to indicate the event, and so its adjectival sense has been forgotten and it has become a noun for a disliked event.

The recitation of the majority thus determines the meaning of general causation of their deeds in respect of the afflictions that befall them, because "mā" in this recitation is either a conditional particle, and the condition indicates causation, or it is a relative pronoun resembling a conditional particle. The relative form indicates an allusion to the cause of the predicate, and its resemblance to the conditional indicates causation.

The recitation of Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir does not determine causation but permits it, because the relative pronoun may be intended to refer to a specific individual by means of the description in its relative clause. It is therefore understood in a general sense by means of the context and by the support of the other recitation, since the basic principle regarding the difference among sound recitations is the unity of meanings.

Both recitations are equal in the possibility that the address is intended for a specific group, and in the possibility that it is intended for all people. Likewise, it is equal whether what is meant is specific afflictions that occurred in the past, or all afflictions that have occurred and will occur.

The meaning of the verse according to both interpretations indicates that among what befalls people of the afflictions of this world is that which is a recompense for them for their deeds, which God the Exalted does not approve, such as the affliction or afflictions that befell the polytheists because of their denial and their harm to the Messenger ﷺ.

Then, if "mā" is a conditional particle, its indication of the generality of its concept, which is explained by the explanatory "min", is more evident, because its past-tense condition can have the meaning of the future, as is common in conditionals formed with the past tense verb; and the conditional linkage makes it purely future. If "mā" is a relative pronoun, its indication is open to both generality and specificity, because the relative pronoun may be definite (for a known referent) and may be generic (for a class).

In any case, it indicates that among the afflictions that befall people in this world is that which God has imposed upon them as a recompense for the evil of their deeds. And if this is established with regard to specific people, it carries a warning and an admonition for others who do the same kind of deeds, that afflictions may befall them in this world as a recompense for their deeds, adding to the punishment they receive. However, this recompense is not invariable, for God may recompense a people for their deeds in this world together with the recompense of the Hereafter, and He may leave a people to the recompense of the Hereafter. So the recompense of the Hereafter, for good and for evil, is the invariable one promised, while the recompense in this world may or may not occur, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And He pardons much﴾, as we shall explain.

This meaning has been repeated in many verses and hadiths, both in general terms and in particular terms. Among what came in a general way is His saying the Exalted: ﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him﴾ [Al-Fajr: 15], ﴿so he says: my Lord has honoured me﴾ [Al-Fajr: 16], ﴿but when He tests him and restricts his provision﴾ [Al-Fajr: 16], ﴿so he says: my Lord has humiliated me﴾ [Al-Fajr: 16], ﴿No! Rather you do not honour the orphan﴾ [Al-Fajr: 17], ﴿and you do not urge one another to feed the poor﴾ [Al-Fajr: 18], ﴿and you devour inheritance, devouring greedily﴾ [Al-Fajr: 19], and the verse.

[Page 101]

His saying ﴿Rather you do not honour the orphan﴾ [Al-Fajr: 17] follows from His saying "No!" (kallā), which follows from His saying ﴿so he says: my Lord has honoured me﴾ [Al-Fajr: 15] and His saying ﴿so he says: my Lord has humiliated me﴾ [Al-Fajr: 16]. This indicates that honour and humiliation are caused only by not honouring the orphan and by not urging the feeding of the poor. And God the Exalted said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return﴾ [Ar-Rum: 41].

In the Sunan of al-Tirmidhi, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "No calamity, great or small, befalls a servant except because of a sin, and what God pardons is greater." He said this while looking to the interpretation of this verse. As for what came in a particular way, among it is His saying the Exalted, recounting Noah: ﴿So I said: ask forgiveness of your Lord, for He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10], ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Nuh: 11], ﴿and will aid you with wealth and sons﴾ [Nuh: 12], ﴿and will make for you gardens and make for you rivers﴾ [Nuh: 12]. And His saying, recounting him: ﴿Worship God, fear Him and obey me﴾ [Nuh: 3], ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and delay you until a specified term﴾ [Nuh: 4], in the Surah of Nuh. And His saying, addressing the Children of Israel: ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 85], the verse, in Surat al-Baqarah. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world; and thus We recompense the fabricators﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 152]. And He said, recounting Moses: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 155], ﴿And when your Lord declared that He would send against them until the Day of Resurrection those who would inflict on them the worst torment; indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾ [Al-Aʿraf: 167], in al-Aʿraf. And He said concerning Pharaoh: ﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first﴾ [An-Naziʿat: 25]. And He said concerning the hypocrites: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice? Then they do not repent, nor do they remember﴾ [At-Tawbah: 126], in "Bara'ah" (Surat at-Tawbah).

In the hadith of al-Tirmidhi the Prophet said: "Walking on foot to the congregations, perfecting ablution in difficult conditions, and waiting for one prayer after another prayer: whoever preserves these lives well and dies well." And in the chapter on punishments at the end of the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, a man is deprived of provision because of a sin that afflicts him."

In al-Bukhari: "Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: We believed in God and strove in His way, so our reward became due upon God. Among us are those who departed without taking anything of their reward, among them Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr, who died and left nothing but… When we covered his head with it, his feet appeared, and when we covered his feet, his head appeared. So the Messenger of God ﷺ commanded us to cover his head with it and to place on his feet some idhkhir (lemongrass)." And among them is one whose fruit was hastened for him, so he is picking it.

And if the affliction in this world is a recompense for doing evil, then likewise the good things of this world may be a recompense for doing good. God the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, the allies of God—there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾ [Yunus: 62], ﴿those who believed and were fearing God﴾ [Yunus: 63], ﴿for them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Yunus: 64]. And He said, recounting the brothers of Joseph: ﴿They said: By God, God has certainly preferred you over us, and we were indeed sinners﴾ [Yusuf: 91], meaning sinful, that is, while you were not a sinner. And He said: ﴿So God gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾ [Al ʿImran: 148], in Al ʿImran. And He said: ﴿And their father had been righteous, so your Lord intended that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [Al-Kahf: 82], in Surat al-Kahf. And He said: ﴿God has promised those who believe among you and do righteous deeds that He will surely make them successors upon the earth, as He made successors those before them﴾ [An-Nur: 55], to His saying: ﴿and He will surely replace their fear with security﴾ [An-Nur: 55], in Surat an-Nur.

All of this does not nullify the recompense in the Hereafter. As for those who deny this and say: recompense occurs only on the Day of Resurrection, by His saying the Exalted: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [Al-Fatihah: 4], that is, the Day of Recompense, and that this world is only a house of obligation (taklif) while the Hereafter is the house of recompense — the answer to their claim is that it is not the case that what befalls one of evil and good in this world is recompense for a deed in an invariable manner, nor is it necessarily so. For there are many causes for that, and many remedies repel it, or repel part of it. And God determines that, as merit and as repelling, but it is among what God increases the recompense by, if He wills.

Righteous people may be struck by calamities, misfortunes and pains, and these are then a trial and an increase in reward, and for reasons known only to God. And those who are excessive may be given good things and blessings as a respite and as a gradual leading toward punishment, and for other reasons that none can count except God, who is the most knowing of the hidden aspects of His creatures, their intentions, the measures of their deeds of good and evil, and the readiness of their souls and minds for the various sources of good and evil. God the Exalted said: ﴿And had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear. And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while being averse﴾ [Al-Anfal: 23].

Among what those of weak knowledge and shallow insight have become confused about is that the advocates of metempsychosis (tanāsukh, transmigration of souls) claimed that these afflictions for which we see no causes, and these good things that appear in places surrounded by the requirements of evil, are only because of the recompense of souls housed in the bodies that we observe, according to what they had suffered from the conditions that befell them in a previous state before they were placed in these bodies that we see. They were blind to the objection to this claim: why evil souls are placed in bodies made easy for righteous deeds, and the reverse. How wretched is what they fabricate!

As for His saying: ﴿and He pardons much﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 15], it is conjoined with the sentence ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and the pronoun in "He pardons" refers to what the pronoun in ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens﴾ [Ash-Shura: 29] referred to. This points to what appears to us as affliction not befalling some of those whose hands have earned crimes, and from the opposite of that, affliction befalling some of those who believed and did righteous deeds. This is a summary which is explained in general by the fact that what God knows of the conditions of His servants, and what of their good deeds outweighs their evil deeds, and what the wisdom of God requires of granting respite to some of His servants or of testing some of those brought near, are many degrees and varied states that conflict and cancel each other out. The one who is granted success searches for the causes, and if they escape him, he entrusts knowledge to God.

The meaning is: He, may He be exalted, pardons, that is, overlooks, so He does not afflict many of His servants who deserve the recompense of evil with worldly punishments, because He knows that this is more fitting for them. Thus what is intended here is pardon from being seized to account in this world, and it has no connection with the recompense of the Hereafter, for there are other proofs for that in the Book and the Sunnah.

"Kathir" (كَثِيرٍ) is an adjective qualifying an omitted noun; that is, "from creation" or "from people."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 31:

﴿And you cannot escape (Allah) on earth, and you have no protector or helper besides Allah.﴾

It is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30], and it is a precaution (iḥtirās), meaning: He pardons while having power over you, for you cannot overpower Him or defeat Him, but He pardons out of grace (tafaḍḍul).

The muʿjiz (the one who escapes, from iʿjāz, "to render powerless") is the one who overcomes another by slipping out of his grasp.

The meaning is: you are not escaping the power of Allah. The address is to the polytheists.

Page 104
The meaning is: Allah afflicted you with the calamity of drought, then He pardoned you by lifting the drought from you, and you cannot escape the power of Allah should He will to afflict you. This is from the sense of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return [to disbelief]﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Abu Sufyan when he prayed for the lifting of the drought from them: "You will return again," and they did return, so Allah struck them with the blow of Badr. [He said:] ﴿On the day We will strike the greatest assault; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [al-Dukhan: 16].

The restriction of the negation by His saying "on earth" is to intend generality, meaning: in any place on earth, lest they think that they are safe by settling in Makkah, which Allah the Exalted had made a sanctuary. That is because the Arabs, when they feared the force of a king or a great man, would dwell in difficult terrain, as al-Nabigha said, recounting his warning to his people about the watch of al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir over them, and advising them:

If you disobey me, I am not one who escapes from me the thieves, so the two sides of the Fire's Harra [are for you]

Or I shall place the house in a deaf, dark valley of wrongs, called "Umm Sabbar"

It repels people from us when we ride it, like a hobbled camel; the night traveler does not pass through it.

The predicate is brought as a nominal clause in His saying ﴿and you are not incapable [of escaping]﴾ to indicate the permanence and continuity of the predicate, meaning: the negation of their being able to escape is established and does not change; they are within the reach of their Creator.

Since His saying ﴿and you cannot escape on earth﴾ conveyed that they would have no refuge from the authority of Allah, by negating that they have a shelter to which they might resort to be helped and protected from the punishment of Allah, He said: ﴿and you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, meaning: you have no guardian who takes charge of you so as to shield you from the authority of Allah, nor a helper who supports you against Allah should He intend to afflict you, so that you might overcome Him. Thus the verse gathers the negation of what was customary among them of the means of protection.

"Min dūni Allāh" is a settled adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) serving as a second predicate concerning (walīyin wa naṣīrin), while the first predicate is "lakum." The fronting of the two predicates serves to emphasize the matter and to hasten their distress over it.

﴿And among His signs are the ships gliding through the sea like mountains.﴾ ﴿If He wills, He stills the winds, and they remain motionless upon its surface. Indeed, in that are signs for everyone who is patient and grateful.﴾ ﴿Or He may wreck them for what they have earned, and pardon much.﴾

When their being reminded was mentioned, namely that what befell them of calamity was caused by the commission of their deeds, and their being reminded of calamities coming at times and being lifted at other times, by His saying ﴿and pardons much﴾, and it was followed by the statement that in both states they are not outside the grip of divine power, this verse was brought, comprising an example of the striking of calamities and the appearance of their frightening signs, which remind them of what they overlook of God's power. These signs may bring what they were warned of, or may pass without harm. It is also a proof of the great power of God Most High, and that there is no escape from what He intends. It is further an incidental reminder of the blessing of sailing the sea and of the sea being made subservient to people, for that is a blessing. God Most High said: ﴿and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:164] in Surat al-Baqarah. So this sentence is a parenthetical insertion, like the sentence ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shura 42:29].

The "ayat" (signs) are the proofs that point to the truth.

"Al-jawari" is the plural of "jariyah," a qualifier of an elided noun indicated by the mention of the sea, i.e., the ships that run in the sea, as in God Most High's saying in Surat al-Haqqah: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose, We carried you in the running vessel﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:11]. He turned from "al-fulk" (the ship) to "al-jawar" as an indication of the locus of lesson, because the lesson lies in the subjugation of the sea for their running and in human reflection on their construction.

"Al-a'lam" is the plural of "'alam," which means mountain. The intended meaning of "al-jawari" here is the great ships that carry many people, and the lesson in them is more evident and the blessing in them is greater.

The word "al-jawar" is written in the Mushaf without a yā' after the rā', and it has many parallels in the Qur'an in both orthography and recitation. The readers differ regarding such cases, and these are what the scholars of the readings call "al-yā'at al-zawā'id" (the supernumerary yā's, i.e., the added yā' letters).

Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read "al-jawari" in this surah with the yā' retained in continuous recitation (wasl) and omitted in pause (waqf). Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read it with the yā' retained in both states. The rest read it with the yā' omitted in both states.

"Iskan al-riyah" (stilling of the winds) means the cessation of their blowing, for the wind is motion and agitation in the air; when that agitation becomes still, there is no wind.

Nafi' read "al-riyah" in the plural form, while the rest read "al-rih" in the singular form. In the reading of the majority there is an indication that the wind may be expressed in the singular form for a favourable wind. What has been said, that "al-riyah" is used for mercy and "al-rih" for punishment in the Qur'an, is a general tendency and not a fixed rule. It has been read in other verses, "al-riyah" and "al-rih," in contexts of mercy and not of punishment.

The majority read "yasha'" with a silent hamzah. Warsh, from Nafi', through the route of al-Isfahani, read it with an alif, as a lightening of the hamzah.

"Al-rawakid" is the plural of "rakidah," and "al-rukud" means stillness and steadfastness.

"Al-zahr" is the back of a human or animal, and it is used commonly for the upper surface of a thing. One says "zahr al-bayt," i.e., its roof. It has already occurred in God Most High's saying: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:189]. Its origin is a metaphor which became so common that it came close to being literal. Thus "zahr al-bahr" is the surface of its water visible to the observer, just as "zahr al-ard" is applied to what appears of it. God Most High said: ﴿He left not upon its back any creature﴾ [Fatir 35:45].

He made that a sign for everyone who is patient and grateful, because in both states there is fear and deliverance; fear calls to patience and deliverance calls to gratitude. The intended meaning is that in that there are signs for every believer who is characterised by the trait of patience in adversity and gratitude in ease, for he takes lesson from the conditions of the ships in the sea, a lesson accompanied by either patience or gratitude.

He made it a sign specifically for the believers because they are the ones who benefit from that sign, so they know that God is singular in divinity. The polytheists, by contrast, pass by it with their eyes and do not take lesson from it.

His saying ﴿or He may wreck them﴾ is a conjunction upon the answer (jaza') of the conditional.

"Yuwbiqhunna" means destroys them. "Al-iyba'" is destruction; its verb is "wabaqa," like "wa'ada." Here it means drowning. It is permissible for the feminine plural pronoun to refer to the ships ("al-jawar"), with "al-iyba'" used metaphorically for drowning, since drowning is destruction. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the passengers, by interpreting the pronoun as referring to groups, as indicated by His saying ﴿for what they have earned﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿and upon every lean camel they come from every deep mountain pass﴾ [al-Hajj 22:27], ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ [al-Hajj 22:28].

The "ba'" is causal, and it has the same meaning as His saying: ﴿And whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 42:30].

His saying ﴿and pardons much﴾ is a conjunction upon "yuwbiqhunna," so it carries the meaning of the answer of an implied conditional, i.e., "and if He wills, He pardons much, so He does not destroy them despite their deserving to be destroyed." This conjunction is a parenthetical insertion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 35:

﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape.﴾

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (wa-ya'lamu) with a *raf'* (nominative) vowel, treating it as a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes it). The rest read it with a *nasb* (accusative) vowel.

As for the resumptive reading of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub, its meaning is that it is a fresh statement with no connection to what came before. It is a threat to the polytheists that they have no escape from the punishment of God. When He said, ﴿And among His signs are the ships gliding in the sea﴾ [al-Shura: 32], the meaning became: and among the signs of His being alone in divinity are the ships gliding in the sea. The polytheists dispute the proofs of God's oneness by turning away and refusing to listen to them, so God threatened them by informing them that they have no escape, that is, from His punishment. He omitted the object of *al-mahis* (escape) to make it indefinite, magnifying the threat so that the mind would go in every possible direction. Thus His words ﴿and those who dispute will know﴾ are a report used to mean a command and a demand. It is in effect ﴿so that those who dispute may know﴾, or "Know, O you who dispute." It is not a report about them, because they do not believe in it until they know it.

As for the accusative reading, according to Sibawayh and the majority of grammarians it is coordinated (*'ataf*) with a verb that follows the *lam* of purpose, and *an* (that) is implied after it. The intended meaning is: ﴿so that He may take vengeance upon them and so that those who dispute...﴾ They called this *wāw* the *wāw al-sarf* (the wāw of diversion), because it diverts what follows from being coordinated with what precedes, to being coordinated with a verb derived from the speech. This is Sibawayh's view in the chapter on what is in the nominative between two jussive verbs and is in the jussive between them. Al-Zamakhshari followed him in *al-Kashshaf*. Al-Zajjaj held that the *wāw* is the *wāw al-ma'iyya* (the wāw of accompaniment), after which the imperfect verb is put in the subjunctive by an implied *an*.

It is also possible to take the report as used to mean the approach of what is reported, as in the saying "The prayer has been established (qad qamat al-salah)." Since their knowledge of it is about to occur, it is treated as though it had occurred, and so it is reported about them. On this reading it is a warning of a punishment that will befall them soon, namely the sword and captivity on the day of Badr.

The verb (ya'lamu) is mentioned to emphasize and draw attention to the report, as in God's words ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿And know that whatever you gain of anything﴾ [al-Anfal: 41] in Surat al-Anfal. It is also like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he saw Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari beating a boy of his, and called out: "Know, Abu Mas'ud, know, Abu Mas'ud." Abu Mas'ud said: "I turned around and it was the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he was saying: 'Know, Abu Mas'ud.' So I dropped the whip from my hand, and he said to me: 'God is more capable over you than you are over this boy.'" Related by Muslim at the end of the Book of Faith. The meaning of ﴿those who dispute concerning Our signs﴾ has already been explained in this surah.

*Ma* (what) is negative, and it suspends the verb (ya'lamu) from governing the two objects.

*Al-mahis* is a noun of place (*masdar mimi*) from *hasa*, meaning to take to fleeing and to swerve in one's course. In the hadith of Abu Sufyan describing the assembly of Heraclius, it says: "they scattered like the scattering of wild asses, and the doors were closed." The meaning is: they have no flight or escape from meeting God. The intended sense is that they have no refuge and no shelter. It was explained earlier in God's words ﴿and they will not find from it any escape﴾ [al-Nisa': 121] in Surat al-Nisa'.

[Page 108]

[p. 109]

﴿Whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of this worldly life; but what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri', a deduction that follows from what precedes) of the sentence ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel...﴾ (al-Shura: 27) to its end, for it implies the existence of one who is favoured and one who is deprived. So they were reminded that what they have been given of provision is a passing accident, and that the good lies in the reward which Allah has stored up for the believers. This also fits what precedes it, His saying ﴿and He pardons much﴾ (al-Shura: 34), in regard to people's safety from many of the terrors of sea voyages, for that safety is one of the blessings of this world. So it is followed by the reminder that this worldly blessing is a short-lived blessing, bound to vanish. Hence the one who is granted success should not make it the ultimate aim of his striving, but should strive for the works of the Hereafter, which bring the great and lasting bliss, namely the bliss which Allah has stored up with Him for His righteous believing servants.

The address in His saying "you have been given" (utitum) is to the polytheists, following the established pattern (nasaq) of the preceding address in His saying ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned﴾ (al-Shura: 30) and His saying ﴿You cannot escape in the earth, and you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾ (al-Shura: 31). The ruling extends to the believers by implication (lahn al-khitab, the implicit meaning of discourse), and it is possible that the address is to the whole community. The first fa' is for consequence, and (ma) is a relative pronoun which has taken the meaning of a conditional. The second fa' in His saying ﴿fa-mata'u al-hayat al-dunya﴾ enters on the predicate of the relative (ma), because it includes the meaning of a condition. We did not make (ma) a conditional because the meaning is one of predication (ikhbar), not of conditional linkage (ta'liq). It only includes the meaning of a condition, which is the mere necessary connection of the predicate with what the relative pronoun denotes, as its parallel was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned﴾ in the recitation other than that of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir.

The phrase "for those who believe" (lilladhina amanu) is related to "best and most lasting" by way of tanazu' (grammatical contention, where two governing words share one complement). The relative clause "those who believe" is followed by what indicates their acting upon their faith in their belief, so the statement that "they put their trust in their Lord alone, not in anyone else" is coordinated to the relative clause. This trust (tawakkul) is the singling out of Allah by turning to Him in everything beyond the power of the servant. Turning to other than Him in that matter contradicts monotheism (tawhid), since the polytheists place their trust in their gods more than in Allah.
