Because this completes the meaning of "those who believe", it is conjoined to the relative clause without a relative pronoun being repeated with it, unlike what came after it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 37:

Page 110
﴿And those who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm) and the indecencies (al-fawahish), and when they are angry, they forgive.﴾

He followed the preceding relative clause with relative clauses that are conjoined one to another, just as descriptive attributes are conjoined to a single described noun. Likewise is the conjunction of these clauses, and their relative pronouns refer to one and the same group of people, namely those who believe in God alone. A parallel to this has already been discussed under His words, exalted is He: "Those who believe in the unseen" (al-ghayb), and then His words: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], the verse, in Surat al-Baqarah.

The purpose of this is to give attention to the relative clauses, so the relative pronoun is repeated so that its clause receives special emphasis, to the extent that the one who holds these attributes, though he is one and the same, is treated as though he were several distinct persons. Thus the meaning is: "What is with God is better and more lasting for the believers who have these attributes," that is, those who make their faith follow from them. These are attributes of the believers according to the different circumstances that befall them, so they are overlapping attributes that may be gathered in a single believer when their causes exist, and may not be gathered when some of their causes do not exist, such as ﴿and whose affair is by mutual consultation among themselves﴾.

The majority of reciters read (kaba'ir) in the plural form. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (kabira) in the singular. So kaba'ir al-ithm are the great acts of the category of sin, which are the grave sins that the Law forbade with a firm prohibition and whose doer it threatened with the punishment of the Hereafter, such as slander, aggression and oppression. On the reading (kabira al-ithm), the meaning is the same as kaba'ir al-ithm, because the singular, when it is annexed to a noun defined by the definite article of genus, is an annexation of a described noun to the noun it describes, so it has the ruling of what it is annexed to.

Al-fawahish is the plural of fahisha, which is: an act described as abominable, against which the religion stressed the prohibition and threatened punishment, or for which it prescribed penalties in this world for the one among its doers who is exposed. Examples are killing a soul, fornication, theft, and brigandage. It was discussed earlier under His words: ﴿And when they commit an indecency, they say: "We found our fathers doing it"﴾ [al-A'raf: 28], in Surat al-A'raf.

The major sins and indecencies may be prompted by the appetitive force (al-quwwa al-shahiyya). And since many of the major sins and indecencies are caused by the irascible force (al-quwwa al-ghadabiyya), such as killing, wounding, insulting and beating,

Page 111
He followed the praise of those who avoid them by mentioning that forgiveness at the time of anger is among their dispositions, that is, restraining themselves from rushing forth under the impulse of anger, so that anger does not overcome their forbearance.

The word (idha), which implies the conditional and indicates that the condition is realized, is used, because anger is a psychological nature from which hardly anyone's soul is free, though to varying degrees. The clause ﴿and when they are angry, they forgive﴾ is conjoined to the clause of the relative.

He placed the subject before the verbal predicate in the clause "they forgive" to express emphasis.

Restricting the predicate by (idha), which conveys the meaning of a condition, indicates that forgiveness recurs whenever they become angry.

The purpose of this is the treatment of Muslims with one another, so that it is not contradicted by His later words: ﴿And those who, when wrong is inflicted upon them, defend themselves﴾, because that refers to their dealings with the enemies of their religion.

This is another relative clause and a further description. Its reference is among the deeds of those who believed, to which their faith calls them. Its primary intended referents are the Helpers (al-Anṣār), as narrated from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd. The meaning is that they are among the believers in whom the trait of consultation (shūrā) was firmly rooted.

As for "responding to their Lord" (al-istijābah li-Llāh), it applies to everyone who believed in God, because responding to God is responding to the call of the Prophet ﷺ. He called them to Islam as one conveying from God, so it is as though God called them to it, and they responded to His call. The sīn and tāʾ in "istajābū" (they responded) intensify the response, meaning that it is a response not mixed with aversion or hesitation.

The lām in "lahu" (to Him) is for emphasis. One says "istajāba lahu" just as one says "istajābahu." The apparent meaning is that a specific response is intended, namely the immediate response of such as Abū Bakr, Khadījah, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and the chiefs (nuqabāʾ) of the Anṣār, the companions of the Night of ʿAqabah (Laylat al-ʿAqabah).

[Page 112]

"And their affair is by consultation among them" (wa-amruhum shūrā baynahum) is coordinated with the relative clause. The Anṣār were known for this, since consultation in affairs was their custom. When a serious matter befell them, they gathered and consulted. Among the consultations for which God praised them was their consultation when their chiefs returned to them and informed them of the call of Muḥammad ﷺ after they themselves had believed in him on the Night of ʿAqabah. When the chiefs conveyed this to them, they gathered in the house of Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī, and their opinion unanimously settled on belief in him and support for him.

Since consultation led to right guidance and correctness, and since one of its finest fruits was that the Anṣār were guided to Islam through it, God praised consultation in an unrestricted way, without limiting it to the particular consultation the Anṣār held about faith. And what affair is greater than the affair of faith?

"Amr" (affair) is a general noun of the category of such words as "shayʾ" (thing) and "ḥādith" (event). The annexation of a generic noun may denote generality by the aid of context, meaning that all their affairs are subject to consultation among them.

Describing the affair as "shūrā" is an instance of describing something by a verbal noun for emphasis. The attribution is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), because consultation is attributed to those who consult, whereas "affair" is a metaphorical container for consultation. Do you not see that one says "they consulted about such-and-such," and God says: ﴿And consult them in the affair﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:159]? So the combination in His words "and their affair is consultation" involves a rational metaphor, a metaphorical substitution (istiʿārah tabaʿiyyah), and emphasis.

"Shūrā" is a verbal noun like "bushrā" and "futyā." It means that one who intends an action seeks from one whom he thinks possesses correct judgment and planning to advise him with what he sees as securing the desired benefit of his action. Its discussion has already preceded at His words: ﴿And consult them in the affair﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:159] in the Surah of Āl ʿImrān.

His words "baynahum" (among them) is a stable adverbial phrase functioning as an adjective to "shūrā." Consultation can only take place among those who consult, so this adverbial phrase is best understood as an indication that consultation should not extend beyond those concerned with the matter among the people of judgment. Thus, one who is not concerned with the matter does not enter it. It also indicates that consultation is a secret between those who consult. Bashshār said:

*"And do not make present at the consultation anyone who is not a keeper of secrets."*

Shaykh al-Islām Maḥmūd ibn al-Khūjah had, in a conversation between myself and him, pointed to considering this indication by a gesture of his hand when he recited this verse. I do not know whether that was an inference from him or something he received from some book or from some of his teachers. Both possibilities are not far-fetched for someone like him.

God praised them for "establishing the prayer" (iqāmat al-ṣalāh). This may be an honoring of the prayer's station among the deeds of faith. It may also be that a specific establishment is intended. If the verse was revealed about the Anṣār, or if the Anṣār were its primary intended referents, then perhaps what is meant is the Anṣār's prompt establishment of congregational prayer after their conversion, when they asked the Prophet ﷺ to send someone to teach them the Qur'an and lead them in prayer. He sent Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr to them, and that was before the Hijrah (the migration).

He also praised them for spending from what God had provided them. The Anṣār had the largest share of this praise, and it is like His words about them: ﴿They prefer others over themselves, even though they themselves are in need﴾ [al-Ḥashr 59:9]. That is because the Anṣār were people of wealth and work. When they believed, they were the first group of believers who had wealth with which they could aid the weak among the believers, both from among themselves and from among the earliest emigrants before the Prophet's Hijrah. As for the believers of Mecca, the polytheists had confiscated their property because of their faith. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Has ʿAqīl left us any house?"

His words: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ are an insertion of a favor-reminder within the praise. Otherwise, spending is not from anything other than what the spender is provided.

﴿Those who, when wrongful aggression (al-baghy) befalls them, defend themselves.﴾ This is the fourth relative clause (mawsul), and its predicate is a disposition (khuluq) that God willed for the Muslims. The first share of it belongs to the believers who were in Makkah before they emigrated, for the aggression of the polytheists befell them in various forms of harm: insult, belittlement, confiscation of property, and torture of their persons. They endured patiently against it.

Al-baghy means transgression against what is right. Its befalling them means that it was imposed upon them, that is, others committed aggression against them. This verse introduces His words in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged, and indeed God is able to give them victory﴾ [al-Hajj: 39] ﴿who have been expelled from their homes without right﴾ [al-Hajj: 40]. Surat al-Hajj was revealed in Madinah.

God praised them for defending themselves to draw attention to the fact that this defense arises in response to the aggression that befell them. Thus each of the cause and the effect merits praise, because defending oneself is a religious virtue, since it serves to repel the aggression directed at them because they are believers. Defending themselves deters the aggressors from pressing further into transgression against their like, and that deterrence helps the spread of Islam, since it cuts off what would otherwise stir in the souls of those who desire Islam the anxieties of fearing that they will be oppressed.

From this you know that there is no contradiction between his words here, ﴿those who, when wrongful aggression befalls them, defend themselves﴾, and his words earlier, ﴿and when they are angered, they forgive﴾, because the two situations differ, as you have learned above.

From Ibrahim al-Nakha'i: The believers used to dislike being humiliated, and whenever they were able [to retaliate], they pardoned.

By his words ﴿they defend themselves﴾ he used the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl, the pronoun that separates the relative clause from its predicate), which separates the relative pronoun from its predicate, to convey the strengthening of the predicate, that is, they should not hesitate to defend themselves.

The verbal predicate was chosen here rather than saying munTaSirun (defending themselves as a participle), to convey the meaning that the defense renews itself whenever aggression befalls them.

As for the verb coming in the present tense (al-mudari'), it is because the present tense is the form with which the separating pronoun comes.

Page 114

[p. 115]

These are three parenthetical clauses, one after another, placed between the clause ﴿And those who, when wrongful oppression afflicts them﴾ (Q. 42:39) and so on, and the clause ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾ (Q. 42:41). The purpose of this parenthetical insertion is to delimit the scope of self-defence (intisar) and to encourage pardon (al-'afw), and then to condemn wrongdoing and aggression. This is a shift from the permission to defend oneself against enemies of the religion to specifying how it is carried out among the community. The evidence for this is that the clause ﴿So whoever pardons and makes amends﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of the clause ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. Abandoning self-defence is called pardon and reconciliation, and there is no pardon or reconciliation with the people of polytheism.

The evidence also includes the promise of a reward from God for that pardon, whereas with the people of polytheism there is no reward for reconciliation.

[p. 115 continues]

The word ﴿sayyi'ah﴾ (evil) is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning an act that harms the one who is treated with it. Its morphological pattern is fay'alah, an intensive form of the adjective, like hayyinah (easy). Its middle radical is a yā' and its final radical is a hamzah, because it derives from sā'a (to harm). When the pattern fay'alah was formed from it, two yā's came together and were assimilated (idgham). That is, the one who requites repays the one who did to him an act that harms him with a harmful act like his act in harm. The word ﴿sayyi'ah﴾ here does not mean the disobedience that God does not approve of, so there is no difficulty in applying the term ﴿sayyi'ah﴾ to the harm inflicted on the wrongdoer.

The meaning of ﴿mithluha﴾ (like it) is that it is equal in measure according to what people customarily recognise. Equivalence may be in the aim and the form, and this is complete equivalence, which is the true meaning of equivalence, such as retaliation (qisas) against a killer who killed unjustly, by the same means with which he killed, and against an aggressor who inflicted a deliberate wound. Complete equivalence may be impossible, and then one resorts to similarity in the aim, that is, the amount of harm. This is approximation. An example is the impossibility of complete similarity in the requital of wars with an enemy of the religion, since harm may fall on persons who did not harm anyone, while persons who did inflict harm on people are spared. So equivalence in war is the revenge of one group on another group to the extent that it satisfies the souls of the victors, as people have agreed upon.

From this also is the destruction of some of the senses by a blow to the head or the eye. Recourse is then made to the blood money (diyah), because the injury to the aggressor's sense cannot be precisely matched with the same injury he inflicted on the one he attacked. Likewise, giving the values of destroyed property consisting of valued goods, since it is difficult to require the offender to give the same thing he destroyed.

Among the problems of equivalence in punishment is the matter of a group who conspire to kill one person deliberately, or to cut off one of his limbs. If retaliation is taken against only one of them, this means the remaining offenders escape the punishment for their crime. If retaliation is taken against each one of them, this is an increase in punishment, because they only wronged one person.

Some scholars did not count that increase and considered that each one of them had wronged the victim, so each deserves requital with the like of what he inflicted on the victim. They treated the plurality as void, and considered the prevention of the means (sadd al-dhari'ah) by which a criminal might contrive to escape his crime by adding a group to himself. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, taking as evidence the judgement of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and his statement: "If the people of Sana'a combined to kill him, I would take retaliation against all of them."

[p. 116]

Others departed from the plurality altogether, and this is the view of Dawud al-Zahiri. Others departed from that plurality in cases of cutting off a limb but did not depart from it in cases of killing. Perhaps this is because 'Umar ibn al-Khattab decided it in the case of killing, and nothing is transmitted from anyone regarding cutting off a limb. Some have at times dropped the plurality when the means of proving the crime is weak, such as the oath of the kinsmen (qasamah) together with a preliminary indication (lawth), according to those who see retaliation by it. Malik did not consider that more than one man may be killed on the basis of the qasamah.

Know that equivalence in such matters is achieved through the value of the compensation, as it is taken into account in blood money (diyat) and compensation for injuries (arsh al-jina'at).

The clause ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾ is in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for an omitted statement indicated by the context, so it is understood as: "Indeed He loves those who pardon," as He said: ﴿And those who pardon people, and God loves the good-doers﴾ (Q. 3:134). His support against the wrongdoer is entrusted to God, and He does not love the wrongdoers. That is, He rewards those who pardon and gives them victory over the transgressors, because He does not love the wrongdoers and so He does not leave the wrongdoer unpunished. And ﴿whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir an authority, so let him not exceed in killing; indeed he is supported﴾ (Q. 17:33). The love of God for those who pardon has been deduced from His saying: ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. On this view, the referent of "the wrongdoers" is those who inflicted wrongful aggression on the believers.

It is also permissible that the reason given by His saying ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾ refers to the implication of the clause ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, that is, without exceeding equivalence in the requital, as in His saying: ﴿And if you punish, punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ (Q. 16:126). Then the referent of "the wrongdoers" is those among the believers who exceed the limit in punishment. This is a warning against exceeding the limit, like the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever grazes around the sanctuary will soon fall into it."

With its parenthetical position, this verse has comprised the principles of guidance concerning what is in self-defence against the wrongdoer and what is in pardoning him of the good for the community. In granting the wronged person the right to defend himself against his wrongdoer there is a deterrent to wrongdoers against committing injustice, out of fear that the wronged person will take his right. So the aggressor takes this into account when he is tempted to transgress.

In encouraging the wronged person to pardon his wrongdoer there is the preservation of the bond of Islamic brotherhood between the wronged person and his wrongdoer, so that it is not broken in its individual details but rather grows stronger through pardon, as the Exalted said:

[p. 117]

﴿Repel with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a close friend﴾ (Q. 41:34).

Yet God, the Exalted, did not neglect the side of deterring the wrongdoer, so He informed that he is in a position of the wrath of God against him, when He said: ﴿Indeed He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. What is contained in this of the terror of threat is not limited.

From the meaning of this verse arises a notable question, over which the early scholars contended in their consideration: the wronged person's absolution (tahlil) of his wrongdoer from his wrong. Abu Bakr ibn al-Mu'arri said in al-Ahkam: Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb transmitted from Malik, when he was asked about the statement of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, "I do not absolve anyone," that he said: "That differs." I said: "A man lends to another man and he dies, leaving no means of repayment." He said: "I think he should absolve him, and this is better in my view, because of God's saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ (Q. 39:18). If there is an excess to be followed." It was said to him: "A man wrongs another man." He said: "I do not think that, and it is contrary in my view to the first, because of God's saying: ﴿The way is only against those who wrong people﴾ (Q. 42:42), and He says: ﴿There is no way against the good-doers﴾ (Q. 9:91). So I do not think you should make him lawful for his wrong."

Ibn al-'Arabi said: So there are three opinions on the question. First: he does not absolve him in any case, said by Ibn al-Musayyib. Second: he absolves him, said by Ibn Sirin; al-Qurtubi added Sulayman ibn Yasar. Third: if it is property, he absolves him, and if it is wrongful oppression, he does not absolve him, and this is the view of Malik.

The reasoning of the first: that he should not make lawful what God has prohibited, which would amount to altering God's ruling.

The reasoning of the second: that it is his right, so he may waive it.

The reasoning of the third: that when a man has overpowered your right, it is kind to him to absolve him, but if he is a wrongdoer, it is right that you do not leave him, lest the oppressors be emboldened and continue in their vile actions.

He mentioned the hadith of Muslim from 'Ubadah ibn al-Walid ibn 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "My father and I set out in search of knowledge among this tribe of the Ansar before they perished. The first person we met was Abu al-Yusr, companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). My father said to him: 'I see in your face a trace of anger.' He said: 'Yes. I had a debt owed to so-and-so. I went to his family and said: "Is he here?" They said: "No." His son came out, and I said to him: "Where is your father?" He said: "He heard your voice and entered my mother's alcove." I said: "Come out to me," and he came out. I said: "What made you hide from me?" He said: "By God, I feared that I would tell you and lie to you, and you are a companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." By God, I was insolvent." He said: He brought his document and erased it with his hand, and said: "If you find the means to pay, then pay; otherwise you are absolved."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 42, verse 41:**

﴿And whoever defends himself after he has been wronged, those—there is no path [of blame] against them.﴾ It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shūrā: 40], in which case it is an excuse for those who did not pardon. It is also permissible that it be a conjunction with the clause ﴿they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shūrā: 39], and what lies between them is an interjection (iʿtirāḍ), as you know. The clause is then either connected to the purpose of a Muslim defending himself against his oppressor from among the Muslims, as a completion of the clause ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shūrā: 40]; or it is connected to the purpose of believers defending themselves against the aggression of the polytheists against them. This defence may be collective, which is war, and then this serves as a preparation (tamhīd) for the permission to fight that was legislated afterwards; or it may be the defence of individuals, if they were able to do so. The Muslims in Mecca on that day had become a people of strength, able to defend themselves individually, as was said regarding the honour of Islam upon the conversion of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

The lām in ﴿And whoever defends himself﴾ is a lām of preparation for an oath (lām al-tawṭiʾa li-l-qasam), and (man) is conditional; or the lām is the lām of initiation (lām al-ibtidāʾ) and (man) is a relative pronoun. The construction of (ẓulmihi) is an idāfa of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: after being wronged.

The meaning of (baʿda ẓulmihi) is an alert that this defence occurs after it has become certain that they were wronged. As for matters other than war: whoever anticipates that someone will attack him does not have the right to strike that person with harm before the latter begins the aggression, saying, "I thought he was going to attack me, so I struck him with harm to protect myself from his expected aggression." This is because such conduct stirs up disorder and corruption. Thus God alerted the Muslims to avoid it with their enemy, unless there is already war between them.

As for the situation of Muslims with one another, it is not within the purpose of the verse. Whoever is attacked by another with an initial act of transgression is permitted to repel him from carrying out his aggression before he can accomplish it, and he should not delay until the harm is inflicted, which may not be remediable by its perpetrator afterwards. This falls under the principle that what is near to a thing is given the ruling of its occurrence, that is, when the strong probability is established by the appearance of its precursors. This is what the jurists stated: "It is permissible to repel an aggressor (ṣāʾil) by any means possible."

The locus of this concession is the cases in which the harm is anticipated to occur in a way that is difficult or hard to remove or remedy. It is known that its locus is the situation in which the act of transgression has not yet been completed. If, however, it has been completed, then the right to retribution for it belongs to referring the matter to the judge, and the wronged person does not take redress into his own hands. This is not among what this verse includes, but it is derived from the various provisions and objectives of the Sharia. We have assumed it here merely to clarify the purpose of the verse, not to explain its meaning.

By (al-sabīl) is meant that which warrants being held to account: blame among the tribes, reproach for aggression, and consequence in the Hereafter for corruption on earth through killing peaceful people. This was called a "path" (sabīl) by way of metaphor (istiʿāra), because it resembles a road in conveying one to the goal, and this usage became so common that it came to equal the literal meaning.

The fāʾ in His words ﴿then those—there is no path [of blame] against them﴾ is the fāʾ of the response to the condition (fāʾ jawāb al-sharṭ). If you take the lām in ﴿to whom He wills﴾ [al-Shūrā: 49] as the lām of initiation, then it is clear. If you take the lām as the lām of preparation for an oath, then the joining of what follows it with the fāʾ of the response is a preference of the condition over the oath when both are combined. The more familiar practice is to give precedence to the first of the two, so that it receives its response, and the response of the second is omitted. It may be said that this applies to an explicit oath, not to an oath implied by the lām of preparation.

The demonstrative (ism al-ishāra) is used at the beginning of the response to the condition in order to distinguish the group mentioned as completely as possible, and to alert to the fact that the reason they are not held accountable is that they defended themselves after being wronged, and did not initiate transgression against people.

[p. 119]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 42:

Page 120
﴿Indeed, the blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. For those there is a painful punishment.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), for when the entire preceding discourse was about permitting those who were oppressed to defend themselves against those who oppressed them, and then it was followed by the statement that those (who defend themselves) have no blame upon them (﴿fa-ulaika ma 'alayhim min sabil﴾, 42:41), this raised the question of a questioner about the party upon whom the negated "sabil" (way/blame/liability) falls.

The restriction conveyed by (innama) ("only") is an emphasis of the content of the sentence ﴿fa-ulaika ma 'alayhim min sabil﴾ [al-Shura: 41]. For the meaning of restriction could have been conveyed by juxtaposing the negation of blame from those who defended themselves after being wronged with the affirmation that the blame lies upon the wrongdoers, since affirming something of one party and negating it of others conveys the meaning of restriction, and this is the basic way of conveying restriction by means of equality or elaboration, like the verse of al-Samaw'al or another:

"Our souls flow along the edges of the swords, and upon other than the swords they do not flow."

As for the well-known methods of restriction in the science of ma'ani (rhetoric), they are concise. So when the restrictive particle is used here, the negation of blame from others is obtained once more through the content of the restriction, thereby reinforcing the first attainment that was achieved by the negation. Its parallel is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawba: 91] up to His saying: ﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your leave while they are rich﴾ [al-Tawba: 93], in the surah "Bara'a."

The intended meaning of "sabil" is the same as its meaning in His saying: ﴿fa-ulaika ma 'alayhim min sabil﴾ [al-Shura: 41], as indicated by the fact that it is repeated in its definite form with the article (al-) after having been mentioned in indefinite form, for repeating an indefinite noun in the definite form with the article indicates that what is meant is what was mentioned first. This "sabil" is the recompense and the consequence in this world and the Hereafter.

The generality of "those who wrong" and the generality of "people" include every wrongdoer, and his recompense corresponds to the measure of his wronging. Included primarily are the wrongdoers being spoken of, namely the polytheists of Makkah, and the people being spoken of, namely the Muslims of that time.

Page 121
Transgression upon the earth (al-baghy fi al-ard) is encroaching upon what God has established on the earth of right, which encompasses the benefits of the earth that were created for people, such as the restricting (of crops and livestock) mentioned in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "These are livestock and tilled land forbidden; none may eat of them except whom we wish," by their claim﴾ [al-An'am: 138], and like the designating of the sa'iba (freed camel) and the cutting of the ear of the bahira (the she-camel). It also encompasses violating what God has laid down in the natural disposition of mankind of upright conditions, such as justice and good companionship. Thus transgressing against these by such things as arrogance, haughtiness, belittling believing people, and expelling them from the gatherings of the people is baghy upon the earth without right.

"Al-ard" (the earth) means the land of Makkah, or the whole terrestrial globe, and the latter is more fitting to the general application of the verse, as the Exalted said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein﴾ [al-Baqara: 205], and He said: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. So every corruption and wronging that occurs in a part of the earth is baghy contained within the earth.

"Bi-ghayr al-haqq" (without right) is connected to (yabghuna) and it is for revealing the state of the baghy, to convey its blameworthiness, since baghy occurs only without right. The designation of baghy is encroachment upon what is right, whereas encroachment upon the wrongdoer on account of his wrongdoing is not called baghy but is called i'tida' (aggression). The Exalted said: ﴿So whoever aggresses against you, then aggress against him in the same manner as he aggressed against you﴾ [al-Baqara: 194]. And it is said: "Fulan asked the judge for redress against his opponent (ista'da)," meaning he requested from him a judgment against him.

The sentence ﴿For those there is a painful punishment﴾ is an explanation of the sentence ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong﴾ if by "sabil" in His saying ﴿ma 'alayhim min sabil﴾ [al-Shura: 41] is meant the way of punishment in the Hereafter; or it is a badal ishtimal (inclusive substitute) of it if by "sabil" there is meant what includes blame in this world, i.e., the sabil upon them is that for them is a painful punishment as recompense for their wronging and transgression.

The ruling of this verse includes the wronging of the polytheists against the Muslims and includes the wronging of Muslims against one another, so that its content harmonizes with all that preceded.

The demonstrative noun (uli'ka) was brought to draw attention to the fact that they deserve what is mentioned after the demonstrative because of what was mentioned before it, while distinguishing them most completely by this threat.

[Page 122]

﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring resolve.﴾

This is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical coordination) with the clause ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged, those — there is no blame upon them﴾ [al-Shura: 41]. The position of this clause is that of an interposed parenthetical (*i'tiraD*, grammatical interjection) between the clause ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾ [al-Shura: 42] and the clause ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾ [al-Shura: 44].

This clause indicates the excellence of the believers who bore harm from the polytheists and endured it, and did not hold accountable those among those who harmed them who later believed, such as the sister of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab before his Islam, and such as his brother-in-law Sa'id ibn Zayd. He said: "I indeed saw myself, and 'Umar was holding me fast in (the matter of) Islam before 'Umar embraced Islam." So there was good in the patience of Sa'id, by which 'Umar entered Islam. And the excellence of the believers is that they are patient toward the wrongdoing of their brothers and forgive them, so they do not take retribution from them and do not seek help against them, in the manner already mentioned in the matter of mutual release (*tahallul*) at His words: ﴿So whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The *lam* that enters upon (*man*) is the *lam* of commencement (*lam al-ibtida'*), and (*man*) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*). The clause ﴿indeed that is of the matters requiring resolve﴾ is the predicate of the relative (*man*). The *lam* in ﴿of the matters requiring resolve﴾ is the *lam* of commencement, which enters upon the predicate of (*inna*), and it is among the *lams* of commencement.

This predicate contains four emphasizers: the *lam*, (*inna*), the *lam* of commencement, and the description by the verbal noun in His words ﴿of resolve (*'azm*) of matters﴾, to draw attention to its content. And (*dhalika*, "that") was added to draw attention through the demonstrative in His words (*inna dhalika*), so there are five points of emphasis in it.

*Al-'azm* (resolve): fixing the intention upon an action and persisting in it. Describing things with *al-'azm* indicates praise of what is described, because the nature of virtues is that their practice is difficult for the souls, since they run against desires. For this reason the most excellent of the messengers were described as "those of firm resolve" (*ulu al-'azm*).

*Al-umur* (matters) is the plural of *amr*. It is meant here as: qualities and attributes. The annexation of *'azm* to *al-umur* is an annexation of an attribute to what it describes, i.e., "of the matters that are resolute."

The description of *al-umur* by *al-'azm* is a description by a verbal noun, for the sake of intensifying the realization of the meaning in them,

[Page 123]

and it is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle, i.e., "matters that are resolute, whose people are resolute," a metonymy of the intellect (*majaz 'aqli*).

The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to the patience and forgiveness, derived from *sabara* and *ghafara*, and they bear the pronoun of (*man*). So the formation of the verbal noun is fitting with the pronoun that accompanies it. The implied sense is: "indeed his patience and his forgiveness are of the matters requiring resolve."

This is an exhortation to pardon and to patience over harm. Its being so among the Islamic community is evident. As for dealings with unbelievers, circumstances vary in them, and the rulings on forgiveness differ accordingly. Its criterion is that the benefit should preponderate, either in pardon or in taking to account.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 44:

﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾ After having related various kinds of the disbelief, obstinacy and denial of the polytheists, and having reminded them of the signs that indicate Allah's sole divinity and the blessings contained within them, and having warned them against being deceived by the fleeting enjoyment of this world, He followed this with His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾, which is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾ [al-Shura: 42].

The meaning is: in what you have heard there is guidance for whoever Allah wills to be guided, whereas for whomever Allah has decreed misguidance, there is no protector other than Allah who could guide him or rescue him. What is intended is the negation of a protector who would set him right and guide him, like His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided; and whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for him any guiding protector﴾ [al-Kahf: 17]. Thus what is intended here is the beginning of a specific meaning of wilaya (protection/guardianship).

Allah's leading a person astray (idlal) means His creating him unready for guidance, or unable to accept it, and withholding from him the tawfiq (divine enabling) by which He would otherwise rectify him each time he sinks deeper into error. So his misguidance is from Allah's creation and Allah's decree concerning him. Allah has called people to guidance through His messengers and His laws. He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [Yunus: 25], meaning He calls every person of understanding, and guides some of those He has called.

"Man" (man) is a conditional particle, and the fa' in ﴿fa-ma lahu min waliyyin﴾ is the connective particle of the response. The negation of a protector

صفحة ١٢٤
is a kinaya (allusive metonymy) for the negation of the means of salvation from error and of the consequences of punishment for it, because a protector's characteristic is benefiting his charge by guidance and rescue. The negation of a protector therefore implies by necessity a need for his charge's benefit, and that entails that his master is in hardship and torment, as indicated by His saying after it: ﴿And you see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment﴾, etc. This is an allusive kinaya, and the explicit form of this meaning appears in His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ [al-Zumar: 23] in Surat al-Zumar, and His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way﴾ [al-Shura: 46], which comes later in this surah.

The pronoun in (ba'dihi) refers to the Name of Majesty (Allah), meaning "after Allah," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So who will guide him after Allah? Will you not then take heed?﴾ [al-Jathiya: 23] in Surat al-Jathiya.

The meaning of (ba'd) here is the meaning of (dun) or (ghayr), the word (ba'da) being borrowed for the meaning of (dun), because (ba'd) is originally used for one who substitutes an absent person in his place or in his work. He likened Allah's leaving the one who is astray in his misguidance to the absence of a protector who abandons his charge without any executor or agent for him. It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-A'raf: 185] in Surat al-A'raf, and His saying: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ [Yunus: 32] in Surat Yunus.

The (min) is superfluous, for emphasis. Among the places where it is added is before non-declinable adverbs of place and time; al-Hariri said: "(ma) is in the accusative as an adverb, and nothing but a particle can put it in the genitive."

* * *

﴿And you see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying: "Is there any way of return?"﴾ This is conjoined to the clause ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾. It is an elaboration and explanation of what was stated in summary in the two verses it is conjoined to, namely His saying: ﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no escape﴾ [al-Shura: 35] and His saying: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾.

The meaning is: they will find neither an escape nor a protector, so they will find only regret over what has passed, and they will say: ﴿Is there any way of return?﴾

صفحة ١٢٥
The interrogation with the particle (hal) is denunciatory, meaning negation, and therefore the superfluous (min) was introduced before (sabil), because it is an indefinite noun in a negative context.

Al-marad is a mimi verbal noun from "radd" (to return), and what is meant by "radd" is return; one says "radda-hu" when one makes him return.

It is also possible that (marad) means repelling, i.e., "Is there any way to repel the punishment from us that is appearing to us, so that we do not fall into it?" It then has the meaning of ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord will surely befall, none can avert it﴾ [al-Tur: 7] in Surat al-Tur.

The address in (tara) is to an unspecified addressee, meaning their state has reached such a degree of manifestness that it is not restricted to any particular addressee; or the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, as consolation for what he encountered from them of denial.

The intent is to inform first of their state, and then to express wonder at it. Thus it was not said "And the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, say," but rather "And you see the wrongdoers" was said for the sake of taking warning from their condition.

The coming of the verb "ra'aw al-'adhab" in the past form serves to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence; the past tense is thus used metaphorically for the future, likening the future to the past in certainty, and the indicator is the verb (tara), which is in the future form; since the sight mentioned is not yet occurring in the present, it is as if it were said: "when they see the punishment."

The clause (yaqulun) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the wrongdoers; that is, you see them saying so, so the seeing is restricted to the state of their saying that, meaning in the state of the seer's hearing their saying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 45:

﴿And you will see them exposed to it, humbled from abasement, looking with a furtive glance.﴾ The verb (tara, "you see") is repeated for emphasis on this sight and to convey its awe, just as the verb (tula'u, "you meet") is repeated in the words of Dawwak ibn Thumayl al-Mazini:

Gently, O Banu Shayban, a little of your threats.
You will meet my horses tomorrow at Sifwan.

You will meet steeds that do not swerve from the battle
when they appear in the crowded, narrow pass.

[Page 126]

Al-'Ard (exposure) originally means displaying a thing and showing it to others. This is why the Arabs said, "I presented the camel to the watering trough" ('aradtu al-ba'ir 'ala al-hawd). Scholars of language and of rhetoric (ulama' al-lugha wa-ulama' al-ma'ani) count this among the inversions (al-qalb) in the construction. From it branch many closely related usages, which are subtle and need careful examination.

Among its usages are the phrases: "the review of the troops before the commander" (ard al-jund 'ala al-amir) and "the presentation of the captives before the commander" (ard al-usara 'ala al-amir). This means having them pass before him so that he may see his opinion regarding their condition and how to treat them. Here the word is used in a metaphorical sense (isti'arah). The word (yu'radun, "they are exposed") is borrowed to mean: they pass by it (the Fire) in a manner whose outcome is that they are brought under its control and judged. It is as though, when they are exposed to Hell, it passes judgment on them with the burning that God has prepared for them. This is explained by His saying in surah al-Ahqaf: ﴿And on the Day the disbelievers are exposed to the Fire: "You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 20].

A different usage of it has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], in surah al-Baqarah.

The verb (yu'radun) is in the passive because the intended meaning is that the act occurs, not the identity of its doer. Those who expose the disbelievers to the Fire are the angels, as other verses indicate.

The pronoun in (alayha, "to it") refers to the punishment, interpreted as the Fire, or to Hell (jahannam), or refers to Hell as understood from the context.

(Khashi'in, "humbled") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun of the third person in (tarahum, "you see them"), since it is a visual sight.

Khushu' (humility) means lowering oneself and the effect of the soul being broken, through submission and abjectness. It may arise from fear, from awe, from obedience, or from inability to resist.

Khushu' is like khudu' (submission), except that khudu' is only ascribed to the body, so one says: "So-and-so submitted" (khada'a fulan), and one does not say: "his gaze submitted" (khada'a basaruhu) except metaphorically, as in His saying: ﴿So do not be soft in speech﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32]. As for khushu', it is ascribed to the body, as in His saying: ﴿humbly before God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199] at the end of surah Al 'Imran. It is also ascribed to some parts of the body, as in His saying: ﴿their eyes humbled﴾ [al-Qamar: 7] in surah al-Qamar, and His saying: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108] in surah Ta-Ha.

What is meant by khushu' in this verse is the visible effect of abasement and fear upon them.

[Page 127]

So His saying: (min al-dhull, "from abasement") is connected to (khashi'in, "humbled"). Its connection to it dispenses with connecting it to (yanzurun, "they look"), and it conveys what its connection to the latter would not convey.

The (min, "from") here expresses cause (lil-ta'lil), meaning: humbled with a humility arising from abasement. That is, their humility is not for the glorification of God and their acknowledgment of His lordship, because that belief was not part of their character in the world.

The clause (yanzurun min tarfin khafiyy, "they look with a furtive glance") is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in (khashi'in), because looking with a furtive glance is a state of the humbled, abased person. The purpose of mentioning it is to depict their dreadful condition.

Close to this meaning is the statement of al-Nabigha, describing captives:

They look sidelong at whoever comes from the side,
with faces that deny slavery, though they are free.

And the statement of Jarir:

So lower your gaze, for you are from Numayr,
you have reached neither Ka'b nor Kilab.

(Al-tarf, "glance," originally is a verbal noun meaning the movement of the eyelid. One says: "tarafa" (he blinked), i.e., he moved his eyelid. It may also be applied to the eye itself, by naming a thing after its act. For this reason it is not made dual or plural. God said: ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾. Its description in this verse as (khafiyy, "furtive") indicates that the movement of the eye is meant, i.e., they look with a hidden look, that is, a look without sharpness. It is like stealing a glance, and this is due to the terror of what they see of the punishment. They shrink from witnessing it because of the fright that afflicts them from it, and what is in a human of love for knowing and seeing drives them to look toward what they are being driven to, like the condition of the fleeing, frightened one from one who pursues him. You see him running hard and looking back from time to time to see whether the one chasing him has come closer, and in that glance he loses steps of his running, yet his love of seeing overcomes him.)

The (min, "from") in His saying (min tarfin khafiyy) is for metaphorical origin (li-l-ibtida' al-majazi). The meaning: they look with a look originating from the hidden movement of the eyelid.

The object of (yanzurun, "they look") is omitted for generality, i.e., they look at the punishment, they look at the terrors of the Gathering, and they look at the bliss of the believers, with a furtive glance.

* * *

﴿And those who believed will say: "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment."﴾

It is more likely that the (waw) here is for a circumstantial clause (hal), not for coordination (atf). The clause is a circumstantial state of the third-person pronoun in (tarahum). That is: you see them in the state of dreadfulness they are involved in, and you see them while hearing the reproachful speech directed at them by the believers in that scene. The (qad) is omitted with the past verb because the contextual indication is clear.

This is the speech of the believers on the Day of Resurrection, when they are at that time at peace from the terrors, thankful for their faith in the world that preceded, aware of the profit of their trade, and contrasting with the state of those who used to mock them in the world, since those mockers were the cause of their own loss on the Day of Resurrection.

The apparent meaning is that the believers say this within earshot of the wrongdoers, so that it increases the wrongdoers' torment with regret, humiliation and shame.

So this statement is used to express joy and delight at being safe from what befell the wrongdoers. That is, they said it as a way of speaking of the blessing and rejoicing in safety, each one of them saying it, or some of them saying it to others.

The particle (inna, "indeed") was used even though the speaker has no doubt about it and the hearer has no doubt about it, for the sake of emphasis on this speech, since their happiness in the Hereafter and their success in the world had become clear by witnessing the opposite of that among their opponents.

The definite article in (al-khasirin, "the losers") is the article of the genus, i.e., none other than them. The meaning: they are the most complete in loss. This article is called (alif-lam) of perfection, and this meaning of perfection is derived from defining both parts (of the sentence), which conveys a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i), since it places the loss of others in the position of no loss. So the meaning is: there is no loss resembling their loss. Therefore, in His saying (inna al-khasirin, "indeed the losers"), there is no use of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (idhar fi maqam al-idmar), as has been supposed. A parallel to this has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Say: "Indeed the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ [al-Zumar: 15] in surah al-Zumar.

Khusran (loss) is the destruction of a merchant's wealth. It is used here metaphorically for the failure to benefit from what its owner had prepared for profit. They used to hope for the bliss of their souls and for companionship with their families wherever they gathered, so there was revealed to them in this gathering the absence of both matters. Or, because they used to think they would not be raised after death, they supposed that they would suffer no pain after it and that the separation of their families would not distress them, so there was revealed to them what disappointed their expectation. They became like the merchant who hoped for profit and was struck by loss.

His saying (yawm al-qiyamah, "on the Day of Resurrection") is connected to the verb (khasiru, "they lost"), not to the verb (qul, "say").

The clause (ala inna al-zalimin fi 'adhabin muqim, "unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment") is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the preceding clauses from His saying: ﴿And you see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 44] and the verses that follow. This is because their state of being in lasting punishment is more general than their state of anxiety to be returned to the world, their humiliation, and their hearing of blame.

The repetition of the word (al-zalimin, "the wrongdoers") is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (idhar fi maqam al-idmar), required by the fact that the nature of a concluding statement is that it should be independently clear in its meaning, since it works like a proverb. This clause is not part of the speech of the believers, because the believers have no standing to pass this judgment. Moreover, the style of its opening indicates that it is the speech of the one who holds judgment on the Day of Resurrection, who is the King of the Day of Judgment. So it is a statement from God's side. That is: while they are in regret, and that abasement and disgrace from hearing what they dislike, they are in continuous punishment.

The clause is opened with the particle of alerting (ala) because this is frequent in concluding statements, for their importance.

Al-muqim ("lasting") is one who does not depart. It is applied to the punishment metaphorically: it likens what is continuous and everlasting to one who has taken a dwelling in which he never leaves.

[Page 130]

﴿And they have no protectors who could help them against Allah﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 45], meaning: they are in a lasting punishment, from which they find no helper. It also refutes their claim that their deities would benefit them with Allah.

The clause ﴿who would help them﴾ is a qualifier (ṣifah) of (awliyāʾ, "protectors"), indicating that the intended sense here is a specific kind of protection, namely the protection of support (wilāyat al-naṣr). This is like the earlier statement ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾ [al-Shura: 44], where the intended sense is the protection of guidance (wilāyat al-irshād).

The (min) in (min awliyāʾ) is extra (zāʾidah) in negation, to emphasise the negation of any protector for them.

The phrase ﴿against Allah﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 93] is a second qualifier of (awliyāʾ), and it is a clarifying qualifier (ṣifah kāshifah).

The (min) in (min dūn Allāh) is extra, to emphasise the connection of the adverbial expression (ẓarf) dūn with the verb.

* * *

﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no way﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) to the clause ﴿They had no protectors to help them﴾. The discussion of its parallel, ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾ [al-Shura: 44], has already passed.

The indefinite noun (sabīl, "way") occurs in a context of negation, so it generalises to every way of deliverance from misguidance and from its consequences. The primary intended meaning here, as the context requires, is the way of escape from the lasting punishment. For this reason, what is said here is not a mere repetition of what preceded in ﴿And whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no protector after Him﴾ [al-Shura: 44].

﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day from Allah that cannot be turned back. On that Day you will have no refuge, and no denial of your sins.﴾ After he had concluded their address following His saying: ﴿Whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Shura: 36], by what he had reached of praise for the groups of believers, and what that entailed of recording the misguidance and punishment upon the polytheists and describing their terrible state, the discourse returned to addressing them with the comprehensive call, seeking to rectify their affair before it is too late. So the speech was resumed in a manner that carries the sense of a conclusion drawn from the preceding admonitions, because the warnings mentioned earlier prepare some souls to accept the call of Islam.

Al-istijaba (response): the answering of the caller. The sin and the ta' are for emphasis. The term istijaba was used metaphorically for complying with what the Prophet ﷺ demands of them as a conveyance from Allah, Exalted is He, because responding to a call entails obeying the one who calls. Thus it has commonly been used for answering one who seeks aid.

The meaning: obey your Lord and comply with His command before there comes the Day of punishment, which is the Day of Resurrection, since the discourse concerns it.

The lam in ﴿li-rabbikum﴾ serves to emphasize the transitivity of the verb to its object, as in: "I praised Him" (hamidtu lahu) and "I thanked Him" (shakartu lahu). It is called lam al-tabligh (the lam of conveyance) and lam al-tabyin (the lam of specification). Its original form is istijaba. Ka'b al-Ghanawi said:

"And a caller called, 'O you who answer the call!' But when that time came, no responder answered him."

Perhaps its original form was istajaba du'a'ahu lahu, meaning "he answered his supplication for his sake," as in His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]. It was then shortened due to frequent usage, so they say istajaba lahu and shakara lahu. This was discussed earlier in His saying: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ [al-Baqara: 186] in Surat al-Baqara.

Al-maradd: a verbal noun with the meaning of al-radd (return). It was mentioned a little earlier in His saying: ﴿Is there any way of return?﴾ [al-Shura: 44]. And ﴿la maradda lahu﴾ ("which cannot be turned back") is an attribute of "a Day." The meaning: there is no averting its occurrence; rather it is certain to happen. "Lahu" is the predicate of the negating "la," meaning: there is no return existing for it, and the lam in "lahu" indicates exclusivity.

The "min" in His saying "min Allah" is for origin, and it is a metaphorical origin, meaning: its judgment is from Allah, as though the Day came from His presence.

The prepositional phrase may be linked to the verb ya'ti (comes). It may also be linked to the existential predicate within the predicate of "la." On this reading the sense is: there is no return existing for it from Allah, and it is not linked to "maradd" as completing its meaning, for if it were so, the noun of "la" would resemble an annexed noun and would be nunated, and would not be built on the fatha. What occurs in al-Kashshaf that seems to imply this is to be interpreted in light of what you have heard. For this reason he called it a complement (silah), and he did not hear it as linked.

The clause ﴿ma lakum min malja'in yawma'idhin﴾ ("you will have no refuge on that Day") is a resumptive clause.

Al-malja': the place of refuge. Al-laja': turning to and leaning upon a thing. Thus al-malja' is the place to which a person turns for protection. It is used metaphorically for a helper, and this is what is meant here, meaning: you will have nothing that protects you from the punishment.

Al-nakir: a verbal noun of ankara, meaning: you will have no denial of what you are being recompensed with. That is, nothing remains for you except acknowledgment, without disclaiming.

Page 131

Page 132

[p. 133]

﴿Then if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey (the message).﴾ The *fa'* here marks a consequence (*tafri'*) of His words ﴿Respond to your Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 47], and so on. This verse gathers up what came before it, as you know, since God commanded His Prophet to call them to faith, from His words at the beginning of the surah, ﴿Thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾ [al-Shura: 7], and then His words ﴿So call (them) to that, and be steadfast﴾ [al-Shura: 15]. Between these, and woven into them, are the explicit and implicit commands up to His words ﴿Respond to your Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 47], and so on.

Then, on the basis of all of that, He informed the Messenger ﷺ of his station and his duty if some of those he calls turn away, and of his excuse for what he has done, that he has not fallen short. This is an allusive (*ta'rid*) consolation for what he has suffered from them. The meaning is: if they turn away after all this, We have not sent you as a guardian over them, responsible for them, since your duty is only to convey (the message).

Since the commands to convey and to call had been introduced at the beginning of the surah by His words ﴿As for those who take protectors other than Him, God is a watcher over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ [al-Shura: 6], it was fitting that, after those commands were complete, He should draw a consequence from them, placing before them the same kind of preface, saying: ﴿Then if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey (the message).﴾

This connection is the reason for the shift (*iltifat*) from address in His words ﴿Respond to your Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 47], and so on, to the third person in His words here, ﴿Then if they turn away﴾. Otherwise it would have said: "Then if you turn away."

The word *hafiz* (guardian) was already introduced at the start of the surah. His words ﴿We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ are not, in meaning, the answer (*jawab*) of the condition, but they indicate it and stand in its place. The meaning is: if they turn away, you have not failed in calling them, and you bear no responsibility for their obstruction, since We have not sent you as a guardian over them. This is shown by the context of His words ﴿Your duty is only to convey (the message).﴾

The clause ﴿Your duty is only to convey (the message)﴾ explains the clause ﴿We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾, insofar as it indicates the omitted answer of the condition.

The second *in* is a negation particle. Its juxtaposition with the conditional *in* in this clause is a perfect paronomasia (*jinas tamm*).

*Al-Balagh* means conveying (*al-tabligh*) and is a verbal noun (*ism masdar*). It is understood from the speech that he has discharged his duty of conveying, because His words ﴿Then if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ indicate the negation of responsibility from the Prophet ﷺ for their turning away, and that the turning away is turning away from his call. Thus it is established that he has conveyed the call, and otherwise He would not have attributed turning away to them.

* * *

﴿And when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it. But if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth, then indeed man is ungrateful.﴾ This sentence is connected to His words ﴿Then if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey (the message).﴾ because of what it contains of an allusive consolation for the Messenger ﷺ regarding what he has encountered from his people, as you know. This connection is signaled by the fact that these two sentences were made a single verse, the forty-eighth in this surah. The meaning is: do not let their turning away from your call grieve you, for they have turned away from My blessing and from My warning, increasing in disbelief. The sentence is therefore coordinated (*ma'tufa*) with the sentence ﴿Then if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾. The opening of the speech with the separate pronoun of the Divine Name, as subject of a verb, rather than saying "And when We let man taste...", is because the intended purpose is to describe this man's exultation over blessings and his disbelief at the time of hardship. The purpose of this sentence here is to console the Messenger ﷺ for the harshness and turning away of his people. The meaning is: their treatment of their Lord in this manner consoles you for their treatment of you, in the manner of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. They had asked Moses for something greater than that﴾ [al-Nisa': 153]. For this reason you will not find similar sentences with this meaning opening with this kind of pronoun, because the position of those similar sentences does not resemble the position of this one, even if their meanings are alike. This particularity is specific to this sentence.

However, the composition of this verse is suitable for conveying this meaning and also another meaning close to it, namely that this is a description of a disposition common to all people, rooted in their innate nature, though its manifestations vary according to the variation of individuals in adopting religious virtues. Thus "man" in both places is taken as the human species (*jins Bani Adam*). "Rejoicing" is taken in its general sense, which admits of gradation, until it reaches the level of exultation. "The evil that their hands have sent forth" is taken in its various degrees of evils, up to the level of associating partners with God. The description "ungrateful" (*kafur*) is taken to include both its derivation from disbelief in God's oneness and disbelief in God's blessing.

For this reason the commentators' interpretations of the verse differ. Some took it as specific to the man who disbelieves in God, such as al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Tibi. Others took it as covering the kinds of people generally, such as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir. Others took it as intending both meanings, with the first being the primary intention and the second included secondarily; this is the method of al-Baydawi and the author of *al-Kashf*. Others reversed this, and this is the method of al-Kawashi in his summary.

On both views, the intended meaning of *al-insan* in the first place and in the second place is one and the same: the definition of the genus (*ta'rif al-jins*) with the intention of comprehensiveness (*isti'ghraq*), i.e., "when We let people taste, and people are ungrateful." This is a customary comprehensiveness (*isti'ghraq 'urfi*), in which the majority of the human genus at that time and place is intended, because most of humanity at that time were polytheists. This is what fits His words ﴿indeed man is ungrateful﴾, i.e., intensely and strongly ungrateful, and His words ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, i.e., of disbelief.

He changed from saying "people" (*nas*) to saying "man" (*insan*) to indicate that this disposition reported of them is one of the dispositions of the species, which nothing removes except adopting the dispositions of Islam. Those who have not embraced Islam remain upon it. This is more effective for consolation, because the word *insan* is a generic noun that includes the attributes of the genus named by it, with variation in that, because of the dominance of desire.

This has been repeated in the Qur'an many times, such as His words ﴿Indeed, man was created anxious﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19], His words ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6], and His words ﴿And man is most contentious of all things﴾ [al-Kahf: 54].

The emphasis of the report by an emphasizing particle (*harf al-ta'kid*) is for the sake of the consolation: the listener, who does not doubt the occurrence of this report, is treated as one who is hesitant about it, because of the magnitude of their turning away from the call to good. He is thus likened to the hesitant one by way of metaphor by implication (*al-makniyya*), and the emphasizing particle is one of the attributes (*rawadif*) of the omitted likened item.

*Al-idhaqa* (tasting) is a metaphor for reaching or befalling.

By "mercy" is meant the effect of mercy, which is blessing. The sense is: "And when We show mercy to man and give him a blessing," by the indication of the contrast of mercy with evil, just as it was contrasted with hardship in His words ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after hardship has touched him﴾ [Fussilat: 50], in the surah Fussilat.

By "rejoicing" is meant what includes rejoicing that exceeds the limit of pleasure to the limit of exultation and arrogance, in the manner of its use in many verses, such as His words, Exalted is He: ﴿When his people said to him: Do not exult; indeed God does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. It is not the rejoicing found in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Rejoicing in what God has given them of His bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170].

The singular pronoun in *fariha* (he rejoiced) is in observance of the wording *insan*, even though its meaning is plural, as in His words ﴿Fight the one that transgresses﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], meaning "the group that transgresses." He took account of the wording *ta'ifa* (group) rather than its meaning, even though He had said before it: "they fought" (*iqtatalu*). For this reason there came after it ﴿But if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾ with plural pronouns of the group, and then He returned to saying ﴿indeed man is ungrateful﴾.

The use of *idha* (when) in this condition is because the nature of *idha* is to indicate the certainty of the frequent occurrence of its condition, while the nature of *in* (if) is to indicate the rarity of its occurrence. For this reason *in* was used in His words ﴿But if an evil befalls them﴾, because their being struck by an evil is rare in comparison with their being struck by a blessing, in the manner of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But when good comes to them, they say: "This is ours." And if an evil befalls them, they ascribe it to bad omen from Moses and those with him﴾ [al-A'raf: 131].

The meaning of His words ﴿But if an evil befalls them because of what their hands have sent forth﴾ was explained earlier at His words, just before: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30].

The ruling contained in the sentence ﴿indeed man is ungrateful﴾ is the intended purpose of the whole conditional sentence. For this reason the emphasizing particle was repeated in it, after the sentence containing the condition had been introduced with it, so that the emphasis would encompass both sentences. This indicates that among the accidents of the human attribute is the accident of disbelief in God. This is because human nature seeks the paths of benefit and blocks the avenues of harm, from what arises from conditions some of whose causes are not within his power. He also has the nature of considering, through the reasoning of sound intellect, the protective means. But it is also his nature to set his imagination in motion in depicting powers that grant him those causes. When his imagination presents to him the existence of powers acting upon the natural laws beyond his control, he takes them to be the lost object he seeks, relies upon them, believes in them, and the evidence of the truth is hidden from him, either because his thinking is too weak to grasp it and there is no guide to it, or because his desire, which dictates to him, makes him disobey the guides among the prophets, messengers and righteous wise men, since only a few people follow them, and only the fewest arrive at guidance by intellect of their own accord, as the wise do. Thus disbelief in God came to dominate over belief in Him among the human species, as we explained just before, in His words ﴿And when We let man taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it.﴾

For this reason He followed this judgment about the species with His words ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 49]. Excluded from this generality are only the righteous among the human species, with variation among them in perfection of character. Their exclusion is established from many verses, such as His words ﴿We created man in the best of stature, then We returned him to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 4-6].

The description "ungrateful" (*kafur*) includes the ingratitude for blessings (*kufran al-ni'ma*), and the two are mostly mutually implicative.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 49:

﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills.﴾

It is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because what precedes it, concerning the wondrous nature of man, whom the divine guidance has not refined, raises in the mind of the listener a question about why man was created with these two dispositions, by which he receives the blessing of his Lord and His trial; and how he was not created with the most perfect disposition, so that he might receive blessing with gratitude and adversity with patience and humble supplication; and also a question about the reason for making man taste blessing at one time and hardship at another, so that he becomes insolent and ungrateful; and how He did not make his state one of sufficiency, with neither pleasures nor afflictions, like the state of the dumb animals. Its answer is: that God, the One who disposes of the heavens and the earth, creates in them whatever He wills of beings and their states. This is a general, persuasive answer, suited to the dignity of refraining from entering into dispute about divine affairs.

In His saying ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ there is a generality that moves the thoughtful and fair observer to seek the wisdom in that. If he seeks it, it yields to him, as the closing of this sentence with His saying ﴿Indeed He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Shura: 50] alludes to. It is as if He says: Look upon the wisdom in the ranks of created beings and the disposal of their Originator. Just as He created the angels upon the most perfect morals in all states, and originated the beasts upon a limit that does not accept perfection of creation, so He created man on a foundation of good and evil, and made him capable of increase in either, according to the differing ranks of the intellects of his individuals and what surrounds them of imitation and emulation; and He created him fully able to distinguish between blessing and its opposite, so that he may rise in degrees and sink in depths according to what he chooses for himself. The creation of man upon the nature of the angels does not suit the condition of his material world, since this world is not fit for its inhabitants to be like the angels, because of the lack of harmony between the world of matter and the world of spirit. Therefore, when the first individual of mankind was completed and the time came for him to act with his companion according to the powers that had sprouted in them both, he was soon transferred from the world of the angels to the world of matter, as indicated by His exalted saying: ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123].

However, God did not close off the avenues of perfection to the species; He created it a middle creation between angelhood and animality, for He composed it of matter and deposited in it the spirit, and He did not leave it without guidance through intermediaries, and their succession through the ages, and the transmission of their guidance among the generations. If he follows their guidance, he joins the morals of the angels until he reaches the stations that place him in a position of equality with some of his individuals and the angels in precedence.

This is indicated by His exalted saying: ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you, some of you enemies to others. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will not go astray nor be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123] ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha: 124], and His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam﴾ [Ta-Ha: 116].

* * *

﴿He bestows female [offspring] upon whom He wills, and bestows male [offspring] upon whom He wills﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ [al-Shura: 50]. It is a substitute (badal) for the clause ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), because His creating what He wills includes His bestowing on whom He wills what He wills.

This substitution is an incorporation (idmaj) of a comprehensive example covering the forms of attaining what is loved and attaining what is disliked. His saying ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ [al-Shura: 50] is, for the majority of people, among what is disliked, and it includes a kind of ingratitude, namely regarding some blessing as evil, as was the custom of the polytheists in their pessimism at the birth of daughters. Allusion to a reproach of them in this is made by placing females before males at the beginning of the enumeration of the blessings bestowed, contrary to the usual practice of placing males before females wherever both are mentioned in the Qur'an, as in ﴿Indeed We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13] and His saying ﴿and made of him the two spouses, the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39]. This is among the subtleties of this verse.

The meaning is: He bestows female [offspring] only upon whom He wills, and bestows male [offspring] only upon whom He wills, by the indication of His saying ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females﴾ [al-Shura: 50].

The indefiniteness of (inathan, "females") is because indefiniteness is the original state of names of kinds, and the definiteness of the males by the article (al-) is because they are the category known to the addressees. So the article is for defining the kind, and recourse to defining the kind is for a purpose: that He bestows that category which you know, speak of, and desire, in accordance with the Arab saying: "Arsalaha al-'Iraku" [the thirst-like-sweat(?) sent her], which was mentioned at the beginning of al-Fatiha. And (aw, "or") is for division.

Tazwij (pairing) is joining one thing with another so that they become a pair. Among its figurative uses is its application to a man marrying a woman, because they become like a pair. Here the meaning is: He makes them a pair in the bestowal, i.e., He gathers for whom He wills, so that He bestows on him males accompanied by females. Thus the meaning is pairing with another category, not the matching of each individual of one category with an individual of the other category.
