The pronoun in (yuzawwijuhum) refers to both the females and the males. And ﴿dhukranan wa inathan﴾ [al-Shura: 50] is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the plural pronoun in (yuzawwijuhum).

Al-'Aqim: the one who does not have offspring from a man or a woman. Its verb is 'aqima, of the pattern fariha, and 'aquma, of the pattern karuma. The original of its verb is that it is transitive to the object; one says 'aqamaha Allah, of the pattern darba, and one says 'uqimat al-mar'a, in the passive voice, i.e., a barren agent made her barren, because the cause of the barrenness is unknown to them. It is among what comes both transitive and intransitive: the intransitive with the first vowel damma and kasra, and the transitive with fatha. The adjective 'aqim is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, so the masculine and feminine are generally equal in it, and occasionally the feminine marker appears rarely; they said: rahim 'aqimah [a barren womb].

**﴿Indeed, He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful.﴾** This is a clause in the position of the cause (*'illah*) for the element it substitutes for (*al-mubdal minhu*, the original term being replaced), which is **﴿He creates whatever He wills﴾** [al-Shura: 49]. So the position of "inna" here is that of the *fa'* of consequence (*fa' al-tafri'*, the resultative "fa" that draws a conclusion).

The meaning is that His creating whatever He wills is not a random creation, empty of wisdom, because He has all-encompassing knowledge: nothing among the knowable things escapes Him. Therefore His creation of things proceeds in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom.

And He is **All-Powerful**, whose power is unrestricted. So when He knows the wisdom in creating a thing, He wills it, and it proceeds according to His measure. Since He combined the two attributes of knowledge and power, it is established that there is an implied attribute, which is will (*al-iradah*), because His power only operates after His will has been directed toward the existent thing.

The detailed meaning is that He is All-Knowing of the causes, the powers, and the influences that He placed in the worlds; of how the effects of some of them agree and of how others differ; of how beings come into existence in the manner He decreed for them in their conditions; of how they cooperate so that effects come in one uniform order; and of how they counteract one another, so that the influence of some of them diminishes in its effects because of the opposition of other influences. All of this is among the manifestations of His knowledge, exalted is He, in the original formation of the universe, and among the manifestations of His power in operating in accordance with His knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 42, verse 51 (part 1 of 3):

[Page 140]
﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾

It is a conjunction to what preceded of their (the polytheists') absurd claims, the conjunction of one narrative to another narrative, and it is a return to refuting the doubts of the polytheists, to which the Exalted's saying indicates: ﴿Thus does He reveal to you and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [al-Shura: 3], and His saying, Exalted is He: "It is grievous to the polytheists what you call them to" (cf. 42:13). We have already pointed to the detail of that in what preceded. It is made clearer by His saying after it: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit by Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. This verse refutes the second doubt among the doubts we have enumerated concerning the Qur'an being a revelation from Allah to Muhammad ﷺ, for they claimed that if Muhammad ﷺ were sent by Allah, there would be angels with him confirming his words, or a ready-made book would be sent down to him from heaven which they would witness descending. The Exalted said: ﴿And they said, "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets? Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner with him?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and He said: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ [al-Isra': 90], up to His saying: ﴿"And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book that we can read"﴾ [al-Isra': 93].

Since the most important purpose of this surah is to establish that the Qur'an is a revelation from Allah to Muhammad ﷺ, just as revelation was sent before him to the messengers, returning to that is of the kind of "repeating the latter part upon the former" (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr).

So Allah made clear to the deniers that Allah's practice in addressing His messengers does not exceed three modes of address. Among them is what the Qur'an came with, and so it was not novel compared with what the earlier messengers came with. And it was not for Allah to address His messengers in the modes the polytheists proposed to the Prophet ﷺ. So there came a restrictive form beginning with a negating formula expressing emphatic negation, which is ﴿It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him﴾, meaning: it was not possible for any of the messengers that a message from Allah should come to him in any of these three forms.

This indicates the negation that the conveying of Allah's intent to the nations of the messengers could be by other than one of these
[Page 141]
types, namely specifically the type of sending a messenger, by the implication of the wording (dalalat fahwa al-khitab). For if the messengers are not addressed by Allah except by one of these three modes, then the nations are more fitting not to be addressed by anything other than that, such as what the polytheists asked: seeing Allah address them, or the angels coming to them. Rather, Allah's address does not reach them except through a messenger from among them who receives Allah's speech in one of the three modes. This falls under His saying: ﴿or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills﴾, for the messenger is an angel, who conveys the revelation to the messengers and prophets.

Allah's address to the messengers and prophets may be for the purpose of conveying to them a matter that benefits them, such as His saying: ﴿O you who wrap yourself, stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1]. It may also be for conveying to them laws for the nations, like most of the Qur'an and the Torah, or conveying to them admonitions, like the Psalms (al-Zabur) and the Book of Luqman (majallat Luqman).

The exception in His saying "except by revelation" is an exception from the general category of types of speaker indicated by the verb in the context of negation, which is "it is not for any human that Allah should speak to him."

So the accusative of wahyan (revelation) is an adjective for a omitted verbal noun (masdar) indicated by the exception, and the estimate is: "except a speech by revelation," i.e., spoken as revealed, just as you say: "I do not speak to him except aloud, or except in a low voice," because loudness and softness are attributes of speech.

By "speaking" is meant the arrival of Allah's intent to the Prophet, whether that arrival is by a speech he hears without seeing its source, or by a speech conveyed to him by the angel from Allah, or by a knowledge cast into the soul of the Prophet, whereby he is certain that it is Allah's intent, by a necessary knowledge that Allah places in his soul.

As for applying the term "speech" to these three types: some of it is literal, like what the Prophet hears as Moses heard; some of it is a close metaphor, namely what is conveyed to the Prophet, for it is a message in speech; and some of it is a pure metaphor, namely what is cast into the heart of the Prophet with knowledge. So the application of the verb "He speaks to him" to all of them is the use of the word in its literal and metaphorical senses, in the manner of using a homonym (mushtarak) in its meanings.

The attribution of the verb "He speaks to him" to Allah is a rational (metaphorical) attribution.

On this basis, the exception of speech described as revelation becomes a connected (muttasil) exception.

[Page 142]
The root meaning of wahy is a hidden allusion, and from it: ﴿So he revealed to them that they should glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 11]. It is also applied to what a person finds in his soul all at once, like the arising of the meaning of speech in the soul of a listener. 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

"And Allah revealed to me that they had conspired / against the camels of Abu Awfa, so I rose on one foot."

This meaning is the one intended here, by the indication of the contrast with the other two types. From here, wahy was applied to the innate inspiration (ilham) that Allah has created in animals, precise and well-formed, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾ [al-Nahl: 68]. Revelation in this sense is a type of the kinds of casting Allah's speech to the prophets, and it is the first type in the count. So wahy is applied to speech that the Prophet hears in an unusual manner. This application is from the technical usage of the Qur'an and is the predominant usage in the Book and the Sunnah. From it is the saying of Zayd ibn Thabit: "So I knew that it was being revealed to him, then it was lifted from him and he recited 'other than those with a harm'," and he did not say "Gabriel descended upon him."

Revelation in this sense is other than the revelation that will come in His saying: ﴿or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills﴾. The meaning of wahy here is: the placing of Allah's intent into the soul of the Prophet, by which he attains the knowledge that it is from Allah. It is thus a proof for the Prophet by virtue of necessary knowledge, and a proof for the community by virtue of protection (ismah) from the whisperings of Satan. It may occur to non-prophets too, but it is not consistent or regulated, although it does happen. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There were among the nations before you muhaddathun (those spoken to / inspired), and if there is any among my community, it is 'Umar ibn al-Khattab." Ibn Wahb said: muhaddathun means "inspired" (mulhamun).

Among this revelation are the visions of the prophets, for they are revelation, though they are not speech cast to them. In the hadith: "I was shown the land of your emigration; it is a lava field with palm trees, and it occurred to me that it was al-Yamama or Hajar, but it was Taba (Madinah)."

A dream may include inspiration and speech, like the hadith: "I saw cows being slaughtered, and I saw—and Allah is best—" (in the narration with the divine name in the nominative, meaning "I saw this word"). The Prophet ﷺ interpreted his vision of the cows being slaughtered as what befell the Muslims on the day of Uhud. As for "Allah is best," it is what Allah brought afterward of good.

[Page 143]
Among inspiration is the vision of the righteous, for it is a part of forty-six parts of prophecy.

Inspiration is not a proof in religion, because one who is not infallible cannot be trusted in the soundness of his impulses, since he is not protected from the whisperings of Satan. Some of the Sufis and the philosophers of illumination (hukama' al-ishraq) act upon it in their own private matters, and claim that there are signs which distinguish for them between the true and false impulses. From this is the saying of Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi in the preface to his commentary on the Miftah: "There has been cast to me, by way of warning from the presence of the Mighty King, through the tongue of inspiration, not as one of the delusions, … " and he continued: "what made me withdraw from the abode of delusion." From it is what has come in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has fully received its term and its provision," according to one of two interpretations of it. There is no doubt that this is what is meant here, because the wording of this hadith follows other than the wording by which the descent of revelation through the speech of Gabriel (peace be upon him) is described.

The second type: that the speech is from behind a veil, which its hearer hears without seeing its source, by Allah creating speech in an object hidden from its hearer. This is what Allah described here with His saying: ﴿or from behind a veil﴾.

The meaning: or [He speaks to] one veiled, the addressee being in the passive (meaning he is veiled) from seeing the source of the speech; so the speech is as if it came from behind a veil. This is like Allah's speaking to Moses in the blessed spot from the tree. The addressee comes to know that this speech is from Allah the first time through a sign Allah shows him, by which he knows that it can only be by Allah's subjugation (taskhir), as Moses knew this through his staff turning into a serpent and then returning to its former state, and through his hand coming out from his collar white, as He said: ﴿another sign, that We may show you of Our greatest signs. Go to Pharaoh, indeed he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22]. Then after that it becomes a habit by which he recognizes the speech of Allah.

This type of speech was specific, among the earlier messengers, to Moses peace be upon him, and it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿He said, "O Moses, I have chosen you over the people by My messages and by My speech"﴾ [al-A'raf: 144]. Yet revelation to Moses was not confined to this type, for the predominant revelation to all prophets and messengers was revealed to him. This type of speech occurred for Muhammad ﷺ on the night of the Isra', for it has come in the hadith of the Isra': "that Allah imposed on him and on his community fifty prayers, then Allah lightened them until they reached five prayers, and that he heard His saying: 'I have completed My obligation and lightened it for My servants.'"

[Page 144]
Surat al-Najm alludes to it in His saying: ﴿Then he was level, while he was on the highest horizon. Then he approached and descended, and was at two bow-lengths or nearer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed. The heart did not lie about what it saw. Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 6]. The view that he heard the speech of Allah on the night he was taken up to the heaven is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, al-Ash'ari, and al-Wasiti, and it is the apparent view, because the superiority of Muhammad ﷺ over all the messengers necessitates that Allah give him of the best of what He gave all His messengers, peace be upon them.

The third type: that Allah sends the angel to the Prophet, and he conveys to him a speech which the Prophet hears and retains. This is the predominant form in which Allah's speech is addressed to the prophets. Allah said regarding Zakariyya: ﴿While he was standing praying in the sanctuary, the angels called to him: "Indeed Allah gives you good news of Yahya"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39], and said regarding Ibrahim: ﴿And We called to him: "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision"﴾ [al-Saffat: 104]. This speech comes in a manner the Prophet ﷺ described to al-Harith ibn Hisham when he asked the Messenger of Allah: "How does revelation come to you?" He said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and this is the hardest on me; it departs from me and I have retained what it said—i.e., from Gabriel—and sometimes the angel appears to me as a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says."

So "the messenger" in His saying: ﴿or by sending a messenger﴾ is the angel Gabriel or other than him. His saying "who reveals by His permission what He wills" named this speech revelation, in observance of the predominant Qur'anic usage as already mentioned, like His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire; it is only a revelation revealed, taught to him by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 3]. This is other than the meaning of His saying "except by revelation," by the indication of the division and the contrast.

Among the subtleties of the composition of this verse is the ordering of what indicates Allah's speaking to the messengers by means of indications. The verbal noun comes first in His saying "except by revelation," then what resembles a sentence second, which is His saying "from behind a veil," and then the verbal sentence third in His saying "or by sending a messenger."

Nafi' read "aw yursilu" with the verb in the indicative (raf'), with the sense: "or He is sending a messenger." And he read "fayuhiya" with the yā' quiescent after the kasra of the hā'.

The recitation of the rest (al-Baqun) reads ﴿أَوْ يُرْسِلَ﴾ with the verb in the subjunctive (naṣb), on the assumption of an elided "an" (أَنْ) which the conjunction implies after the verbal noun (maṣdar). Because the conjoined verb then takes the force of a verbal noun, it requires the insertion of a particle of "sabk" (the particle that converts the verb into a verbal noun). They read ﴿فَيُوحِيَ﴾ with a fatḥah on the yā', as a conjunction to ﴿يُرْسِلَ﴾.

The relative clause ﴿مَا يَشَاءُ﴾ ("what He wills") is a sentence that explains what is meant. That is, ﴿فَيُوحِيَ﴾ means "so He reveals speech that He wills." This sentence therefore functions as a descriptive clause (ṣifah) for the elided noun "kalām" (speech). The linking element (rābiṭ) is ﴿مَا يَشَاءُ﴾, since it refers back to "kalām." This is like linking a clause by repeating the word it refers to, or by a synonym, as in ﴿الْحَاقَّةُ مَا الْحَاقَّةُ﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 1] ("The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?"). The full sense is: "or except speech characterized by the fact that Allah sends a messenger who reveals, by His permission, speech that He wills, for sending is a kind of speech intended in this verse."

The verse clearly indicates that these three types are kinds of the speech of Allah with which He addresses His servants. The mention of the first and third types clearly indicates that when speech of this kind is ascribed to Allah, or attributed to Him, wherever it occurs in the terminology of the Sharia, as in His words ﴿until he hears the speech of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6], and His words ﴿He said: "O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech"﴾ [al-A'raf: 144], and His words ﴿And Allah spoke to Musa directly﴾ [al-Nisa': 164], this indicates that it is speech with a specific characteristic: Allah brought it into existence in a manner that breaks the customary order, so that by this it would be a proof that the meanings of its words are intended by Allah and are what He means. Just as the spirit by which 'Isa came into being was called "the spirit of Allah," because it came into being in a way that breaks the customary order, Allah created speech that indicates His intention, in a manner not following the normal pattern by which speech comes into being, so that people may know that Allah intended to inform them that He intended the meanings of that speech. This is a sign that He broke the customary way of bringing speech into being. It was therefore an origination not produced from ordinary causes and means, like the origination of the heavens and the earth, and of Adam, in that it is not produced from natural causes and means.

Know that the reality of divinity does not, in itself, require that Allah be speaking, just as it requires that He be one, living, knowing, powerful, and willing. Whoever attempts to make the attribute of speech a requirement of divinity, by analogy of God to a king, on the basis that kingship requires addressing subjects with what the king wants from them, has brought a rhetorical argument. Rather, the truth is that what requires the affirmation of the speech of Allah is the establishment of the divine laws (al-wad' al-ilahi), that is, the connection of Allah's will to guiding people to avoid what disrupts the soundness of their affairs, through His commands, prohibitions, admonitions, promises and threats. This has been since the day He forbade Adam from eating from the tree and threatened him with misery if he ate from it, and then since the sending of messengers to people and their conveying to them the command and prohibition of Allah through establishing the laws. This is without doubt from the time of Nuh, or from the time of Adam if we say that Adam conveyed the command and prohibition of Allah to his family.

Therefore it is necessary to believe that Allah is the one who commands, prohibits, promises, and threatens, and informs through His messengers and prophets, and that His intention in this was conveyed to the prophets through speech that is cast to them, and that they understand, and which is not familiar to them before prophethood. It varies in kind in its resemblance to familiar speech.

Since the Book and the Sunnah do not mention describing Allah as a speaker (mutakallim), nor the affirmation of an attribute called speech for Him, and since the reality of divinity does not require it, there was no reason among the later scholars of ta'wil (interpretation) to affirm that, such as the Ash'aris and the Maturidis, who said that Allah is a speaker and that He has an attribute called speech. Especially the Mu'tazila, who said that He is a speaker but denied the attribute of speech. The matter of the Mu'tazila is more astonishing, for they affirmed the rational attributes (al-sifat al-ma'nawiyyah) on account of the decisive verses of the Qur'an, but denied the attributes of meanings (sifat al-ma'ani), out of scruple and to escape the resemblance to the claim of a plurality of eternal beings, without any reason. They had an alternative to not affirming the attribute of the speaker, because there was no reason to affirm it, unlike what prompted them to affirm other rational attributes. Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi), in his commentary on this surah, related the consensus of the community that Allah is a speaker.

The most that is found in the Qur'an is the attribution of the act of speech to Allah, or the attribution of its verbal noun to His name. This does not require that a descriptive attribute be derived from it for Allah, for they did not say that Allah has the attribute "the one who breathes souls" on account of His words ﴿and I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [Sad: 72]. What moved those who affirm the attribute of speech for Allah is the strong connection of this attribute to the attribute of knowledge, so they gave this connection a specific name, and made it an independent attribute, as they did with the attributes of hearing and sight.

Furthermore, know that those who affirm the attribute of speech have differed about its reality. The early generation (al-Salaf) held that it is an eternal attribute like the rest of Allah's attributes. When they are asked about the words that constitute speech, "Are they eternal or originated?", they say, "Eternal." Fakhr al-Din al-Razi marveled at them and reproached them, and I do not think they were anything but averse to explicitly stating that it is originated, lest that lead the common folk of the community to believe that Allah's attributes are originated, or lest it lead to nullifying that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. For clarifying the true meaning of the idafah (annexation) in their saying "the speech of Allah" is extremely subtle, and whoever grasps it needs to sharpen his mind with the rules of the sciences, and the common people are far from that.

Among the people of this method, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, may Allah have mercy on him, is well known, at the time of the trial of the createdness of the Qur'an. The jurists of the Malikis during the time of the 'Ubaydids also adhered to this method. Shaykh Abu Muhammad Ibn Abi Zayd said in al-Risalah: "The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, not created, lest it perish, and not an attribute of a created thing, lest it be exhausted." They engraved on one of the pillars of the Great Mosque in the city of Sousse this phrase: "The Qur'an is the speech of Allah and is not created." It is still standing to this day.

Fakhr al-Din said: "It happened one day that I said to some of the Hanbalis: 'If Allah spoke with these letters, either He would speak them all at once or in succession. The first is false, because speaking them all at once would not produce this composed arrangement in succession and sequence. The second is false, because if Allah spoke them in succession, they would be originated.' When he heard this from me, he said: 'It is obligatory upon us to affirm and let pass (nuqirru wa numurru),' meaning that we affirm that the Qur'an is eternal, and we let this speech pass as we heard it." He said: "So I marveled at the simplicity of that speaker's heart."

Very strange is what is attributed to Muhammad ibn Karram and his followers, the Karramiyyah, of saying that the speech of Allah is letters and sounds subsisting in His essence, the Exalted. They said: "It does not follow that every attribute of Allah is eternal." Such a view is also attributed to the Hashwiyyah. As for the Mu'tazila, they affirmed that Allah is a speaker, but denied that He has an attribute called speech. What led them to this was the combination of what is widespread in the Qur'an and the Sunnah and among the early generation of the attribution of speech to Allah and its annexation to Him. They said: "The derivation of a descriptive term does not necessitate that the verbal noun subsist in the one described," and this is their method for all attributes of meanings. They added and said: "The meaning of His being a speaker is that He is the creator of speech."

As for al-Ash'ari and his companions, they did not differ that the speech that we say is the speech of Allah, composed of letters and sounds, recited by our tongues and written in our copies of the Qur'an, is originated, and that it is not the attribute of Allah, the Exalted. Rather, the attribute of Allah is the meaning indicated by that composed speech of letters and sounds, namely commands, prohibitions, promises and threats. My approximation of this is that the originated speech which Allah created indicates the intention of Allah, the Exalted, and that the intention of Allah is an attribute of Allah.

Abu Bakr al-Baqillani said, quoting the Shaykh (al-Ash'ari): "The eternal speech of Allah is recited by our tongues, preserved in our hearts, heard by our ears, and written in our copies, without inhering in any of that, just as Allah is known by our hearts, mentioned by our tongues, and worshipped in our prayer niches, and He does not inhere in any of that. The recitation and the reciter are created, just as the knowledge and the knower are created, and the known and the object of knowledge are eternal." End of quote. He means that the spoken and written words are signifiers and are created, and the signified, which is Allah's willing the meanings of those compositions, is the attribute of Allah, so that it is valid that Allah intended for people to act upon the meanings indicated by those compositions. Al-Ash'ari named that signified "inner speech" (kalam nafsi), which is the will for the meanings that the verbal speech indicates. He found support for this in the verse of al-Akhtal:

"Indeed, speech is in the heart, and the tongue was made only a sign of the heart."

As for Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, al-Razi reported from him a speech mixed from the words of al-Ash'ari and the words of the Mu'tazila, and some reported from him something like the statement of the early generation. The cause of the difference in transmission from him is that al-Maturidi followed Abu Hanifa in the principles of religion. His followers disagreed about understanding his expression in the creed attributed to him, called al-Fiqh al-Akbar (if its attribution to him is correct), since it is an expression that appears contradictory, and perhaps this was intended. Interpreting it in a way that agrees with the words of al-Ash'ari is the verified position.

The verification of this matter in a clear and near way is to say: the establishment of the attribute of speech for Allah is like the establishment of the attribute of will and the attribute of power for Him, the Exalted, in pre-eternity, and it is most similar to His being characterized by will. Just as the meaning of the attribute of will for Allah is that, whenever His knowledge relates to bringing into existence a thing that did not exist, or to annihilating a thing that existed, nothing prevents or hinders the execution of what His knowledge has related to, whether bringing it into being or annihilating it. And whenever His knowledge relates to keeping the non-existent in non-existence, or the existent in existence, no compeller forces Him to the opposite. Likewise, the establishment of speech for Allah means that whenever His knowledge relates to commanding or prohibiting someone, nothing stands between that and the bringing into existence of what conveys His intention to those commanded or prohibited, and whenever His knowledge relates to leaving the directing of a command or prohibition to people, no compeller forces Him to command or prohibit them.

Just as will has a potential eternal relation (ta'alluq salahi) and a actual originated relation (ta'alluq tanjizi), which arises when the will is directed to bringing something into being through power, so we find that the speech of Allah has a potential eternal relation and an actual relation that arises when the knowledge of Allah calls for the directing of His command, prohibition, or the like to some of His servants.

So the speech that the Messenger utters and attributes to Allah, the Exalted, is originated, and it is the effect of the originated actual relation. The speech that we believe Allah intended, and intended that people act upon, is the eternal, pre-eternal attribute, and it has the eternal potential relation. In the Khaqaniyyah treatise of the great scholar 'Abd al-Hakim al-Sialkuti, he reported from some scholars that the speech of Allah has an originated actual relation, and this is of great verification.

The verified position is that this eternal speech branches out into types of signified meanings: command, prohibition, information, promise, threat, and the like.

The essence of the meaning of the verse is that God may create in the soul of Jibril (Gabriel) or of another of the angels knowledge of God's intent, in a manner we do not know. He also creates knowledge that God has commissioned him to convey that intent to the Prophet. The angel conveys to the Prophet what he has been ordered to convey, on behalf of the one who commissions him, through fixed words that God has cast into the angel's soul, like the words of the Qur'an. Or the words may be of the angel's own composition, as in what God related about Zakariyya when He said: ﴿The angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: God gives you good news of Yahya﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39].

Or God creates in the Prophet's hearing speech which he knows with certain knowledge did not come to him from a speaker. He is then certain that it is from God, by the evidence of the miracle at the first occurrence, and by the evidence of his becoming accustomed to it afterwards. This is like the speech with which God addressed Musa (Moses). Do you not see His saying, ﴿O Musa, indeed I am God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Qasas: 30], ﴿and throw down your staff﴾ [al-Qasas: 31], and the rest of the verse? Here He joined His address, which is beyond custom, to the miracle, which is beyond custom, so that Musa would be certain that this speech was from God.

Or God creates in the Prophet's soul definitive knowledge that God intends such-and-such from him, just as He creates it in the soul of the angel in the case mentioned first.

Page 150

Through these modes, revelation (al-wahy) comes to the prophets. The Qur'an is distinguished by the feature that God Most High creates speech which the angel retains and is commanded to convey to Muhammad (ﷺ) word for word, without alteration.

The discussion of the placement of the clause ﴿Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise﴾ is the same as the discussion of the earlier clause ﴿Indeed He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Shura: 50]. The attributes Most High and All-Wise were chosen here because they suit the context of both. Highness in the attribute "Most High" is a highness of supreme majesty, which human souls are not fit for, since they have not been purified by the sanctity of holiness. Thus they could not receive His intent directly from God. His loftiness therefore required that His address to mankind be directed through intermediaries, some of which lead to others, because, as the philosophers say, the receiving of the recipient from the source is halted by the lack of correspondence between the two.

As for the attribute All-Wise, its meaning is one who perfects the making of things and knows their subtleties. His address to mankind is only for the wisdom of reforming them and ordering their world. And His occurring in these three modes is only an effect of wisdom, to facilitate the reception and comprehension of His address without any disorder in it and without exceeding the capacity of those who receive it.

Refer to what preceded at His saying, ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], in the chapter of al-A'raf, and at His saying, ﴿then grant him protection until he hears the words of God﴾ [al-Tawba: 6], in the chapter "Bara'a" (al-Tawba).

**[Page 151]**

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 42, verse 52:

﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whomever We will of Our servants﴾. This is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾ [al-Shura: 51], and it is an argument against them that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah. By it, he follows up on the refutation of their doubt, which the statement ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾ [al-Shura: 51] had been introduced to refute. That is, Our revelation to you was like Our speech with which We spoke to those before you, as he stated in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa: 163]. The intended meaning of this is His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was﴾.

The demonstrative refers to something preceding in the speech, which is what was mentioned just before in His saying: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾ [al-Shura: 51]. That is, and like what was mentioned of Allah's speaking, Our revelation to you is a spirit from Our command. This is then in the manner of the saying of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

*"Like it, advice goes forth to the people, a wasteland with no camels (afla') beyond it."*

That is, like our advice, which we gave to the king 'Amr ibn Hind, the advice of peoples to one another is [given] because it is the advice of kin, those bound by ties of blood.

It is also possible that the demonstrative refers to what comes afterward, namely the revelation derived from "We have revealed to you" (*awḥaynā ilayka*). That is: like Our revelation to you, We have revealed to you. In other words, if one wished to compare Our revelation to you in terms of loftiness of rank and guidance, nothing would be found to resemble it except itself, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a midmost community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning is: what We have revealed to you is the most honored and noble revelation, such that nothing else is comparable to it.

Both meanings are suitable here, so it is appropriate that both be taken as the interpretation of the verse, in the manner that we devised in the ninth introduction to this commentary. It is derived from this verse that the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was given the three types of revelation, and this is also what the purpose of the context of these verses requires.

The *rūḥ* (spirit) is that by which a person has life. It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the spirit﴾ [al-Isra': 85], in Surat al-Isra'. Here the spirit is used figuratively for the Sharia (sacred law), by which souls are guided to what benefits them in their first life and their second life. The guidance of their intellects after error is likened to the entry of the spirit into the body, so that it becomes living after having been a corpse.

The meaning of "from Our command" (*min amrinā*) is: from that which We have singled out for creation and have withheld from people. The command (*amr*) attributed to Allah means a great matter, as in the saying of people: "The matter of so-and-so has become grave" (*amira amru fulān*), that is, his affair, and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the permission of their Lord, for every matter﴾ [al-Qadr: 4].

What is meant by the spirit from Allah's command is what was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) of guidance and direction, whether it was by the inspiration of a specific speech, commanded to be conveyed to people in its exact wording without change, which is the Qur'anic revelation whose purpose is two matters: guidance and inimitability (*i'jāz*); or whether it was not restricted to that, but the Messenger was commanded to convey the meaning without the wording, which is that which comes in speech not intended for inimitability; or by the conveying of meaning to the Messenger through direct address from the angel. The Messenger has latitude in this, to express in his own words what was revealed to him in the manner he wishes to express it, or through a dream vision, or through inspiration into the soul, as has been mentioned earlier.

The closing of this surah with this verse, together with its opening with His saying, ﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾ [al-Shura: 3], contains an embellishment of the type called *radd al-'ajz 'alā al-ṣadr* (repetition of the end at the beginning).

The clause ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to the pronoun in "We have revealed" (*awḥaynā*). That is: We revealed to you while you did not know the Book or faith. In other words, We bestowed upon you the gift of revelation while you were devoid of knowledge of the Book and knowledge of faith. This is a challenge to the obstinate, so that they may reflect upon the condition of the Messenger (ﷺ) and know that what he was given of the Sharia and of ethical manners is one of the gifts of Allah, exalted is He, which he had not practiced before. It also contains a favor upon him and upon his Muslim community.

The meaning of not knowing the Book is that his knowledge did not extend to reading or understanding a book.

The meaning of not knowing faith is that his knowledge did not extend to what the true legal reality of faith contains of the attributes of Allah and the foundations of religion. Faith is sometimes used in the sense synonymous with Islam, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and it is the faith that increases and decreases, as in His saying: ﴿So that those who believe may increase in faith﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]. Thus there is added to the meaning of not knowing faith the absence of the Messenger's (ﷺ) knowledge of the precepts of Islam. The absence of his knowledge of faith is like the absence of his knowledge of the Book, that is, the absence of knowledge of its realities. For this reason He said "you did not know" and did not say "you were not a believer."

**[Page 153]**

Neither of these two possibilities requires that the Messenger (ﷺ) was not a believer in the existence of Allah and the oneness of His divinity before the revelation came to him. For the prophets and messengers are protected from polytheism before prophethood. They are monotheists devoted to Allah and renouncers of the worship of idols. But they did not know the details of faith. Our Prophet (ﷺ), in the period of his people's ignorance, knew the falsehood of idol worship. Since his people associated others with Allah in divinity, the falsehood of the divinity of the idols was, in his view, a purification leading him to affirm the singling out of Allah in divinity without doubt.

He reported this about himself in what Abu Nu'aym narrated in *Dala'il al-Nubuwwa* from Shaddad ibn Aws, and 'Iyad mentioned it in *al-Shifa'* without attribution: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When I grew up, that is, when I reached the age of reason, idols were made hateful to me and poetry was made hateful to me. I did not intend to do anything of what the Jahiliyya used to do except twice, and Allah protected me from both, and then I did not return to them."

Despite the intensity of the Quraysh's dispute with him over the matter of monotheism, they did not argue against him that he used to worship idols with them.

In this verse there is evidence for those who hold that the Messenger (ﷺ) was not a worshipper under any sacred law before his prophethood.

The insertion of the negative particle (*lā*) in His saying "nor what faith was" is an emphasis on the negation of his knowledge of it. That is: you did not know the Book nor faith, to make explicit that what is negated is knowledge of each of the two.

His saying, ﴿But We made it a light﴾, is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾. The pronoun in "We made it" refers to "the Book" in His saying "You did not know what the Book was." The estimated meaning is: We made the Book a light. The corrective conjunction (*istidrāk*) is introduced into the coordinated clause to draw attention to the fact that the content of this clause is the opposite of the content of the clause ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾.

The *istidrāk* arises from what the clause ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾ implies, since the apparent sense of negating knowledge of the Book is that its absence is continuous. So He corrects this by saying that Allah guided him by means of the Book, and through him guided his community. So the corrective conjunction falls exactly in its place. The estimated meaning is: You did not know what the Book was nor faith; then We guided you by means of the Book initially, and We made you know faith through it, and you guided people through it secondarily,

**[Page 154]**

so that whomever We will guide is guided by it, that is, whoever We did not will to be guided remains in error, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By it He leads many astray and by it He guides many﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26].

The Book is compared to light because of the relation between guidance and it, since faith, guidance and knowledge are likened to light, while misguidance, ignorance and disbelief are likened to darkness. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He brings them out from the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. When a traveler is in darkness, he goes astray from the road; when it is illuminated for him, he finds the road. So light is the means of guidance, but only one who has no barrier preventing guidance is guided by it. Otherwise the means of guidance does not benefit him. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By it We guide whomever We will of Our servants﴾, that is, We create guidance by its means in the souls of those whom We have prepared for guidance from among Our servants.

So the guidance here is a special guidance, namely the creation of faith in the heart.

* * *

﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path, the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 52–53].

That is: by it We guide whom We will, through your call and your mediation. When He established the guidance to Allah and made the Book a means to attain guidance, He then coordinated the mediation of the Messenger in conveying that guidance, to honor the Messenger (ﷺ).

So the clause ﴿And indeed you guide﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿by it We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾. In the speech there is an allusion to the polytheists, since they were not guided by it, and since what calls them to it was grievous to them, even though it guides them to a straight path.

The guidance in His saying ﴿And indeed you guide﴾ is general guidance, namely guiding people to the path of good. It thus differs from the guidance in His saying ﴿By it We guide whom We will﴾.

The object of "you guide" is omitted for generality, that is, you guide all people, that is, you direct them to a straight path. This is like His saying: ﴿And We showed him the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10], ﴿but he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11].

The emphasis of the statement with *inna* (indeed) is for the sake of attention to it, because the statement is used to strengthen the heart of the Prophet (ﷺ) by bearing witness to him in this great station. So the statement is used with its implied meaning, and it is also used as an allusion to those who deny his guidance. Thus the emphasis carries the purpose of confirming it and nullifying their denial.

Just as the statement is used with two of the implications of its meaning, so too the emphasis with *inna* is used for two of its purposes, and both are of the kind that is attached to the use of a homonym (*mushtarak*) in both of its meanings.

The indefiniteness of "a path" (*ṣirāṭ*) is for magnification, like the indefiniteness of "bone" (*'aẓm*) in the verse of Abu Kharash:

*"No, by the father of the bird that is raising its young in the forenoon, they have indeed fallen upon a bone of Khalid."*

Also, because indefiniteness is more suitable to the context of allusion to those who did not care about his guidance.

He departed from the construct of "path" to the Name of Majesty (Allah) at the outset in order to intend a general statement, which is followed by detail, by substituting after it "the path of Allah," so that the intended meaning settles most firmly by this style, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha: 6], ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7].

The description of the Name of Majesty by the relative pronoun and its clause indicates that the reason for the straightness of the path to which the Prophet guides is that it is the path of Him who owns whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, so nothing escapes Him of what befits His servants. When He sent to them a messenger with a Book, there is no doubt that what He sent to them contains their welfare.

**[Page 156]**

﴿Is it not to Allah that all affairs will return?﴾ This is a concluding summation (tadhyil) and an ending of the surah, bringing to a close what it contained of disputation and argument with a decisive, comprehensive statement that warns those who turn away of a grievous threat and gives good news of the promise to every humble believer.

The sentence opens with the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih) to draw the attention of people.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) conveys exclusivity (ikhtisas): to Allah and not to anyone else.

*Al-masir* means return and arrival at an end. It is used here metaphorically for the manifestation of realities as they are on the Day of Resurrection, when the deception of deceivers will vanish, the tyranny of tyrants will weaken, and whoever was among the obstinate opponents will acknowledge the truth. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belongs the final outcome of affairs﴾ [Luqman: 22], and His saying: ﴿And to Him all matters are returned﴾ [Hud: 123]. *Al-umur* (affairs) means circumstances, conditions, realities, and everything existing, whether of essences or of meanings.

Al-Kumayt took up this meaning in his verse:

"Now I have come to Umayyah,
and affairs lead to their destinations."

In ending the surah with this verse there is an embellishment of good conclusion (husn al-khatam), a rhetorical device.

**[Page 157]**

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Surah al-Zukhruf**

It is named *al-Zukhruf* in both ancient and modern copies of the Qur'an. Likewise, I found it so in a fragment of an ancient Qur'an in Kufic script, of what was written at the end of the fifth century. On this basis al-Tirmidhi titled it in the Book of Tafsir in his Jami'. It is also named so in the books of tafsir.

al-Bukhari named it in the Book of Tafsir of his Sahih "Surah Ha Mim al-Zukhruf." The attachment of the word *Ha Mim* to *al-Zukhruf* is in the manner I explained in naming the surah *Ha Mim al-Mu'min*. al-Tabarsi narrated from al-Baqir that he named it so.

The reason for the name is that the word *wa-zukhrufan* (and ornament) occurs in it and does not occur in any other surah of the Qur'an, so they identified it by this word.

It is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyyah reported a consensus that it is Meccan. As for what was narrated from Qatadah and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, that the verse ﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers: Did We appoint gods besides the Most Gracious to be worshipped?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 45] was revealed at al-Masjid al-Aqsa, then if it is authentic, it does not contradict this, because what is meant by "Meccan" is what was revealed before the Hijrah.

It is numbered as the sixty-second surah in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surah Fussilat and before Surah al-Dukhan.

Its verses, according to the counters from most of the regions, are counted as eighty-nine, while the people of Syria counted them as eighty-eight.

**[Page 158]**

**Its Purposes**

The greatest of the purposes this surah contains are: the challenge by the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, because it is the sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brought, and the emphasis on this several times, and that Allah revealed it for their admonition and the repetition of their admonition, even if they turn away, as those before them turned away from their messengers.

Since what drove them to attack the Qur'an was their attachment to the worship of idols, which the Qur'an had forbidden them, it was among the most important purposes of the surah to express wonder at their state, in that they combined acknowledgment that Allah is their Creator, their Benefactor, and the Creator of all creatures, with taking gods that they worship as partners to Allah. Thus, when the foundation of their obstinacy collapsed, their falsehood became clear to them and to others.

They attributed daughters to Allah while believing that daughters are of lower rank than males. Thus they combined through this both polytheism and belittlement.

The nullification of the worship of whatever is other than Allah, despite the variance in the degrees of the worshipped in nobility, for they are all equal in lacking divinity, and in the sonship of Allah, Exalted is He.

It turned to the refutation of their proofs and excuses, and it ridiculed their fancies and nonsense.

It reminded them of the conditions of the earlier nations with their messengers, warned them of the same consequences, and cautioned them against being deceived by Allah's respite. It specifically mentioned the messages of Ibrahim, Musa, and 'Isa, peace be upon them. It singled out Ibrahim in that he made the word of monotheism remain among a group of his descendants. It threatened the polytheists and warned them of the punishment of the Hereafter after the Resurrection, the denial of which was among the nourishments of their disbelief and their turning away, because they believed that they would be safe after death.

These purposes and their branches have been arranged in a wonderful structure and a splendid style, in advancing and delaying, in the primary and the digressive (istitrad), according to the occasions demanded by eloquence, and to renew the listener's energy to accept what is presented to him. Within this there were interspersed arguments, parables, proverbs, thunderous warnings, encouragement and intimidation, something wondrous, together with the dispelling of the doubts of the obstinate through varied modes of persuasion, showing the degradation of their disbelieving creed and the crookedness of their deviant conduct.

Within all of that was incorporated (idmaj) what the proofs of divine oneness contain of the blessings upon people, along with warning and good news.

The verses of this surah follow the style of attributing speech to Allah, Exalted is He, except where evidence indicates attribution to someone else.
